title: Colombia earthquake death toll rises as frantic search for survivors continues
summary: The devastation has tested Colombia's new president and his government as it scrambles to respond to the disaster and civil society as it pushes to provide aid to the most affected communities.
story: Tons of aid from regional partners began to roll into Colombia on Wednesday, as the search for survivors in the rubble of a powerful earthquake grew more desperate after the temblor razed buildings, buckled roads and crushed cars.

The devastation has tested Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, and his government as it scrambles to respond to the disaster and civil society as it pushes to provide aid to the most affected communities.

De la Espriella said Wednesday evening that at least 265 people died in the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the country's west on Monday. The president said nearly 500 people were reported missing, though civilian-run databases put that number at more than 4,100. In total, more than 25,800 families were impacted, de la Espriella said.
"Our efforts are focused on the disappeared," he told journalists in Colombia's capital.

Teams continued to pick through the rubble in the hardest-hit cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo, as time ticked away for victims to be found, and rescued, alive. Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours crucial for retrieving survivors, though that threshold can be extended if those trapped have access to food and water.
On Wednesday afternoon, Alejandro Eder, the mayor of Cali, told reporters that rescue teams continue to find signs of people alive under the rubble and are racing to save them.
"The next 20 hours are the most critical to find and rescue people alive," he said. "Every minute is vital."

Social media videos showed a baby being rescued Monday from the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali. In the videos, a survivor can be heard telling rescuers, "I'm with a baby," as the cries of the infant are heard.

In Pereira, rescuers pulled 32-year-old Daniela Largo alive from the rubble late Tuesday, capping a complex 12-hour rescue in which crews carved a small opening in the debris to free her pinned arm and a doctor administered IV fluids to stabilize her. Wrapped in a blue blanket, the young woman was carried to an ambulance as firefighters embraced and onlookers cheered.

Craig De Meillon, a search-and-rescue volunteer from Miami, Florida, was part of the rescue effort.   "It was kind of like a football moment, when everyone is like shaking hands, like, 'Yes, yes!'" De Meillon told CBS News when asked how it felt to see the woman freed.
Another moment was marked by mourning, as a man was pulled from a building in the same city, lifeless and covered in a white blanket.
During search operations, hundreds of onlookers and volunteers must be kept quiet enough in the middle of a bustling city to listen for the faintest sign of life.

In one instance in Pereira, CBS News cameras captured volunteers forming human bucket brigades, passing piece after piece of rubble by hand for hours. And then, during one of those moments of silence, a Colombian army unit, using specialized equipment and sniffing canines, spotted signs of life, prompting hundreds of people to erupt in cheers.
Colombians fear possibility of aftershocks

Across the coffee-growing region, among the areas worst affected by the quake, authorities have converted sports arenas, schools and other public buildings into shelters for thousands of displaced Colombians. In Pereira and Cali, families have been sleeping in parks, some fearing aftershocks or the collapse of their damaged homes, others without homes to return to.
Colombia's geological service has documented 130 aftershocks since the quake.

"We have the most important things: a roof over our heads, food, water and, in my case, medical care," said Edith Penagos, 48, who was staying with her teenage son in one of the white tents set up in a Pereira park.

Rodrigo León Loya, a seismologist and geosciences professor at the University of the Andes, said the probability of an earthquake of a similar magnitude occurring in the same area is low but he would not rule out more seismic activity.

"Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," he said. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia's seismic sources."

In many areas, including the epicenter of the quake, Choco, the official response to the disaster has been complicated by the ongoing crises of deep poverty and civil warfare that have created waves of forced displacement for decades. The true impact of the earthquake in the jungled northwest remained largely unknown because cell service has been lost and many of the likely affected communities are remote, accessible only by river.

"This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.
Earthquake prompts large international aid response

Many aid organizations were already on the ground in Choco supporting a 2016 peace accord between the government and leftist rebels, and responding to violence in the region involving other armed groups that has persisted since then.
Those humanitarian workers were able to quickly pivot to disaster relief, said María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator in Colombia.
"We have a presence on the ground. Therefore, our ability to be there, present with the people, I think, has increased exponentially," Torres said in a statement Tuesday.
At the same time, aid from other countries and nonprofits abroad continued to roll in.
The U.S. State Department posted on its website that disaster response teams started to arrive in Colombia on Monday. The U.S. has also offered over $15 million in aid.

Mexico, meanwhile, said it had sent two military aircraft carrying 19.5 tons of nonperishable food and 19 members of Mexican security forces to Pereira, and it plans to send another 39 tons of aid in the coming days. A further 255 military specialists and 20 dogs are on standby to be sent to Colombia if needed.
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to send two planes loaded with 100 tons of aid.
On Wednesday, Pope Leo XIV thanked those contributing to recovery efforts and said he is praying for those killed, injured or otherwise affected by the earthquake.
"I want to express my solidarity with my Colombian sisters and brothers who have suffered the effects of the recent earthquake," he said.

On Aug. 16, artists Marc Anthony, Luis Fonsi, Chayanne, Feid, Jay Wheeler and others will perform a concert in Miami to benefit victims of both the Colombia earthquake and the two earthquakes that hit Venezuela in June and killed thousands of people.

title: Stunning photos show total solar eclipse over Europe
summary: The only total solar eclipse of 2026 crossed the Northern Hemisphere Wednesday, with a path of totality across parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain. See photos and video from the best viewing locations.
story: The only total solar eclipse of 2026 brought darkness across a swath of the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday. Crowds gathered all across Europe to see it, with northern Spain a prime viewing location in the path of totality.

First, if you've never had the opportunity to see a solar eclipse, what you are watching is the moon passing in front of the sun. It occurs somewhere on Earth about every 18 months, but in any one particular spot on the globe they could happen hundreds of years apart.
Where was the solar eclipse visible?
Many places along the path of totality are not inhabited, like northern Greenland. But western Iceland and northern Spain were also right in the path for a peak eclipse experience.
In Spain, they had not experienced a total solar eclipse since 1905.

Even though totality only reached a relatively narrow slice of the hemisphere, a partial solar eclipse was visible in a much wider area. About 230 million people live in areas getting 90% totality, according to population data from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network at Columbia University.
That includes most major cities in Europe, including Madrid, London and Paris.

Even some of North America got a chance to see a partial solar eclipse, though it won't be nearly as impressive as when the U.S. got to see a total eclipse in 2024. The best place to see it in the U.S.: Fairbanks, Alaska, reaching 37% totality.
Boston saw about 16% totality, while New York City reached 9% totality, Toronto about 8% and Philadelphia about 7%.
What time did the eclipse happen?
Since the eclipse crossed just the northern part of the globe, the path of totality was fairly short from start to finish, about an hour and 45 minutes.

The first glimpse of the total eclipse became visible in extreme northern Russia at 1 p.m. Eastern time. It reached northeast Greenland about half an hour later and western Iceland 15 minutes after that.

The eclipse crossed the northern Atlantic for 45 minutes — giving the U.K. its best view, with London reaching its max of 91% at 2:13 p.m. ET — then totality reached northern Spain at about 2:30 p.m. ET.
It was all over by 2:45 p.m. ET.
This animation from NASA shows the path of totality for the eclipse:

For those in North America seeing a partial eclipse, it reached its maximum in Toronto at 1:40 p.m. and New York City at 1:54 p.m. local time. In Fairbanks, people could see its fullest point at 8:27 a.m. local time.
Watching the eclipse in person
If you were lucky enough to be in one of the locations where the solar eclipse reached totality, plunging the day into sudden darkness, it lasted for about two minutes.
Enthusiastic viewers came out to watch across Europe, with most seeing a partial but still dramatic view.
Wearing solar eclipse glasses is essential to protect your retinas from damage when viewing an eclipse. It's only safe to take the glasses off for the brief period of totality.
During a partial eclipse, you have to keep those glasses on the whole time to avoid eye damage.
When is the next total solar eclipse in the U.S.?
If the total solar eclipse in Europe gets you excited for the next one in the U.S., you have some time to wait.
The next total solar eclipse over the U.S. will be in 2044, but that one will only be visible in three states: Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota.

The next year, there will be another opportunity visible in many states as it moves from coast to coast. The eclipse will start in Northern California and move in an arc toward the east, ending in Florida, similar to one in 2017. There will be numerous U.S. cities where eclipse watchers can view the total eclipse, including Reno, Nevada; Colorado Springs; Tulsa, Oklahoma; Little Rock, Arkansas; Jackson, Mississippi; and Orlando, Florida.
There will be another in 2052 that crosses the Southeast, including Florida, Georgia and South Carolina.
To see a total eclipse in the northeastern U.S., you'll have to wait all the way until May 1, 2079.

title: Baby rescued from earthquake rubble in Colombia as death toll rises
summary: Footage shared on social media shows a baby being rescued from the bloody arms of a man trapped underneath a destroyed building in Cali after a powerful earthquake struck Colombia.
story: Footage posted on social media shows a young baby being pulled alive from the rubble of a destroyed building in Colombia after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck the country Monday.

The video, posted by Brian Osorio Zuluaga on Monday night, shows a group of people combing through the rubble of a building in Cali, asking a survivor trapped underneath if he is alone. "I'm with a baby," the man can be heard saying in a muffled voice.

As they race to remove pieces of concrete with their bare hands, the muffled cries of a child are heard. Another video shows a man holding the crying infant, with his arms covered in blood and the lower half of his body still trapped in rubble.

The five men in the video slowly remove the baby then shout for a paramedic before erupting in a euphoric cheer. The last video posted by Zuluaga shows the workers continuing to help free the man who had been holding the baby.
"Today I understood, more than ever, that no one is really prepared to live through a situation like the one we are experiencing today," Zuluaga wrote on the post accompanying the videos.
He described being among the first people at that location and helping a group of people rescue others.
"A helping hand can make the difference between life and death," Zuluaga wrote. "In moments like this, differences don't matter, what matters is helping."
The conditions of the baby and the adult who held him were not immediately clear.
Search teams and volunteers across the country are racing against time to save anyone who may still be alive under the rubble.

Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella, who had only been in power for days when the disaster struck, said at least 181 people had died and 2,595 were injured. On Wednesday, authorities in Cali said the current death toll stands at 216.
Civilian-run databases estimate nearly 4,000 people are still unaccounted for.
The U.S. has offered over $15 million in aid and Mexico's president said she is prepared to send hundreds of search and health workers, tons of health supplies and other equipment.
On Tuesday afternoon, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said his country would send two planes loaded with 100 tons of aid in the coming days.
"Our prayers are with the families of the victims, the wounded and all the Colombian people," Bukele wrote on X.

title: At least 1 dead, 172 rescued from ferry fire near Bali, Indonesia
summary: One Indonesian teenager was killed when the vessel caught fire in rough seas.
story: Crews rescued 172 people and recovered the body of a passenger from a ferry that caught fire in rough seas Wednesday near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, authorities said.

The fire started at about 4:15 a.m. while the Putri Yasmin ferry was en route from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the neighboring island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara province, according to the search and rescue office in Mataram, the provincial capital.
The agency received an emergency report almost half an hour later and immediately deployed personnel and rescue vessels.
"Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members," said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.

Initial reports said the ferry was carrying 131 people, including 17 crew members, based on the ship's manifest, when the fire broke out in the Lombok Strait. However, hours after the incident, officials said more people were aboard than listed. It is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers on a boat or ferry to differ from the manifest. The ferry was also transporting 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles.

The National Search and Rescue Agency, or Basarnas, said rescuers evacuated 172 people from the burned vessel, including two Australian tourists, and recovered the body of a 19-year-old Indonesian girl.
Syamsurizal, head of the Lembar Port Authority, said at least two injured passengers were rushed to a nearby hospital.
"The response operation is ongoing, and authorities are continuing to account for all victims," said Syamsurizal, who like many Indonesians uses a single name.
Wednesday's incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.

title: Cartel sought to buy weapons in exchange for fentanyl, U.S. says
summary: "In exchange for the weapons, the defendants paid in the form of fentanyl and methamphetamine imported into the United States for distribution," the Justice Department said.
story: The U.S. Justice Department unsealed indictments on Tuesday against four members of one of Mexico's most powerful drug cartels accused of seeking to purchase arms and ammunition in exchange for drugs in the Czech Republic.
The four alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation cartel, known by its Spanish acronym CJNG, were arrested in the Czech Republic in June, Justice Department officials said.

Two of the defendants — Edgar Alejandro Lopez Velasco, 44, and Jose Miguel Alvarado Morales, 23 — have been extradited to the United States and made a court appearance in Tampa, Florida, on Monday, they said.
Extradition is pending for the other two accused — Noe Diaz Jimenez, 33, and Leobardo Gaxiola Lopez, 63, also known as "Bado," the officials said.
The four alleged CJNG members are charged with drug importation conspiracy, firearms trafficking and other offenses which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison.

Lopez Velasco and Diaz Jimenez negotiated the sale of weapons in the Czech Republic "to commit acts of violence against rival cartels, civilians, police forces, and military personnel in Mexico," the Justice Department said in a statement.
"These weapons included different kinds of European machineguns, rocket-propelled grenade launchers, mortar launchers, and accompanying ammunition and ordnance," it said.
"In exchange for the weapons, the defendants paid in the form of fentanyl and methamphetamine imported into the United States for distribution," it said.

The United States last week announced charges against several high-ranking members of CJNG and increased reward money for the capture of its leaders to more than $100 million, including  $25 million for information leading to the capture of the cartel's alleged leader, Juan Carlos Gonzalez, or "Pelón." According to the State Department, Gonzalez was born in Santa Ana, California, on Sept. 12, 1984.

The State Department said the charges and reward money were aimed at "crippling the organization's leadership" while President Trump has ramped up pressure on Mexico and other Latin American nations to carry out his security agenda.

CJNG is among eight Mexican cartels designated as foreign terrorist organizations. The group was dealt a blow in February when leader Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or "El Mencho," was killed by the Mexican military. The U.S. provided intelligence for the operation, which resulted in a burst in violence in the state of Jalisco.

Last month, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on 50 people and companies linked with the cartel, including González. The sanctions froze assets and blocked U.S. financial transactions with those cited.
In June, the U.S. Treasury announced a new bank alert targeting the cartel.

title: Trump secretly switched to different plane in Turkey amid Iran threat
summary: Ahead of a flight from Turkey, President Trump secretly left Air Force One and was moved to another plane with the help of a catering truck, according to a source, as the U.S. grappled with a threat from Iran.
story: Shortly before Air Force One took off from Turkey at the end of last month's NATO summit, President Trump secretly slipped away from the presidential jet and was whisked to another plane with the help of an airport catering truck, according to a U.S. official with direct knowledge of the matter.

The ruse was employed because the U.S. had learned of a threat from Iran and its allied proxies. U.S. intelligence had detected a credible plot to fire a missile at the plane Mr. Trump was on as he left the Turkish capital of Ankara, CBS News reported exclusively.
The president had expressed awareness of the risks posed by the U.S.-Iran war, calling himself Iran's "number one target" during the NATO summit.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday he switched to a different plane at the military and Secret Service's request, saying, "I guess there was a threat out there."
The Washington Post was first to report on the secret plane-switching.

Multiple Trump administration officials expressed frustration Monday night that highly classified tactics and procedures leaked into the public eye, potentially limiting future protective operations for U.S. presidents.

Hours before the move, on July 8, Mr. Trump announced he would leave Ankara in the old Air Force One rather than a newer Qatari-donated jet that he had taken to the NATO summit. The president said he was switching planes "for old time's sake," and U.S. forces stationed at a U.K. refueling stop would be able to check out the new plane, but CBS News has reported that the Secret Service advised he take the older plane for security reasons.

Video footage captured by the press showed the president walking up the stairs of the old Air Force One and disappearing into the plane, with a catering truck visible on the other side of the jet. Several minutes later, the truck pulled away and drove off to another U.S. government plane, which The Post reported was an Air Force C-32A.

Mr. Trump then flew from Ankara to a refueling stop in the United Kingdom on the separate plane while members of the press and the president's staff traveled the same route on Air Force One — and believed they were on board the same aircraft as the president.

While in Ankara, members of the press were told to keep the window shades in Air Force One's press cabin closed, reporters said at the time. Asked why the shades needed to be closed, Mr. Trump later told reporters they were "probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags that we have to deal with."

In the United Kingdom, Mr. Trump switched to the newer Air Force One, which was donated by the government of Qatar last year and retrofitted by the U.S. Air Force to serve as the new presidential plane. Mr. Trump spoke to members of the press while they flew across the Atlantic toward Washington, D.C.
The Trump administration has never publicly disclosed that the press and some members of the president's staff were flying on a decoy plane.

Asked Tuesday about his ride in a catering truck, the president told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes the decision was made by the military and Secret Service, who "wanted me to go in a different flight."
He said it was in response to a threat, which he called unsurprising, noting that he gets "a lot of threats."
"Any consequential president has a lot of threats," Mr. Trump told reporters.

Reporters asked Mr. Trump on Tuesday why it was too dangerous for him to fly on Air Force One, but not staff or members of the press. He said: "I think, actually, the plane that I flew on was at greater risk."

Last month, the new Air Force One — which debuted in June — was sent off to be "maxed out" with additional upgrades, the president told reporters, after questions arose about the newer plane's security features.

Asked Monday about the decision to secretly switch planes in Turkey, White House communications director Steven Cheung didn't respond directly to the question, saying in a statement: "The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff. As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats."
The Air Force has also called the new presidential plane "safe, secure and equipped with the most advanced technologies necessary to meet the requirements of the presidential mission."

title: Rescuers race to find Colombia earthquake survivors as death toll rises
summary: Over 1,100 homes were destroyed when Colombia was struck by its strongest earthquake on record.
story: Rescue workers and volunteers rushed to clear rubble as they searched for survivors in Colombia on Tuesday after the country was struck by its strongest earthquake on record.
At least 181 people died and 1,595 were injured in the earthquake, according to the country's president, Abelardo de la Espriella.

De la Espriella said 195 people were reported missing. Civilian-run databases suggest the number of missing could be as high as 3,900. Many families posted information about loved ones online, hoping for information about their fate.
Over 1,100 homes across the country were destroyed, and over 8,300 damaged, de la Espriella said. Rescue workers and volunteers were seen clearing rubble by hand in some places.
The 7.4 magnitude quake struck cities across Colombia's western region shortly after 7:30 a.m. local time Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets.
Electricity was all but gone in the hardest-hit city of Pereira, with a population of over half a million.
Many residents spent the night sleeping on the street, fearing more deadly aftershocks, or because their homes had sustained damage.
"Since yesterday we've been wondering what will become of our lives," 38-year-old housewife Gloria Giraldo, whose neighborhood had tumbled around her, told French news agency AFP.
The city was plunged into darkness Monday evening as volunteers combed through the remains of collapsed buildings searching for survivors.
Throughout the night, residents navigated blacked-out streets with torches.
Volunteers searched the ruins of a six-story building of shops and offices where two girls were believed to be trapped.
"It's so sad to see the whole city like this, knowing that there may still be people alive under there," said Juana Marin, 25, who joined dozens of volunteers clearing rubble by hand.
"We're without power. This seems honestly like a zombie city," resident Juan David Gaitan said.
At the airport in Pereira, videos showed pieces of ceiling falling down on travelers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.
De la Espriella, who had been on the job for only three days, declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort.
"Someone whistled back"
In Cali, volunteers quickly went to work with picks, basic tools and their own hands to try to find survivors.
Rescuers formed human chains to remove bricks and masonry, stopping every few minutes to listen for signs of life from those trapped below.
Andres Felipe Mejia was among those who joined a makeshift crew.
"One of the rescuers asked anyone trapped to whistle, and someone whistled back," he said near a pancaked building.
"They pulled out a man and a baby, but the wife is still in there," he said.
Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, according to local authorities.
"It felt like the end of the world — cars and motorcycles driving the wrong way, everyone searching for their loved ones," said volunteer rescue worker Nelson Moreno.

Dana Carolina Zamora posted an image of her missing 60-year-old uncle, Miguel Ángel Zamora, cradling his dog. The farmer was living in a rural area of El Cairo, not far from the quake's epicenter in San Jose Del Palmar.
"We are afraid. We hope that is not the case, that he is all right and that it is only a communication failure. But we haven't heard anything from him," Zamora said.
De la Espriella announced Monday night that he had mobilized "the entire military and police apparatus" to respond to the temblor.
World responds to Colombia earthquake
The Vatican said Tuesday that Pope Leo XIV is "deeply saddened" by the earthquake.

"The Holy Father, deeply saddened to learn the painful news of the earthquake that has seriously affected several areas of Colombia ... offers prayers for the eternal rest of the deceased and raises his prayers to the Lord for the prompt recovery of those affected by this tragedy," the Vatican's secretary of state, Pietro Parolin, wrote in a note to the archbishop of Cartagena, Francisco Javier Munera Correa.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post on Monday that the Trump administration was closely monitoring the earthquake response and "stands ready to support the people of Colombia." The U.S. announced $15.5 million in emergency relief.
South Florida organizations are among U.S.-based humanitarian groups mobilizing to send aid to Colombia.

"There's a lot of damage, and we are waiting for information as to what the needs are. The first is rescue and recovery," Fabio Andrade, a Weston city commissioner and a Colombian American, told CBS News Miami.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had mobilized Copernicus, a satellite service, to help with rescue operations.
Israel, Mexico, Ecuador and France also offered assistance.

title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak viewing on Wednesday night
summary: The Perseid meteor shower is the best viewing all year, according to NASA.
story: The Perseid meteor shower is set to provide a late-summer show in the skies over the United States.
The meteor shower, which NASA calls the best of the year, is set to peak on Aug. 12 and 13.

"With swift and bright meteors, Perseids frequently leave long 'wakes' of light and color behind them as they streak through Earth's atmosphere," according to NASA. "The Perseids are one of the most plentiful showers with about 50 to 100 meteors seen per hour."

For those who are trying to see the meteor shower on Wednesday night, the best time for viewing in the Northern Hemisphere is during the predawn hours on Aug. 13, but if you don't want to get up very early, you can still see them as early as 10 p.m. the night before.

Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.

The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and isn't scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.
The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.
"We don't have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors," said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.
The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids' peak, making viewing conditions even better.

"The moon is beautiful, but it's such a diva," said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. "New moon means we don't have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result."
To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights. Venkatesan plans to drive to the Sierra Nevada.
The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.

Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by — even in your peripheral vision — and to avoid looking at your phone.
"There's just something magical about it," Vanderbosch said.

title: Matthew McConaughey's piece of relationship advice that keeps his marriage to Camila Alves strong
summary: Matthew McConaughey reveals the marriage advice that has kept him and Camila Alves connected through nearly two decades together as a couple.
story: The Academy Award-winning actor tells Fox News Digital the biggest lesson that he's learned in his 14-year marriage to Camila Alves.
Matthew McConaughey is sharing the key to making his marriage work.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 56-year-old actor spoke about his new film, "The Rivals Of Amziah King," which arrives in theaters on Aug. 14, and the biggest lesson he learned that has contributed to his decades-long marriage.

"You got times where one seems to be affirming and sprinting ahead," he said. "And you got times when somebody else may be a little more insecure or a little more unstable on their feet about their choices and what they're doing."
He explained that when in a relationship, it is important to "try not to get too much of a gap between those two" stages.
Matthew McConaughey shared the biggest lesson he has learned that has helped his marriage. (David Parry/PA Images via Getty Images)

"Is there a way to go, 'I'll slow down so you can catch up, or 'You slow down so I can catch up a little bit?'" he added. "Not asking you to not be in the lead because I want you to be in the lead because when the fire's hot, keep it burning. Go, go, go, go, go. But just keep me in arm's length over here. Keep me in arms length."

McConaughey and Camila Alves got married in June 2012, six years after they first met in a nightclub in West Hollywood in 2006.
Over the course of their relationship, the couple has welcomed three kids together; sons Levi, 18, and Livingston, 13, and daughter Vida, 16.

In his new film, also starring Kurt Russell and Cole Sprouse, the "Dallas Buyers Club" star plays Amziah King, a musician, beekeeper and pillar in his community in Oklahoma whose life is turned upside down when his former foster daughter returns as he is also dealing with threats to his honey business.

While the actor grew up in Texas rather than Southeast Oklahoma, he was able to relate to his character in the movie, as "it's got a lot of the same characters in it" as he saw growing up.

"There's a lot of people in a lot of places all across the United States where music is how you communicate, it's how you survive, it's how you keep belief alive, it's how they keep hope alive, because if you look at logic, and you look at the facts every single day, all we got to do is look at the news," he said.

"Oh, that doesn't do a lot for keeping your belief and hope alive. If anything, it puts a damper on it," he added. "So music and belief are like, 'Hey, we're gonna play through the struggle. We're going to sing through it. We're gonna dance through it, we're going to say that any time is a good time to put you in the spotlight and say, you're on, go.'"
McConaughey told Fox News Digital he had the opportunity to play the instruments himself and sing in the film, noting, "singing and playing at the same time is not as easy as I thought."

The actor shares that "musicality" is important to him in all his roles, saying, "There is a rhythm for every character," and while he always has "a set of djembes in my trailer," he found that when singing and playing at the same time, "my hands couldn't keep up with my mouth."
"It's a very musical character and I actually got to play and sing in this and that was a hell of a lot of fun," he said. "And I had a lot of help from the real musicians that were there."

Last week, McConaughey and Alves were photographed meeting Pope Leo XIV at St. Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City.
The actor and his model wife grinned during the moment, which took place during the pope’s weekly general audience.
The actor has been in Italy filming his new Netflix movie "Positano." McConaughey stars in the movie alongside Zoe Saldaña.
The Texas-born movie star has been open about his faith over the years, and has even published a book called "Poems & Prayers" in 2025.
McConaughey told Fox News Digital he felt "a little nicely anxious" about meeting the Pope.

"Yeah, as the man in the world that represents most cleanly the moral aperture and judgment. What an awesome position," he added. "And, you know, the Pope has had different amounts of power through the history of time in politics. There were paintings there where… actually the kings in the past came to kiss the Pope's feet for the blessing, you know what I mean?"

The movie star noted that the Pope is still "the moral compass," which he says is "really important, especially... as politics has gained so much power and popularity and has been sort of our fulcrum for which we look at, for almost where our values come from. Politics is part of the values of whether you want to call it religious or not."

"He noted that while there's a separation between church and state, there's still "values of politics" that "need to come down through certain religious aspects, I believe. And they're even built on those in some way. Yeah, I understand law is separate from belief or values, so to speak, but they're always going to be intrinsically aligned and should be in some way," McConaughey said.

"And it's something we're going through now. We're trying to figure out the standards of AI, you know, what are the morals and ethics and the values that we need to set as a standard within AI –  that's becoming this new power and platform and tool in our lives," he said.
When asked what he talked to the Pope about, he said, "That's between he and I."

title: Matthew McConaughey gives update on rumored 'Yellowstone' spin-off series, years after reports first surfaced
summary: Matthew McConaughy says his conversations with Taylor Sheridan about a "Yellowstone" spin-off are ongoing but confirms nothing is officially real yet.
story: Matthew McConaughey told Fox News Digital that he likes to have a good time with his wife.
Matthew McConaughey is clearing the air about his rumored "Yellowstone" spin-off.

During a recent appearance on The Playlist’s "Discourse" podcast, the 56-year-old actor discussed the status of the rumored "Yellowstone" spin-off he was meant to star in, giving fans some hope that they might still see him in that universe.

"No, I mean, it’s not any more of a thing than it was or probably any less of a thing than it was that did hit the headlines there for a while," McConaughey said. "Taylor and I have spoken and have continued to have conversations about what [it could be] and if that would be whatever. But nothing’s real yet."

Rumors of a potential collaboration between McConaughey and Taylor Sheridan first sparked in 2023, when Sheridan was still trying to figure out the end of "Yellowstone" and whether its star, Kevin Costner, would return.
McConaughey gave his fans an update on his rumored collaboration with Taylor Sheridan. (PG/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)
LIONESS STAR MICHAEL KELLY CALLS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'ONE OF THE GREATEST STORYTELLERS' IN ENTERTAINMENT
During the gap between the first half of the show's final season and the second, rumors began swirling that McConaughey and Sheridan were in talks for a potential spin-off of the show.
Sheridan told The Hollywood Reporter in June 2023 that McConaughey "seems like a natural fit."

"We had a few conversations over the years and spitballed a few ideas," Sheridan said. "Then he started watching 'Yellowstone' and responded to it. He was like, ‘I want to do that.’ And by ‘that’ he meant diving into a raw world clashing up against the modern world. And then I said, ‘Buddy, that we can do.’"
"Yellowstone" aired its series finale in December 2024 without Costner, Sheridan giving his character an off-screen death.
Costner did not return to film the second half of Season 5 of "Yellowstone." (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Airbnb)

It was announced in August 2024 that two of the show's stars, Cole Hauser and Kelly Reilly, who played Beth Dutton and Rip Wheeler, would star in their own spin-off series, "Dutton Ranch," which saw the two characters leave Montana to start fresh in Texas.
While this show is an extension of the "Yellowstone" universe, Sheridan stepped away from the writers' room during the first season, although he is still an executive producer.

"There were challenges, you know?" Hauser told Film Inside NYC in July. "Not having Taylor [Sheridan] there for us to really kind of be able to work with these new writers, these new directors, these people ... everything had changed."

Kelly Reilly as Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser as Rip Wheeler in "Dutton Ranch." (Lo Smith/Paramount+)

In the end, Hauser said he is "proud of what we accomplished" on the show, crediting everyone on set for having to "figure out on our feet how to really perform and tell a story," noting, "I look forward to doing it again."

title: Nicole Kidman admits she was ‘very fearful and deeply vulnerable’ after Keith Urban divorce
summary: Nicole Kidman says her divorce from Keith Urban left her future "completely unknown," despite surviving her split from Tom Cruise decades earlier.
story: Nicole Kidman, nominated for her leading role in "Babygirl," greeted fans and photographers as she walked the carpet at the Golden Globes.
Nicole Kidman has been through one highly scrutinized Hollywood divorce before — but she says splitting from Keith Urban hasn't made heartbreak any easier.
"It's all new," the actress said in a cover interview with British Vogue. "Every time!"

Just months after her 19-year marriage to Keith Urban officially ended, the Oscar-winning actress is opening up about the emotional journey of starting over — admitting there was a point when she was "very fearful and deeply vulnerable" but ultimately decided she had to move forward.
NICOLE KIDMAN FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM KEITH URBAN CITING 'MARITAL DIFFICULTIES'
Nicole Kidman tells British Vogue she was "very fearful and deeply vulnerable" after her divorce from Keith Urban. (Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for The Mark Hotel)
"Free falling?" she asked herself, as she searched for the right words to describe this chapter of her life. "Jumping off?"
Then came the question that seemed to capture her life at the moment.
"Like, where am I going? And what’s next?"

Kidman, 59, filed for divorce from Urban, 58, last September in Nashville after nearly two decades of marriage. Their divorce was finalized in January, with irreconcilable differences cited and Kidman named the primary residential parent of their two daughters.
The former couple agreed to make major decisions involving the girls jointly. Neither party sought spousal support, and both waived their right to appear at the divorce hearing.
NICOLE KIDMAN PLANS ON BECOMING A DEATH DOULA AS SHE ADMITS IT 'MAY SOUND A LITTLE WEIRD'
Nicole Kidman says her divorce from Keith Urban hasn't made heartbreak easier the second time around. (James Devaney)
While Kidman didn't get into the details of what led to the split, she revealed what it felt like to be on the other side of a life she thought she understood.
"I’ve approached my whole life like that," she said of her "feelings first" philosophy.

"That’s just who I am. I don’t overthink things and I’m probably not that analytical. I’m far more feeling-centred and I lead with my heart. I just go, ‘OK, what do I feel here? I’ll give it a go.’ It throws people, because I think they think I’ll be far more measured and I’m not."
Kidman has never been one to let her head overrule her heart, she suggested in her interview.

"I can still approach things intellectually," she continued with a smile, "but my desire is not to be ruled by my head. I’ve always wanted to live a well-examined life, so what does that entail? Trying things, making mistakes, failing, getting back up, moving on, embracing love, staying open, keeping the heart open and the possibilities."
Nicole Kidman and Keith Urban split in 2025. (Stefanie Keenan / Getty)

The "Practical Magic" star added, "But at the same time, I’m like, ‘OK, I didn’t expect this. I had a different view of what my life was going to be, but this is what it is now.’ You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not. You have to adjust. You adapt. The future, it’s completely unknown to me right now."
She paused and added, "Strange."

When asked whether the uncertainty was frightening, Kidman replied, "There was a point where I was very fearful and deeply vulnerable," adding, "which is exposing. And then at the same time [I'm] going, 'Well, I can either really not confront it and just curl up, or I can just go forward with an enormous amount of hope.'"
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I know my character. I know my talent. I know who I am. If I make a mistake and it doesn’t connect, or something goes wrong in my life where it’s humiliating, it’s OK. Other people have had that and that’s OK. Take the onus off it."
But if Kidman thought her first very public divorce had prepared her for the second, she quickly learned otherwise.

The actress was famously married to Tom Cruise for more than a decade after meeting him on the set of "Days of Thunder." They married in 1990 and adopted two children, Isabella and Connor, before divorcing in 2001.
Nicole Kidman opens up about life after Keith Urban, reflecting on her Tom Cruise marriage at 22. (Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic/Getty Images)

Her marriage to Cruise began when Kidman was barely into adulthood. She has previously described being swept up in the romance and largely ignoring warnings that becoming the wife of one of Hollywood's biggest stars could affect her own career.
"Yeah, I got married so young," Kidman said. "Suddenly, I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband, but it just seemed completely natural."
"We just fell madly in love and it was that simple," Kidman recalled.
When people warned her that marrying Cruise could overshadow her career, she didn't hesitate.
"I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’"
She remembered the people who later said, "‘See, we told you.’"
Her response was just as defiant.
"I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course, I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’"
"But you have to remember literally, because of who I married at such a young age, I was thrust into it since I was 22."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
After Cruise, she found love with Urban, the New Zealand-born singer-songwriter and guitarist. They married in 2006 and welcomed two daughters, Sunday Rose and Faith Margaret.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Dan Aykroyd details 'medieval times' reality of California while praising life in Canada
summary: Dan Aykroyd described driving through Santa Monica's beauty alongside 60,000 homeless people, saying we are living in "frankly medieval times."
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Dan Aykroyd praised his Canadian roots while pondering world atrocities in a recently unearthed podcast.

Aykroyd, 74, admitted in a resurfaced clip from "The Adam Carolla Show" that he "loved going around the world," boasting that his Crystal Head Vodka was "made in Canada" where he was born – a place he believed to have a stark contrast to life in California.

"It's great to be living in the western world," he said before singing an old blues song with lyrics including, "Oh, this world is in an uproar, things all going wrong. The way the reds is cutting up, we ain't going to be here long."
DAN AYKROYD SURVIVED 50-FOOT FALL, CREDITS 'DIVINE INTERVENTION' FOR SAVING HIS LIFE
Dan Aykroyd boasted about life in Canada during a resurfaced appearance on "The Adam Carolla Show." (Kevin Winter)
The "Ghostbusters" actor recalled a visit with a friend from Israel who stayed on his farm and once asked, "Dan, what is it like to live in a land where there's no war?"

"Here I am driving through the bucolic countryside ... and we're in Canada," he said. "We're driving to the drugstore to get an ice cream, and he tells me, 'What it is like to live in a country without war?' I thought to myself, ‘Boy, do I take things for granted, you know, around this place.’"

After Carolla reminisced on failed promises for the future, Aykroyd insisted there were "pockets of the world that are at peace and that there is harmony, you know, Santa Monica, California – harmony, peace, joy by the sea."
"It's beautiful there, beautiful houses and beautiful shops and lovely wide boulevards and 60,000 homeless," he said. "So the underside and the overside will always, always be there."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Aykroyd is known for his roles in comedies like "Ghostbusters." (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

"We're living in frankly medieval times. You go, I drive very carefully in the car. I don't drive prison hours at night, have a gated place to live ... lock up at night. Bring my family close, whereas really I would like to take my family and let them run in the park at 1 in the morning."

He added, "But, no. We have to be so guarded now."

Carolla added, "Well, what we're living in, especially in California, is you have Jay-Z and Beyoncé buy a $200 million house in Malibu, but in order to get there, you have to drive through a homeless encampment."
"They got a deal, by the way," Aykroyd joked. "It's worth $700."
John Bellushi and Dan Aykroyd founded the famous Blues Brothers duo in the late '70s on "Saturday Night Live." (Getty Images)
"That's where we're at, which is ultra rich and then people just expiring on the streets in squalor," Carolla noted before the actor jumped back in.

"Well, thankfully, knowing people like that, they're going to drive through their driveway, see that, and immediately start to act to try to alleviate and help in some way, because that's the kind of people they are," Aykroyd said.

title: 'Deadpool' star Rob Delaney reveals how losing 2-year-old son changed his approach to fame
summary: Rob Delaney reveals how losing his son Henry to a brain tumor at age 2 reshaped his entire approach to Hollywood and his career priorities.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

The death of Rob Delaney's son, Henry, fundamentally changed the way he approaches Hollywood, prompting the "Deadpool" star to limit his workload and spend as much time as possible at home with his children.
Delaney lost his two-and-a-half-year-old son in 2018 after battling a brain tumor. Henry had been diagnosed with cancer shortly after his 1st birthday.

"I had a son, his name was Henry, and he died, and he's dead," he said during an appearance on Ted Danson's podcast, "Where Everybody Knows Your Name." "You know, does he live on inside of me and in the smile of my wife and in the gaze of my other boys who are alive and vibrant? Yes, he does. But he died, and I don't like to sugarcoat that, you know. And that affected how I work now."
RYAN GOSLING'S FAMILY-FIRST PHILOSOPHY RESHAPED HIS HOLLYWOOD CAREER: EXPERTS
Rob Delaney said the death of his son Henry in 2018 reshaped the way he approaches his Hollywood career. (Imeh Akpanudosen/Getty Images)
Rather than building a production empire or juggling numerous projects like some peers, he chose to prioritize being physically present with his family.

"...they've got their fingers in other pies," he said. "I don't do that. I just do one, maybe two things at a time to the best of my abilities, and then I just spend the rest of the time at home, you know, smelling my kids and having as many of them sit on me at one time as possible, you know."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
The "Deadpool" star said he limits himself to one or two projects at a time to prioritize time with his family. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)
For Delaney, that shift in priorities is inseparable from the grief he continues to carry.

"That's a big part of me is metabolizing that the pain of the loss of Henry and then trying to be smart enough to let that inform how I do my career, because I think it would be a real shame if that happened and I didn't change how I work, you know," he explained. "That would be folly."

Delaney spent years working in stand-up before gaining a major following on Twitter, where his offbeat comedy helped turn him into one of the platform’s earliest breakout comedians. In 2012, he was named "Funniest Person on Twitter" at Comedy Central’s Comedy Awards.
Rob Delaney said the grief of losing Henry continues to inform how he balances work and fatherhood. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images)

title: Matthew McConaughey prompts priceless reaction from Ella Langley after Oscar winner covers ‘Choosin’ Texas’

"I love that song ‘Choosin’ Texas’ by Ella Langley," Fallon read. "And I’m really excited to see Matthew McConaughey’s new movie ‘The Rivals of Amziah King,’ where he performs in a bluegrass band. If there was only a way to combine those things, that would be a dream come true."

ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100
The country anthem recently scored its 17th nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the longest-running non-holiday No. 1 by a solo female artist in the chart's history.
The milestone pushed Langley past Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" and Mariah Carey's "We Belong Together," which each spent 14 weeks at the top of the chart.

title: ‘X-Men’ star Tyler Mane says wife ‘saved my life’ after seemingly harmless lump led to breast cancer diagnosis
summary: Tyler Mane credits his wife Renae with saving his life after she insisted he get a breast lump checked that turned out to be Stage 1 cancer. They're now co-hosting a new podcast, "Mane AF."
story: The "X-Men" and "Halloween" actor discusses his rare male breast cancer diagnosis and urges men to advocate for their health and get unusual lumps checked. He is launching a new podcast, "Mane AF."
Tyler Mane, who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer, believes his wife may have saved his life.

The actor is teaming up with his wife, Renae, for a candid new podcast, "Mane AF," tackling the realities of "midlife, marriage and mayhem." The couple will also open up about one of their most personal challenges yet: navigating his diagnosis of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC).

Mane made his feature-film debut as Sabretooth in 2000's "X-Men" and later reprised the role as Wolverine's nemesis in 2024's "Deadpool & Wolverine." He also starred as Michael Myers in 2007's "Halloween" and 2009's "Halloween II," and appeared as Ajax in 2004's "Troy."
FORMER WRESTLER, ACTOR REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS: 'ONE IN 750 MEN'
Tyler Mane, who was diagnosed with breast cancer, is co-hosting a new podcast with his wife Renae titled "Mane AF," which is launching Aug. 27, 2026. (Courtesy of Jenny Brezinski)

"She just kept insisting," the former wrestler told Fox News Digital about seeing a doctor. "I kept talking about it, 'I have this lump here still, and it's hard.' And she was very insistent because women are trained from a certain age that if they feel something in their breast area, go get it checked out."
"I have to thank her," he said. "She saved my life by saying, 'Get in there and get tested.'"
Tyler Mane as Sabretooth in "X-Men," circa 2000. (Maximum Films)

When the 59-year-old first noticed a lump in his breast area, he assumed it was a lipoma — a soft, fatty growth he'd had removed before. But this lump felt different. Mane initially brushed it off, but Renae kept urging him, "Go in and get checked." Eventually, he listened.
WATCH: TYLER MANE SAYS WIFE ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS

"To be honest, even my doctor said, 'Oh, it's probably nothing. It's probably just a lipoma,'" Mane recalled. "And then, when I went in for the [surgery], he said, 'You probably want to get that removed, but it's probably nothing.' It's just dismissed so much that you have to be an advocate for your own body. And I'm just so thankful that she was an advocate for my body. Otherwise, it could have been a whole different story."
Mane said a 28-millimeter tumor was removed.
Known for his roles in "X-Men" and "Halloween," Tyler Mane shared the news publicly to help raise awareness about a condition that is frequently overlooked in men. (Bobby Bank/Getty Images)

"It was removed, I think, on a Thursday," Mane said. "I went on a trip and thought nothing of it. I came back, got up and started working at 6am, and then I got the news: invasive ductal carcinoma. I went and woke my wife up. She's like, 'This is not good.' She was half-asleep but woke up very quickly. And that's when our journey began."
Tyler Mane is undergoing chemotherapy. (Courtesy of Tyler Mane)

Because breast cancer is predominantly associated with women, many men are unaware that they are also at risk. The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2026, about 2,670 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer and about 530 will die from the disease.
According to the American Cancer Society, the average lifetime risk of breast cancer for men is about 1 in 755.
Tyler Mane attends the "Playing With Fire" New York premiere at AMC Lincoln Square Theater on Oct. 26, 2019, in New York City. (John Lamparski/FilmMagic)

The most common symptom of male breast cancer is a firm, usually painless lump under or near the nipple, according to experts. Other signs can include skin dimpling, nipple retraction and nipple discharge. Mane said the lump was the only symptom he experienced before his diagnosis.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Tyler Mane credited his wife Renae for urging him to seek testing. (Stephen Shugerman/Getty Images)

Male breast cancer is rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of breast cancers in the U.S. Screening mammograms are not usually recommended for men, even those at increased risk, according to the National Cancer Institute.

"This is a cancer that anyone can get," Mane said. "If you feel something different in your chest than the norm, you have to go get it checked out and tested. You have to insist on getting tested and checked. You have to be the best advocate for yourself."
Tyler Mane appears at a meet and greet in Dortmund, Germany, on Nov. 3, 2018. (Alamy Live News)

"For sure, I wanted to keep my diagnosis private at the beginning because I felt a bit ashamed," Mane admitted. "I was like, 'How can I have breast cancer?' But then I quickly turned to, 'No, I got to talk about this because this is a very serious issue that men don't usually deal with.'"

Initially, Tyler Mane struggled with shame after his diagnosis. Today, he’s turning that experience into advocacy — speaking out to break the stigma and raise awareness for other men. (Courtesy of Tyler Mane)

While male breast cancer can occur at any age, the risk increases with age, according to the American Cancer Society. Treatment usually starts with surgery, while other common treatments include chemotherapy, hormone therapy and radiation therapy, according to Mayo Clinic. Treatment depends on factors including the cancer's stage and the patient's overall health.

Actor Tyler Mane and his wife arrive for Universal Studios Hollywood's Halloween Horror Nights and Eye Gore Awards Kick Off Party on Sept. 21, 2012, in Universal City, California. (Albert L. Ortega/Getty Images)

"I was a Stage 1, so we got it early," Mane said. "Now we're into the chemotherapy ... to make sure that it's completely out of my system ... and then after the chemotherapy, I have some radiation to make sure we hit that area specifically."
For Mane, some days are easier than others.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Actor Tyler Mane attends the premiere of the movie "X-Men" at Ellis Island. (NY Daily News via Getty Images)

"Chemotherapy is hard on your system," he said. "Unless you've gone through it, you can't even imagine what it does to your body, and it's a repetitive cycle. It's not like you get an injury, and you rehabilitate it, or like when I had my hips replaced, and it's one and done. With chemotherapy, it's ongoing. You have your chemo treatment, where they put all of the chemicals into you."

"You feel like c--- for about the first week, and then you have a couple of weeks where you're like, 'I'm just getting back to normal now,'" he continued. "And then you have to go in, sit in that chair again and have that pumped into your body again to kill off the cancer cells. It's about the hardest thing to psych yourself up for."
Writer-director Rob Zombie and actor Tyler Mane pose at the after-party for the premiere of MGM's "Halloween" at the Geisha House on Aug. 23, 2007, in Los Angeles. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

"Right now, I want to take a nap, but I've got the metal mouth. And that's one thing: every round I've had something different thrown at me. I couldn't lift my shoulder over my head. One time I broke out in hives. But it's just your body trying to kick it out and get ready for the next round."
Tyler Mane attends the "Deadpool & Wolverine" New York premiere on July 22, 2024, in New York City. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)
Known for playing some of Hollywood's most intimidating characters, Mane said he's bringing that same fighting spirit to his cancer treatment, with Renae by his side every step of the way.

"I knew I had it in me," he said with a smile. "You have to have a positive attitude, and I've stayed positive no matter what. You have to stay positive. As soon as you let yourself get down, then it's a downhill slide from there. And I need to stick around for my wife and my family. It's time to step up and do what I have to do."
Tyler Mane told Fox News Digital that his cancer was caught at Stage 1. (Taylor Hill/WireImage)

As Mane continues to talk publicly about his diagnosis, he hopes to use the podcast to raise awareness about breast cancer in men, including by bringing his oncologist on as a guest. But he wants other men to take another lesson from his experience to heart: listen to your wife. She just might save your life.

Actress Renae Geerlings-Mane and actor Tyler Mane arrive at the premiere of Dimension Films' "Halloween II" at Grauman's Chinese Theater in Hollywood, on Aug. 24, 2009. (Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images)
"All you guys out there, listen to your wives when they tell you to get checked," he said.

title: John Rich warns Nashville's famed Broadway could go dark as businesses face tax ‘death nail’
summary: John Rich warns Nashville's Lower Broadway honky-tonks face closure as property tax bills soar, threatening the live music culture that defines Music City.
story: Country music star John Rich told Fox News Digital that soaring property appraisals and higher taxes could force longtime businesses on Nashville’s famed Broadway to "turn out the lights."

Country star John Rich is warning that Nashville’s Lower Broadway, the iconic entertainment district famous for its glowing neon signs, packed honky-tonks and live country music, could soon begin going dark.

In a video that Rich shared on Facebook last week, the 52-year-old Big & Rich member sounded the alarm, declaring that "the lights are going out on Broadway" as Nashville businesses struggle under mounting property tax bills.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Rich, who owns Redneck Riviera Bar & BBQ on Lower Broadway, argued that sharply higher property assessments along with increased taxes have pushed longtime Broadway establishments to a breaking point, which he said threatened not only the businesses themselves but the live music culture that earned Nashville its "Music City" nickname.

"It was a one-two punch," Rich said. "So the first thing he did was they reappraised everybody's property in the county, in the city, and as soon as they got that done, which was an extremely inflated appraisal rate, then they come in and raise the taxes aggressively on top of these extremely inflated appraisals."
COUNTRY STAR JOHN RICH JOINS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ADVOCATING FOR LANDOWNERS' RIGHTS
John Rich of Big & Rich warned that Nashville's famed Broadway could go dark due to soaring property assessments along with increased taxes. (Getty Images)

"And with those two things, what you've done is you've now put a death nail in a vast majority of the businesses," he continued. "It's only a matter of time before you're going to see large percentages of the businesses downtown turning out the lights."
"We've already had three in the past two weeks have to shut down. I'm talking major, major, major places that have been there for decades," Rich added.

Though Rich blamed Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell for the overall tax burden, the city's regularly scheduled four-year reappraisal, which took place in 2025, was conducted by the independently elected Davidson County assessor of property.
WATCH: JOHN RICH WARNS TAX ‘ONE-TWO PUNCH’ THREATENS BROADWAY

The 2025 reappraisal resulted in a 45% median increase in property values countywide. Under Tennessee law, the reappraisal itself is revenue-neutral, meaning the tax rate is adjusted so higher property values don't automatically generate additional revenue for local government.

However, O’Connell and the Metro Council subsequently set the Urban Services District tax rate at $2.814 per $100 of assessed value, 26% above the revenue-neutral certified rate, according to the assessor’s office.

The increases were particularly steep on Lower Broadway, where a 400% increase in real estate values was common, according to a report by Axios Nashville. The outlet also reported that many honky-tonk operators rent their buildings and are responsible for the property taxes under their leases, leaving them to shoulder rising tax bills without benefiting from the increased equity in the properties.
Rich warned that the establishments might have to charge "$50 a beer." (Jason Kempin)
Rich pointed to several Lower Broadway establishments while describing what he sees as a broader threat to businesses in the district.

He cited Nashville Underground, which permanently closed in May after roughly eight years in business, and Acme Feed & Seed, whose owner, Tom Morales, has warned it could close amid a steep increase in its property tax bill. Rich also said he has heard Hard Rock Cafe Nashville, a Broadway fixture since 1994, is considering closing, though Fox News Digital has not independently confirmed that claim.

Acme Feed & Seed, in particular, has emerged as a flashpoint in the debate over the rising tax burden. In February, Morales said the popular four-story restaurant, bar and live music venue's annual property tax bill had jumped from $129,000 to nearly $600,000.

Morales told Nashville's NewsChannel 5 that Acme Feed & Seed ended 2025 about $500,000 "in the red," while he and his daughter Lauren Morales later told the Nashville Scene that closure was "imminent" if they could not find a solution to the tax increase.
O’Connell addressed Morales' warnings at the time during an interview with Nashville's Fox 17.
"It’s not up to me whether he keeps that business open," O’Connell told the outlet. "The market evolves. New businesses start even as beloved old businesses close."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Rich expressed his concerns regarding the Super Bowl. (Jason Kempin)

The comments drew criticism, including from Metro Councilmember Jacob Kupin, who told Fox 17 he was "appalled" by the mayor's response. O’Connell’s office later accused the station of selectively editing and misrepresenting his remarks and released a longer version of the exchange.

In the fuller answer, O’Connell said the state comptroller had reviewed downtown valuations and determined they reflected market value. He called Acme's location "an incredibly valuable piece of property" and said it was up to the owner to determine how to capture that value.
Rich argued that Acme’s concerns are far from isolated, pointing to a recent meeting he attended with other Lower Broadway business owners.

"Then we had this meeting with all the business owners down there," Rich told Fox News Digital. "And in that meeting, all the ownership of Broadway was represented down there, and every single person said it's only a matter of time before we literally have to just close the doors because we're running at a deficit."
"We'd have to charge $50 a beer, which you can't do that," he continued. "I mean, there is no business model that exists that allows the businesses down there to stay open."
WATCH: JOHN RICH SAYS NASHVILLE BARS WOULD NEED TO CHARGE ‘$50 A BEER' TO SURVIVE
Rich emphasized that the bar and restaurant operators sounding the alarm include some of the most experienced in the city.
"You're not talking about a bunch of amateurs here," he said. "You're looking at the best of the best, and they can't survive it."
For Rich, however, the bigger concern is what the financial pressure could ultimately mean for Nashville’s identity.
"The bigger story to me is live music in Nashville. I mean, it's called Music City," he said.
Rich described the unique concentration of live music along Broadway, where honky-tonks line both sides of the street and bands perform throughout the day and into the early morning hours.

"You walk down Broadway, the doors are all open to all the honky-tonks, you're hearing music from the right side of your head and the left side of your head for five blocks in a row," Rich said. "There's 60, 70, 80 live music venues in that one concentration. It's the only place like it in the world."

"The French Quarter doesn't have that. Las Vegas doesn't have that. Times Square doesn't have that," he continued. "There's nowhere in America that has what downtown Nashville has when it comes to live music. And it is absolutely under threat."
Rich painted a dire picture of what he fears the entertainment district could eventually look like when Nashville hosts the 2030 Super Bowl.

"Can you imagine when the Super Bowl comes to Nashville here in a few years, and everybody's packed in on Broadway and there's only 30 or 40% of the neon signs that are even still lit up, if you're lucky?" he said. "That's what you're looking at happening. I mean, what a travesty that would be."

Rich, an outspoken conservative and longtime supporter of President Donald Trump, placed much of the blame for the situation on O’Connell, a Democrat, suggesting the mayor's approach to the issue is driven by ideology. However, Rich maintained that concerns among Broadway business owners cross political lines.
"This is not just a bunch of conservatives yelling about it," Rich said. "The group of business owners that I sat with were from both sides of the aisle."
"There's all kinds of things we don't agree on amongst each other," he continued. "But this right here brought unity amongst left and right and middle. It's that bad."
Rich also accused O’Connell of using tax policy to reshape the character of Nashville, offering his own view of the mayor's motivations.
Rich criticized Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell, suggesting that his approach to the issue is driven by ideology.  (Getty Images)

"It is a tactic to tax things out of existence that you don't like and replace them with things that you'd rather have there," Rich said. "Can you imagine the neon signs on Broadway replaced with government buildings and corporate offices? I think that's what he wants."
Fox News Digital has reached out to O’Connell’s office for comment.
The five-time Grammy Award nominee is now calling on Tennessee state leaders to intervene.

Rich said Broadway business owners have appealed to Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson and urged Gov. Bill Lee to work with lawmakers on a solution. He told Fox News Digital that the governor has the opportunity to become a "honky-tonk hero."
WATCH: JOHN RICH FEARS NASHVILLE’S NEON LIGHTS COULD GO DARK BEFORE SUPER BOWL COMES TO MUSIC CITY

"Governor Lee, who's still here, has an opportunity to do a special session with the Senate, with the House, and come with some solution that, if nothing else, will buy us some time until we can go in and make the more permanent moves," Rich said.

State leaders are considering taking action. Sexton's office confirmed to Axios Nashville on Wednesday that the House speaker has spoken with Lee's office about the issue and that they are "looking at all possible solutions," including the possibility of a special legislative session.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Despite his warnings, Rich said the culture that draws crowds to Broadway has not changed, at least not yet.
Rich said that Broadway's culture hasn't changed yet. (Johnny Louis/Getty Images)
"The culture on Broadway hasn't changed at all," he said. "The crowds that come there, the bands that play there, the owners of those businesses, they're the same as they've always been."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It is all about the music," Rich continued. "It's all about people coming to town to have a good time and look at what some of the most talented people you've ever seen in your life play on these tiny little stages."

title: Paris Jackson says dad Michael’s unusual rule helped protect her childhood
summary: Paris Jackson revealed on "Call Her Daddy" that Michael Jackson required his kids to finish homework and chores before enjoying Neverland attractions.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Behind the glitz of Michael Jackson’s larger-than-life world, Paris Jackson said her father enforced a strict rule to protect his children’s sense of normalcy.

The late King of Pop kept a tight rein on his children despite their unusual upbringing. Jackson recalled her father requiring them to finish their homework and chores before earning weekend fun, limiting television and movies and having them wear masks in public to shield their identities from the intense spotlight surrounding his fame.

"The cool, like very congruent line throughout my childhood that kind of started there and then just continued on wherever we went was, if you're good, and you do your chores, and you do your homework, and you do the things that you're supposed to do. Then on the weekends you can go see some animals, and you can go ride some rides, and you can go to the movies," she told "Call Her Daddy" host Alexandra Cooper.
VICTORIA BECKHAM REVEALS STRICT NO-PHONES RULE AT FAMILY DINNER KEEPS HER KIDS GROUNDED
Paris Jackson said her father, Michael Jackson, required homework and chores before his children could enjoy weekend outings. (Evan Agostini/Invision/AP, File)

"It was made very, very clear that all of the attractions [at Neverland] were not for us," she added. "That it did not belong to us. That was for, you know, underprivileged children and children that were terminally ill that couldn't go to like Disneyland."
Paris said the rule remained in place as the family moved frequently and rarely stayed anywhere for more than a year.

"If we were living in Vegas, and it's like, 'OK, if you're good you can go to Circus Circus on the weekends.' Or like we were in like some random place in Virginia. Like, 'OK, if you're good you can go to Chuck E. Cheese this weekend,'" she recalled.
Michael’s rules extended to television. Paris said his children could watch movies or TV after completing their responsibilities, with an exception of studying film without sound.
Paris Jackson recalled wearing masks in public as part of Michael Jackson’s effort to protect his children from the spotlight. (Dave M. Benett/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Michael also took steps to protect his children from the spotlight, having them wear masks in public so they could go unnoticed.

"I mean it just, it made sense because it was like, 'Oh yeah, if you do this now, then you can go to Chuck E. Cheese and be normal this weekend 'cause no one will know who you are,'" the "Wilted" singer recalled. "Like that made sense to me."
The masks helped Paris maintain some anonymity, but she still understood that her father was famous. What she didn’t grasp was the sheer magnitude of his celebrity.
Michael Jackson’s Neverland Ranch attractions were meant for visiting children, not his own family, Paris Jackson said. (Mohamed Hadid/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I just didn't know how famous ... There was definitely part of me that, like when I looked out my hotel window, and it was one of the times where like the alias didn't work and there's just like a sea of people with signs and stuff – I'm not so naive to think, yeah, everyone experiences this, you know?" Paris admitted. "I just didn't understand the lengths."
Jackson, the only daughter of late pop superstar and Debbie Rowe, built an entertainment career through modeling, acting and music.

Paris Jackson has since built her own career in modeling, acting and music, releasing her debut album, "Wilted," in 2020. Her brothers, Prince and Bigi, have also built careers in the entertainment industry. (Alan Chapman/Getty Images)

After making highly publicized appearances with her family following Michael Jackson's 2009 death, she pursued modeling and landed acting roles before signing with Republic Records and releasing her debut album, Wilted, in 2020.
She has two brothers, Prince Jackson and Bigi Jackson.

title: Jeffrey Dean Morgan nearly quit acting after miserable ‘Star Trek’ experience: ‘I hated it so much’
summary: Jeffrey Dean Morgan says his Xindi alien role on "Star Trek: Enterprise" nearly ended his career due to claustrophobia from 14-hour prosthetics sessions.
story: The "Doc Meets World" star spoke with Fox News Digital at Tribeca Festival about nearly leaving Hollywood and the lasting passion that kept drawing him back.
Jeffrey Dean Morgan's miserable experience playing an alien on "Star Trek: Enterprise" nearly convinced him to quit acting for good.

Long before his breakout roles on "Supernatural" and "Grey's Anatomy," Morgan appeared as a Xindi alien named Damron on the sci-fi series — a job that required extensive prosthetics and left the actor struggling with claustrophobia.
"I hated it so much," Morgan recalled during an appearance on Josh Horowitz's "Happy Sad Confused" podcast. "I was like, 'That's it. I've got to do something else.'"

Jeffrey Dean Morgan detailed a horrifying experience that made him nearly want to quit acting.  (Getty Images)
