title: Molly Sims calls out Hollywood for lying about beauty secrets
summary: Molly Sims slammed Hollywood's fake beauty secrets, saying stars lie about drinking water and sleep when facelifts and peptides tell the real story.
story: Model Molly Sims reveals her favorite wellness routines and why feeling good matters most at the Super Bowl.
Molly Sims is getting real about Hollywood spewing fake beauty secrets.
During a recent interview with US Magazine, the 53-year-old model slammed people in Hollywood for lying about how they maintain their camera-ready look.

"Early on, other models would help you. Like, 'I’m getting shots in my a--,' or 'I’m only going to drink grapefruit juice,'" she explained. "Hollywood people would say, 'I just drink a lot of water, and I slept eight hours.' I’m like, 'No, you f---ing didn’t.'"
She went on to say that while out to dinner with a group of girlfriends recently, "all we did was talk about everybody’s facelift."
Sims slammed Hollywood for spewing fake beauty secrets. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Baby2Baby)
MARTHA STEWART GETS CANDID ABOUT PLASTIC SURGERY, DATING AS SHE TURNS 85

"We’re like, 'She looks amazing. She did the upper lip, the lower. She did the CO2,'" she said. "It’s refreshing for a woman in Kentucky or Ohio to know that it’s not just drinking water and getting a good night’s sleep. You too can be on the peptide."
The model also spoke about how her approach to her appearance has evolved from her early days in the modeling industry to now, as a woman in her 50s.

Sims recalled coming into the industry "during a difficult era called 'heroin chic,'" saying the expectation was to be "about 20 pounds underweight and very goth," noting the scrutiny she received was "devastating."

"I went from Vanderbilt with my sorority sisters, where you’re dipping your fries in a Wendy’s Frosty and you think nothing of it," she said. title: Nick Reiner indicted in murders of parents Rob Reiner, Michele Singer Reiner at Brentwood home
summary: Nick Reiner faces two murder charges and special circumstance allegations in the stabbing deaths of his parents at their Brentwood home in December.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Nick Reiner pleaded not guilty Wednesday after a grand jury indicted him on murder charges in the stabbing deaths of his parents, actor-director Rob Reiner and photographer-producer Michele Singer Reiner.

The indictment, returned July 20 and unsealed Wednesday, charged Nick, 32, with two counts of murder and included special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and lying in wait. Prosecutors also alleged he used a knife.
"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said.
ROB REINER'S FINAL ROLE DRAWS FIERCE CRITICISM 6 MONTHS AFTER LEGENDARY DIRECTOR'S TRAGIC DEATH
Nick Reiner during his arraignment in Los Angeles County Superior Court in Los Angeles. (Chris Torres/Pool)

"The indictment unsealed today also adds a special circumstance allegation that the defendant committed the murders by means of lying in wait. We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."
Prosecutors claimed Nick fatally stabbed his father, 78, and mother, 70, on Dec. 14, 2025, at their Brentwood home.
ROB REINER'S SON NICK FIGHTS FOR $1.5M TRUST FUND ACCESS TO BANKROLL HIGH-POWERED MURDER TRIAL DEFENSE
Multiple agencies worked to find and arrest Nick, who was apprehended near the University of Southern California at approximately 9:15 p.m., hours after his parents' bodies were discovered.
Nick Reiner appeared in court earlier this year during an arraignment with Deputy Public Defender Kimberly Greene. (Chris Torres-Pool)
The 32-year-old initially pleaded not guilty to the double murder charges in February, one month after his powerhouse attorney, Alan Jackson, stepped down from the case.
Jackson told reporters during a news conference he had "no choice" but to withdraw from the case, citing circumstances beyond his and Nick's control as to why he abruptly resigned from the case.
NICK REINER LOSING POWERHOUSE DEFENSE ATTORNEY MAY COME DOWN TO MONEY, EXPERTS SAY
"Circumstances beyond our control, but more importantly, circumstances beyond Nick's control have dictated that," Jackson said during a news conference outside the courthouse.
"Sadly, it's made it impossible for us to continue our representation of Nick. I'm legally and I'm ethically prohibited from explaining all the reasons why."
Jackson remained adamant that Nick was "not guilty" of murdering his parents.
Attorney Alan Jackson said he had "no choice" but to resign from Nick's counsel earlier this year. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"We've investigated this matter top to bottom, back to front," Jackson said. "What we've learned — and you can take this to the bank — is that pursuant to the laws of this state, pursuant to the law in California, Nick Reiner is not guilty of murder."
Jackson arrived at the Reiner home less than 24 hours after the couple's bodies were discovered. Soon after, he signed on to represent Nick.
Kimberly Greene, the deputy public defender assigned to the case, spoke briefly with Nick after Jackson resigned and said Nick "was understanding that there was going to be a change in counsel."

Nick is being held without bail and remains in custody at the Twin Towers Correctional Facility in downtown Los Angeles after formally being charged with two counts of first-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of his parents.

Rob Reiner and wife Michele Singer Reiner were found dead at their Brentwood home in December. (Stefanie Keenan)

title: Brooks Nader ditches bikini top in front of dad and sparks fierce fan debate
summary: Brooks Nader went topless during a Sardinian beach day with her dad and family, sparking heated debate over the Sports Illustrated model's bold move.
story: Brooks Nader tells Fox News Digital about growing up with conservative parents who banned two-piece bikinis and reveals why her "Baywatch" swimsuit gets the family seal of approval.

Brooks Nader turned a sun-soaked Sardinian getaway into a full-on family spectacle when the model ditched her swimsuit top in front of her dad and relatives – leaving everyone with nowhere to look but straight at the drama.

The Sports Illustrated model arrived at the seaside outing in a billowy white dress before peeling it off to take a dip in the Mediterranean.

title: ‘Grease’ star Stockard Channing says she’s ‘happy being a recluse’ after leaving America
summary: Stockard Channing revealed her reclusive London lifestyle, morning routine with her dog and why her longtime partner's death shifted everything.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Stockard Channing admitted she's "happy being a recluse" as she reflected on her quiet lifestyle after fleeing the states for the United Kingdom.
The "Grease" star began living in London "just before COVID," a move she envisioned after the 2014 death of her partner of 25 years, producer Daniel Gilham.
"I've lived alone since I lost Daniel and I'm happy being a recluse," Channing wrote in an essay for The Sunday Times. "I was married four times before Daniel, and they all represent epochs of me.
HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE
Stockard Channing is content away from Hollywood, she explained in a new essay. (Alan Chapman)

"I grew up in the sixties, reacting to that repressed notion of marriage and sexuality from the fifties kinda like Rizzo," she noted. "Children were thought about and, yeah, I think about them now because it'd be great to have someone taking care of me. But, hey, children can be just as selfish as everybody else out there."
Channing, 82, confessed that Gilham's death "was more devastating than I realized; it had a lag effect."
‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’
"The pattern of my life shifted, so I shifted my life from Maine," she wrote of the move, which also vaguely coincided with Trump's second presidential bid.

"When I started playing 'The West Wing's first lady, Abbey Bartlet, in 1999, we were about to move to the second Bush administration," she wrote. "The cast had a good look at that Washington world, and there seemed to be a level of honest, intelligent discourse that is missing from 2026.
Channing starred as Rizzo in the classic 1978 film "Grease." (Paramount Pictures)
"People look at 'The West Wing' and go, 'Wow, wasn't it great when politicians had an ounce of integrity?' Abbey didn't suffer fools, and she's the character most like me in real life."
Channing reflected on an interaction with director Aaron Sorkin, who said he "wrote Abbey as the person he saw in me."

"I was quite short with him the first time we met," she wrote. "He was saying all these nice things, and I said, 'Look, I don't have time for flattery.' I didn't mean to be rude it was just one of those days."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Her days of stardom are slightly different from now as the "Six Degrees of Separation" actress detailed her morning routine, which begins at 7 a.m. when her dog wakes her up.
"After he's had his breakfast and I've made a strong pot of coffee, my dog walker takes him out and I go back to bed," she wrote. "My ideal morning."
Olivia Newton John, left; Didi Conn, right; and Channing, center, were part of the "Pink Ladies."  (Getty Images)
John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John captured the hearts of America with "Grease." (CBS )
"My duvet is covered in ink spots because for many years I've been keeping a diary. I sit there with my fountain pen and my thoughts. What do I feel about this or that?
"I only leave the bed when I need to go to the bathroom. At my age life is guided by bodily functions."
By 10 a.m., Channing pursues a "bit of exercise," but admitted that her "favorite exercise days are when I play hooky."

"I know that exercising is the right thing to do but my brain tells me to go hide behind the bike sheds," she wrote. "Lunch is my first meal of the day and I can follow a recipe, but if my ramen doesn't work out I give it to the dog.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"If I'm leaving the apartment I comb my hair, but I don't have a wardrobe of designer outfits. Well, I do, but they're all from the Eighties and Nineties. Do I care how I look? Most actors do although part of your job is not being self-conscious.
Stockard Channing earned an Academy Award nomination in 1994 for her role in "Six Degrees of Separation." (Gregg DeGuire/WireImage)
"But I've never considered myself as beautiful. And I'm not a celebrity 'tart.' I'm just me, take it or leave it."
Channing's fan base is vast, and she recognized how different age groups remember her as different characters.

"For younger girls it's 'Practical Magic,' for grown-ups it's 'The West Wing,' and for real grown-ups it's 'Grease,'" she wrote. "Although the critics weren't kind about Grease, it made tons of money and it still gets streamed a lot.

"I guess films are like songs: they take you back to a particular time in your life. Maybe a more innocent time."

title: John Hinckley Jr gives his thoughts on Jodie Foster 45 years after shooting Ronald Reagan to impress her
summary: John Hinckley Jr. reveals that Jodie Foster could have been a target herself, saying "fate went the other way" toward former President Ronald Reagan.
story: Jodie Foster spoke to Fox News Digital about being honored at a hand and foot ceremony on Friday.
John Hinckley Jr., the man who shot former President Ronald Reagan in 1981 to impress Jodie Foster, said he wants nothing but good things for the actress.

"I just wish Jodie Foster well," he said. "I don’t really see her movies, but I wish her well, and I know she’s doing quite well. And that’s all I can say: I just, I wish Jodie well, and I hope she has a good life."

The 71-year-old explained on the "Mark Joseph Show" in an exclusive preview shared with Entertainment Weekly that when he shot Reagan 45 years ago in a delusional state, he believed he would spend the rest of his life with the "Silence of the Lambs" actress.
REAGAN SHOOTER CALLS LINK TO WASHINGTON HOTEL ‘SPOOKY’ AFTER ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AT SAME SITE
John Hinckley Jr., at left in his 1981 mugshot, spoke about Jodie Foster in a new interview. (Bureau of Prisons/Getty Images; Jamie McCarthy/WireImage)
The full episode will air on Wednesday.

"I wanted to have like this union with Jodie Foster and live the rest of my life with her and all these things that, of course, were delusional, but I was believing those things at that time. So, the best outcome would have been to just have like this union with Jodie Foster," Hinckley told Joseph after the host asked what he believed at the time would be the best thing that could come out of the shooting.
John Hinckley Jr. said he wishes Jodie Foster well. (Getty Images)

He explained that he believed at the time that Foster would "join me wherever I was. You know, I didn’t know if I was going to be in jail or hospital or what, but after things settled down, I had this notion that she was going to join me wherever I was."

It came out shortly after Hinckley’s assassination attempt that left Reagan with a broken rib, punctured lung and internal bleeding, that Hinckley was obsessed with Foster after seeing her in "Taxi Driver" and thought the shooting would make her notice him.
JODIE FOSTER HAUNTED BY HORRIFIC DOG TRAGEDY, BELIEVES SHE GAVE UP WHAT SHE LOVES MOST FOR SUCCESS
John Hinckley Jr. stands for a portrait in Williamsburg, Va., in 2022. (AFP via Getty Images)
Hinckley was found not guilty by reason of insanity after shooting the former president outside the Washington Hilton two months after he was elected.
Former White House press secretary James Brady was shot in the head and suffered brain damage and partial paralysis, which led to his death in 2014. His death was ruled a homicide.
Two other men were also wounded in the shooting.
Hinckley was committed to a psychiatric hospital after the trial and released in 2016. By 2022, he was living in Virginia without any court restrictions.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
President Ronald Reagan waves to the crowd outside the Hilton Hotel in Washington, D.C., just before an assassination attempt on March 30, 1981. (Consolidated New Pictures/AFP via Getty Images)
Hinckley admitted to Joseph, however, that, in his delusional state, Foster could have been a target herself.
"She definitely could have been a target. It’s just fate went the other way," Hinckley said. "But, yeah, she could have been a target. But, as fate turned out, it was Reagan instead of her."

In a 2022 interview with CBS, Hinckley apologized for his actions.
Jodie Foster on the set of "Taxi Driver" with Robert De Niro and director Martin Scorsese. (Corbis via Getty Images)
"I shot four people, and I’m sorry to the Reagan family, the Brady family, the other families of the victims," he said at the time. "I’m sorry to Jodie Foster for bringing her into this."

title: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr reveals where she now lives after leaving Los Angeles behind
summary: Diane Farr reveals she left Los Angeles after 30 years for rural Washington and plans to split time between Vancouver and Spain in her "third act."
story: After long, 14-hour workdays, Diane Farr told Fox News Digital that she makes her Sundays count—spending time with friends, paddleboarding, e-biking and soaking up life on the water in the Pacific Northwest.
"Fire Country" star Diane Farr has revealed where she is now living after leaving Los Angeles behind.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Farr explained that once her children went off to college, she didn't feel tied to California anymore and decided to put down roots in rural Washington. She also plans to split her time between Vancouver and Spain.

"So I actually moved to rural Washington because I could buy this pretty house, and it wasn't very expensive in comparison to living in LA for all those years," she said. "I live right on the water, so there's a lot of stand-up paddling and there's a lot of e-biking and really drinking in this gorgeous Pacific Northwest weather."
"Fire Country" star Diane Farr shared that she left LA for rural Washington after living in California for 30 years. (Sergei Bachlakov/CBS via Getty Images)
Farr stars in "Fire Country," which is filmed in Vancouver. Farr plays Sharon Leone on "Fire Country," a Cal Fire Division Chief and the mother of Bode Leone.
"Fire Country" Season 5 is scheduled to premiere on October 9, 2026, airing Fridays at 9/8c on CBS and streaming the next day on Paramount+.
Farr told Fox News Digital that once her children went off to college and left California, she felt like she had "permission" to do the same.
'FIRE COUNTRY' STAR DIANE FARR LEAVES LOS ANGELES AFTER 30 YEARS TO START HER 'THIRD ACT'
"So I actually moved to rural Washington because I could buy this pretty house, and it wasn't very expensive in comparison to living in LA for all those years."

"The permission came from my children being old enough that they live somewhere else. You know, they go to college, they live in other states, and I know women always talk about empty nest syndrome, and mine was unique," Farr began. "I didn't leave LA for 15 years when I had babies. I was afraid of working out of town. I was afraid of missing everything. I was afraid to do a one-hour drama."
WATCH: Diane Farr finds her joy in the Pacific Northwest
The actress explained that she had her children when she was nearly 40 and "really wanted to be there."

"After the pandemic, 15 years had gone by. We spent two years at home and everybody was a teenager and mean to mom. And I thought, I can leave, I could go to Vancouver. I'm taking that drama," she continued.
Shawn Hatosy as Brett Richards and Diane Farr as Sharon Leone in "Fire Country." (CBS via Getty Images)
Farr said that her "third act" was focused around how she could get more joy out of her life.
"My third act is gonna look like six months of the year in Spain and six months of the year in Vancouver, because it's really like how to get the joie de vie. It's how to live the most," Farr said.
WATCH: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr teases Sharon’s 'off the rails' era in Season 5
At the end of July, Farr shared with her Instagram followers that she was leaving Los Angeles after 30 years.

"I wasn’t born here, I didn’t go to school here — I just had a chance for representation as an actor and I moved out of NYC the summer I was 26," she wrote. "I came like most of the people I love in Hollywoodland — none of which I saw this week bc moving sucks."
'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'
She went on to say that she came to Los Angeles "chasing a dream that I am still shocked worked out."
Michael Trucco as Luke Leone and Diane Farr as Sharon Leone in "Fire Country." (CBS via Getty Images)

Farr's acting career began in the '90s, with the actress landing her breakthrough role in "Roswell" in 1999. She later earned leading roles in "Numb3rs," "Splitting Up Together" and, most recently, "Fire Country."
In addition to her acting career, Farr also reflected on the many other positive experiences she had while living in Los Angeles, including starting a family.

"I also got to raise babies in the sun and the mountains and enjoy this beautiful home and attend public schools ??" she said. "Pinch me I’m overwhelmed by the blessings and hope, really hope I gave enough back. LA will always be where my family is from."
WATCH: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr is choosing joy in her 'third act'
Farr shares three children with her ex-husband, Seung Yong Chung: son Beckett, 18, and twin daughters Coco and Sawyer, 17.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Farr explained what fans can expect from Sharon in season five.

"Well, last year was a lot of grief, right? Because she had lost Vince and this year she seems to have gotten some action with a very handsome man at the end of last season. So, I was sort of looking at it like Sharon hasn't dated or been single or been a party of one since she's about 20," she began. "So she's a little off the rails, you know, like she's kind of behaving like a 20-year-old. Which isn't good when you're the boss, and you have children and people responsible for you."
Farr shares twin teenage daughters and a son with her ex-husband. (Francis Specker/CBS via Getty Images)
Farr concluded, "So, she's not making her best choices this season."

title: Meghan Markle’s royal exit had warning signs years earlier, veteran correspondent reveals
summary: Simon Vigar's new book details how Meghan Markle's 2018 royal tour of Australia exposed the first cracks in her relationship with palace staff.
story: Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," says a "culture clash" and mismatched expectations contributed to Meghan Markle’s difficulties adjusting to life in the British royal family.
Meghan Markle’s rocky tenure as a working royal may have stemmed from a "culture clash" with palace aides, according to a veteran royal correspondent who covered her time as a working royal.
Simon Vigar, one of Britain's longest-serving royal correspondents, examines those tensions in his new book, "The Four Wives of Windsor."
Kensington Palace told Fox News Digital it does not comment on books. A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex told Fox News Digital, "This is not something we would comment on."
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex visit a local farming family, the Woodleys, on Oct. 17, 2018 in Dubbo, Australia. Simon Vigar looked back on the couple's royal tour in his new book, "The Royal Wives of Windsor." (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)

"There was a culture clash there," Vigar told Fox News Digital. "I think it's a crying shame. It was avoidable, and egos got in the way on both sides. I think she thought that there would be more control over events, public events, than there was. ... The narrative now is that the British media was always against Harry and Meghan. That is not how I remember it, and many of my colleagues remember it."

"Harry and Meghan were great," Vigar said. "I saw her on her first engagement in Nottingham. She was brilliant with the crowds. She was an absolute natural, which is why it's so sad that they're not part of [the working royals] now. The tour of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and Tonga [in 2018] went really well.
Meghan Markle visits Nottingham for her first official public engagement with then-fiancé Prince Harry on Dec. 1, 2017, in Nottingham, England. (Jeremy Selwyn - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"The crowds were massive. But ... the palace press officers were trying to spin three different stories after that. One person was in tears from the Kensington Palace team because of how it had all gone pear-shaped, as we say in the U.K."
WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE FACED ROYAL FAMILY ‘CULTURE CLASH’: AUTHOR

Meghan, a former American actress who starred in the legal drama "Suits," became the Duchess of Sussex when she married Prince Harry in 2018. The palace announced Meghan's pregnancy shortly after the couple arrived in Sydney for their royal tour that October.

Vigar covered the royal tour and wrote that it exposed some of the first significant cracks in Meghan's role as a working royal. According to Vigar, Meghan was accustomed to a public life where "everything was micromanaged in a far more controlled environment."
Meghan Markle on the red carpet for "Suits," circa 2015. (Mike Coppola/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"Those levels of Hollywood control-freakery, as courtiers say, are incompatible with the public service role of the monarchy," he wrote. Vigar also quoted an anonymous senior staffer as saying, "My overall sense is Meghan realized it was hard work and not that glamorous. It's not about you."
Simon Vigar's "The Four Wives of Windsor" is available now. Vigar is one of British television's longest-serving royal correspondents. (Penguin)

Vigar wrote that during the royal tour, Meghan was scheduled to visit Suva Market in Fiji for an engagement highlighting women's economic empowerment. She planned to meet with vendors connected to the cause, but the visit ended earlier than planned.

"There were all these people queuing up to meet her," Vigar recalled. "... In the first few minutes, it all ended very quickly. Team Sussex said it was a security issue. That is denied by other people."

Meghan Markle’s first pregnancy was officially announced on Oct. 15, 2018, when Kensington Palace confirmed that she and Prince Harry were expecting their first child, due in spring 2019. She was reported to be around 12 weeks pregnant at the time. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Reports at the time attributed the shortened visit to security concerns as crowds gathered to see Meghan.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, visits Suva Market to meet female vendors involved in the U.N. Women's project "Markets for Change" on Oct. 24, 2018, in Suva, Fiji. (Pool/Getty Images)

"... If it was a security issue, the Scotland Yard bodyguards would never have allowed her to arrive. They have an advanced team there. They have a team with her. They wouldn't have let her get out of the car if they thought it was a big security issue."

"Was it because it was too chaotic or too hot? Well, it wasn't chaotic really," Vigar said. "It was a very well-planned route through the market. It may have been illness, although that's not what Team Sussex said. In which case, why come down in the first place? And she looked OK. [But] there was a moment in the market where she looked at one of her assistants and the whole mood changed. It all went fast-forward. And my cameraman was being pushed out of the way."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attend the unveiling of The Queen's Commonwealth Canopy in Redvale, New Zealand, on Oct. 30, 2018. (New Zealand Herald - Pool/Getty Images)

"The women I was with had been waiting for ages to see her," Vigar continued. "One of them had handmade raffia fans with Harry and Meghan in them. She didn't get to meet her. She just zoomed past her, and that was that. Meghan was off. It was very strange. ... And I suppose that was an early sign in retrospect. That was an early sign that there was a mismatch in expectations."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex attends the official opening of the ANZAC Memorial at Hyde Park in Sydney, Australia, on Oct. 20, 2018. (Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)
Vigar noted that the Duchess of Sussex was working on "an intense schedule" while pregnant during the overseas tour.
"Meghan understood ‘the show’ bit but not the cultural side of the royal family," one senior aide told Vigar.
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex attends the Jaguar Land Rover Driving Challenge at the Invictus Games on Oct. 20, 2018, in Sydney. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Valentine Low, then royal correspondent for The Times of London, reported in 2021 that Jason Knauf, who had served as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s communications secretary, had submitted a bullying complaint concerning Meghan in 2018. Meghan Markle is seen here being interviewed by Oprah Winfrey on March 8, 2021. The bombshell report concerning bullying allegations was published shortly before the televised tell-all. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"The press team at Kensington Palace is pretty small, let's say, compared to a movie premiere in Hollywood or a movie premiere in London," he explained. A royal aide told Vigar that working royals are expected to fulfill public engagements even when they do not feel their best: "Even if they are feeling grotty, they turn up and they do the job."
In the book, Vigar wrote that there is nothing "showbiz" about "cold palaces and a life of smiling, waving and turning up."

title: ‘Twilight’ star Kellan Lutz traded California for Tennessee land and Bible studies
summary: Kellan Lutz explains how his wife's need for a support system after their second child led the family from Orange County to Franklin, Tennessee.
story: Dennis Quaid reflects on leaving Los Angeles for Nashville, saying residents are frustrated with high taxes, poor services and the fallout from devastating wildfires.
Kellan Lutz said this week that he left California three years ago for Tennessee after the pandemic.
"I love California, I really do," he explained on "Inside of You" with Michael Rosenbaum. "The whole Tennessee move happened when we had our second kid."
The "Twilight" actor said they moved from Orange County – and his wife, Brittany Lutz, hopes to eventually move back there or at least to be "bi-ish coastal."
‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’
Kellan Lutz said that his family moved to Tennessee three years ago. (WireImage)

Lutz’s wife was born and raised in Orange County. "Her family is awesome. But post-COVID, a lot of people flew, like fled California. A lot of people lost jobs and wanted to move somewhere a little bit more peace given."

His wife’s family chose to leave California, and he said they followed them to Tennessee, mainly because otherwise she wouldn’t have had a support system when he goes on location for work, and she’s left at home with the children.
"We got some land, got great Bible studies that we're a part of, great churches, great community,"

"And one of the kids got sick. She felt really out of control as far as not being able to bring both kids there or just kind of helpless. So, she's like, ‘Can we move?’ I'm like, ‘Yeah, of course," he explained.
He added that other men with kids in his life told him that new moms usually wanted to move to where their mom lives "just to help with the kids."
Kellan Lutz is seen at an event with wife, Brittany, in 2019. (WireImage)
'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'

"Then when they decided to move, I was like, "OK, well, we're going to do it. We're going to give it a couple years and we have, and it's great. There's a lot of great things about Tennessee, especially Franklin where we live."
The family moved to Tennessee three years ago, but he acknowledged he doesn’t know how long they’ll stay.
Kellan Lutz signing autographs for "Twilight" fans in 2009. (WireImage)

"We got some land, got great Bible studies that we're a part of, great churches, great community," he said. "There's a lot of actors. I've gone to probably more movie premieres in Franklin, Tennessee, than I have in L.A., you know, the last couple years since I lived there."
Admittedly though, there are adjustments.

title: ‘The Office’ star Lucy Davis ‘at peace’ with 'incurable' cancer diagnosis after nearly ignoring warning sign
summary: Lucy Davis revealed her breast cancer has metastasized to her spine, hip and ribs, with chemotherapy no longer an option for "The Office" actress.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Lucy Davis revealed a devastating Stage 4 breast cancer diagnosis after quietly battling the disease for the past year and a half.
"The Office" actress said the cancer had metastasized to her spine, right hip and ribs and was now "incurable," with chemotherapy no longer an option.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny," she wrote on Instagram. "I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out."
Rather than dwell on her prognosis, Davis said she was determined to embrace whatever time she had left.
BARRY MANILOW RESCHEDULES CONCERT 45 MINUTES BEFORE START AMID ONGOING LUNG CANCER RECOVERY
‘The Office’ actress Lucy Davis is opening up about her private battle with incurable Stage 4 breast cancer – and the subtle symptom she almost ignored. (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

"As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can," she explained. "I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that."
Davis said maintaining that outlook had not made the physical realities of cancer any easier.

"As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else," Davis wrote. "Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!)"
Despite the pain, Davis said she had found peace with what could come next.
"The Office" star Lucy Davis says she’s choosing joy, purpose and peace as she continues acting and advocating for animal rights amid her cancer diagnosis. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

But Davis made clear she had no plans to stop pursuing the work and causes she loved.

"I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights," Davis noted. "It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life."
After an 18-month battle kept largely out of the public eye, Lucy Davis shared an emotional update on cancer’s physical toll and the outlook keeping her going. (Dave Benett/Getty Images)

title: Riley Green shares how Luke Grimes unexpectedly launched his acting career
summary: Riley Green reveals how Luke Grimes encouraged him to audition for "Marshals," helping the country star land his first acting role as a Navy SEAL.
story: Riley Green told Fox News Digital that he doesn't get nervous going on stage anymore, but his nerves were wrecked when he walked on the "Marshals" set.
Riley Green may be one of country music’s rising stars, but his latest on-screen career move came with a little help from a famous friend.

During an appearance on "CBS Mornings" on Monday, the 37-year-old Alabama native revealed that "Yellowstone" star Luke Grimes helped open the door to his first acting role, encouraging Green to step outside his comfort zone and eventually helping land him a part on the CBS drama "Marshals."

"It happened so organically because he was starting his music career and coming to Nashville a little bit. We wrote together," said Green, who made his acting debut as Garrett — a former Navy SEAL struggling with PTSD — alongside Grimes in the "Yellowstone" spinoff.
TAYLOR SHERIDAN SHOCKS 'YELLOWSTONE' FANS WITH NEW SPINOFF SERIES, PROVIDES VIEWERS WITH DARK RIDE
Riley Green opened up about how his friendship with Luke Grimes led to an unexpected career move. (Getty Images)

"He mentioned something about maybe I should act. I said, 'Well I'm interested.' He said, 'I've got this show.' A couple months later, I went out and read for a part. They said I got it. I flew back out to Utah and we filmed the show."
Earlier this year, Green admitted it's not every day an opportunity like that presents itself.

"I guess that doesn't happen all the time, where the star of the show sits in with somebody trying out for a part," Green told USA Today. "But man, I've got to be such good friends with Luke, and it makes it so much easier to step into a world that I wasn't necessarily comfortable in."
It was a dramatic change for a performer accustomed to playing sold-out concerts.
TAYLOR SHERIDAN’S 'YELLOWSTONE’ FORMULA TURNS COUNTRY STARS INTO SCENE-STEALERS AS MORGAN WADE MAKES HER DEBUT
Green previously admitted acting was considerably more intimidating than taking the stage.
Riley Green as Garrett and Luke Grimes as Kayce Dutton appear in a scene from the CBS original series "Marshals." (Cam McLeod/CBS)

His Hollywood debut was the latest unexpected chapter in a career Green never necessarily envisioned for himself.
Long before he found fame, Green was earning his living as a construction worker, framing homes until he signed a record deal in 2018.

title: Bella Thorne says Hollywood treated her like a kid on screen and an adult off camera
summary: Bella Thorne opens up about the moment she turned 18 and finally felt free after years of navigating Hollywood's impossible child star expectations.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Bella Thorne's life as a child star came with a harsh reality: Hollywood expected her to be a kid on screen and an adult everywhere else.

Thorne began working in entertainment as a child, appearing as a model before taking on television roles in shows including HBO’s "Big Love." Her major breakthrough arrived in 2010 when she was cast as CeCe Jones opposite Zendaya’s Rocky Blue in Disney Channel’s "Shake It Up."
"You're ... spending all of your hours a day on set with adults, you know, that is – it's like such a different, the brain's like how do I–" Thorne explained during an appearance on "Call Her Daddy."
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Bella Thorne reflected on the pressures of growing up in Hollywood during a recent appearance on Alexandra Cooper’s podcast. (Getty Images)

"And I'm expected to be this child, but I'm also working like hours like an adult and being in adult conversations," she added. "And when I f--k up it's my bad, not like a child – It's my bad. Like you're an adult, it's your bad."
But navigating those adult expectations while growing up in the public eye didn't come easily for Thorne.

"Well, I think people can see how I've managed it publicly," she told host Alexandra Cooper. "They can see it, they've got photos of it. Oh, they got all the photos. Oh, wow. I don't know that I ever handled it or balanced it out correctly."

"I don't think that I ever had that mental clarity," Thorne acknowledged. "I've worked a lot on the more recent side. I got to a point where I just needed to kind of change things in my life and get better at – I was working so much and yet was leaving very little time for the things that I really, really cared about."
Bella Thorne rose to Disney Channel fame alongside Zendaya after starring in "Shake It Up" as CeCe Jones. (Craig Sjodin/Disney Channel via Getty Images)
FORMER DISNEY STAR MAITLAND WARD SAYS YOUNG ACTORS WERE TREATED LIKE A 'PRODUCT' IN HOLLYWOOD FACTORY

Thorne said she spent the past two years working to prioritize her mental health, a shift that became especially important after "Color Your Hurt" left her feeling emotionally drained. The now 28-year-old actress revealed she finally gave herself "some space to breathe" along with grace.
"I don't think I ever did that when I was younger," she said.
While Thorne struggled to give herself that same grace as a child star, she recalled feeling a dramatic shift when she turned 18.
Bella Thorne said she felt a sense of freedom when she turned 18 after years of working as a child actor. (Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images)
"...I was like, 'I'm free,'" the "Midnight Sun" star recalled.

"Like I'm literally free. Like I'm walking into this house and no one's asking me when I'm like, when I'm gonna be there, when this time or when I'm gonna leave. It ... was such a weird – and you don't know what's weird until someone else tells you it's weird."
Thorne also spoke candidly about being compared to her fellow Disney Channel stars, including Selena Gomez, Miley Cyrus and Demi Lovato.

title: When is a mental health crisis too severe for telehealth? Warning signs families shouldn't ignore
summary: Lindsay Clancy's psychiatrist had 14 virtual visits but never met her in person, raising questions about telehealth mental health treatment limits.
story: Jonathan Alpert, a New York psychotherapist, said virtual care can work very well, but that "there comes a point where a screen may not be enough."

As the Lindsay Clancy murder trial spotlights the psychiatric care she received before the killings of her three children, the case has raised broader questions about the growing reliance on telehealth for mental health conditions.

Nearly half (48.3%) of American adults with serious mental illness now receive some type of mental health treatment via telehealth, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA).

Clancy reportedly had 14 virtual visits with her primary psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, over a five-month period, from September 2022 through Jan. 23, 2023, according to testimony reported by The Associated Press. The final appointment was on Jan. 23, the day before the killings. The two never met in person.
POSTPARTUM MOM LINDSAY CLANCY ON TRIAL FOR MURDER BRINGS COURT TO A HALT WITH SUDDEN BREAKDOWN
During cross-examination, Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, questioned Tufts about her reliance on virtual appointments, per AP.
Nearly half (48.3%) of American adults with serious mental illness now receive some type of mental health treatment via telehealth. (iStock)
"Did you ever suggest to her that 'maybe you should come in and see me, rather than on the computer?'" Reddington asked.
"Talking to her over the video didn't seem like an issue," Tufts responded. "It didn't seem like there was something I was missing."
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT

Jonathan Alpert, Ph.D., a New York psychotherapist — who was not involved in Clancy's care and was speaking generally about telehealth rather than the specifics of her treatment — said virtual care can work very well, but that "there comes a point where a screen may not be enough."
"The sicker and more unstable someone becomes, the less comfortable I'd be relying exclusively on a screen."

"If someone is becoming suicidal, psychotic, manic, unstable or unable to function, the clinician has to consider whether that person needs to be seen in person or needs a higher level of care," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation: How America Got Hooked on Therapy and Why It's Left Us More Anxious and Divided," told Fox News Digital.
"The priority has to be getting an accurate picture of what’s going on and keeping the patient safe."
Benefits and drawbacks of virtual care
Telehealth plays an important function in mental healthcare and offers many benefits, Alpert noted.
"As a provider, I can see far more people in a day doing virtual therapy than I could if I were doing in-office treatment," he told Fox News Digital.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE
For the patient, it eliminates the commute to the therapist's office, which could be a limitation for those with busy schedules.
"So it does allow more and better access to care in many cases, but it does have its limitations if someone has a severe psychiatric disorder," Alpert said.
Lindsay Clancy sits next to her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
There are certain things about a patient’s appearance — such as hygiene, movements, agitation, intoxication or general behavior — that aren't as obvious on Zoom, he noted.
"Someone can pull themselves together for an appointment and look relatively fine for 30 minutes even though they're falling apart outside of it," he said.
Signs that in-person is best
If the patient keeps getting worse despite frequent appointments, that's a big warning sign, according to Alpert.
"At some point, the treatment plan has to change, whether that means seeing the person in person, getting an emergency evaluation or moving them to a higher level of care," the expert said. (iStock)

"More appointments aren't necessarily more treatment," he told Fox News Digital. "If someone is becoming more suicidal, paranoid, manic, disorganized, aggressive or simply unable to function, you can't just keep scheduling another video call and assume that's enough."
"At some point, the treatment plan has to change, whether that means seeing the person in person, getting an emergency evaluation or moving them to a higher level of care."
"It's helped a lot of people get care who otherwise might not."
In cases where there is any concern about suicide or violence, Alpert said it’s important for the therapist to be direct and to ask the following questions.

Are they having thoughts of hurting themselves or someone else?Do they have a plan?Do they have access to weapons or other lethal means?Have they done anything recently that suggests the risk is escalating?
Are they having thoughts of hurting themselves or someone else?
Do they have a plan?
Do they have access to weapons or other lethal means?
Have they done anything recently that suggests the risk is escalating?
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"If someone says they just want to die, that's one thing, and it's very concerning, but if they have a plan, say a weapon or pills, that brings it to the next level and would certainly warrant intervention, whether it's through the police or emergency services," he said.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
It’s also important for the therapist to know where the patient is located during the appointment so that if there is an emergency, they can take action, Alpert advised.
"And sometimes you need information from family or other people in the patient's life, because the patient may not be giving you the whole picture."
A good clinician can identify serious risk over video, and at the same time, someone can miss serious risk sitting across from a patient in an office. (iStock)
The expert also emphasized the distinction between postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis.
"With postpartum psychosis … there may be delusions, disorganized thinking, hallucinations — and if that's what's going on, that definitely warrants inpatient treatment."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Overall, Alpert said, telehealth itself is not the problem.

"It's helped a lot of people get care who otherwise might not," he said. "The bigger issue is whether the clinician is doing a thorough assessment and whether the level of care still fits the patient's condition."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
A good clinician can identify serious risk over video, he noted — but at the same time, someone can miss serious risk sitting across from a patient in an office.
"The sicker and more unstable someone becomes, the less comfortable I'd be relying exclusively on a screen," he added.

title: Beer, wine or liquor? Massive study reveals which was linked to lower death risk
summary: Heavy alcohol use raised death risk by 24%, but wine at low levels was linked to lower mortality than beer or spirits in a UK Biobank study.
story: Addiction expert Jessica Steinman discusses a recent study comparing mortality risks of various types of alcohol and why wine’s potential health benefits should be interpreted cautiously.
Heavy drinking has been shown to raise mortality risk, but, at lower levels, what’s in your glass may also matter, a new study suggests.
In recent research of data from 340,924 participants in the UK Biobank, wine was linked to lower mortality, while beer and spirits were tied to higher death risk.
Data were collected between 2006 and 2022, with more than 13 years of average follow-up. The findings were presented at the American College of Cardiology’s Annual Scientific Session in New Orleans.
WINE EXPERT SAYS ONE COMMON HABIT COULD BE SABOTAGING EVERY SIP
In the study, participants reported their alcohol intake as never/occasional, low, moderate or high.
High consumption was defined as more than 40 grams per day for men (about three standard drinks) and more than 20 grams per day for women (about 1.4 standard drinks).
Heavy drinking has been shown to raise mortality risk, but, at lower levels, what’s in your glass may also matter, a new study suggests. (iStock)

Participants with high alcohol consumption had a 24% higher risk of all-cause death, 36% higher risk of cancer death and 14% higher risk of cardiovascular death when compared to people who never or occasionally drank, according to the study findings.
With low or moderate alcohol consumption, however, the mortality risk appeared to differ according to the type of beverage.
AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

Spirits, beer and cider were associated with significantly higher mortality, the researchers found, while the same amount of wine intake was linked to significantly lower mortality. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death than those who never or occasionally drank.
Conversely, those who drank low amounts of spirits, beer or cider were found to have a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.
In new research of data from 340,924 participants in the UK Biobank, wine was linked to lower mortality, while beer and spirits were tied to higher death risk. (iStock)

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," Dr. Zhangling Chen, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author, said in a press release.
"These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed but also on the type of beverage."
"Not everybody should have daily consumption of an alcoholic substance, whether it's wine, beer or certain liquors."

One potential reason for wine’s lower mortality association could be that it contains compounds such as polyphenols and antioxidants, which could have beneficial effects on blood vessels, inflammation and cardiovascular health, the researchers noted.

Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles addiction specialist and chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery, said the study’s information is "helpful" but cautioned against broadly applying the findings to individuals, particularly those with a history of substance misuse.
HOME COCKTAIL MAKER SAYS GEN Z ISN'T GIVING UP ALCOHOL — THEY'RE CHANGING HOW THEY DRINK
While certain ingredients or substances might help someone with a specific issue, she expressed her concern when it comes to mental health issues and addiction.

"When we hear these stories or get this research, it becomes a ‘black and white’ larger generalization for the population, and we want to be careful with that," Steinman, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
Different substances have different levels of alcohol in them, and each person metabolizes alcohol differently, the expert noted. (iStock)

"Not everybody should have daily consumption of an alcoholic substance, whether it's wine, beer or certain liquors. … If there's someone who’s struggling with substances, then they really shouldn't be having it at all."
Different substances have different levels of alcohol in them, and each person metabolizes alcohol uniquely, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"All those kinds of things are so specific to one person or a small sect of people," she said. "So, we want to make sure anytime there's research given about something, that we're not taking it as a society and saying, ‘Let's do this,’ and not keeping it as black and white.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Overall, more is not better, but also the higher potency of alcohol and higher percentages of alcohol is going to affect people negatively as well."
Steinman recommended consulting with a medical professional for individual guidance.
There was the chance that wine drinkers may have different dietary or other lifestyle habits that could impact their health outcomes, the researchers noted. (iStock)

The researchers acknowledged some limitations of the study. Because it was observational in design, the study could not prove that drinking wine led to lower mortality or that other alcoholic beverages directly caused higher mortality.
Also, the participants reported their baseline alcohol intake at the start of the study, which means any changes in drinking patterns during the follow-up period were not recorded.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
There was also the chance that wine drinkers may have different dietary or other lifestyle habits that could affect their health outcomes, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The UK Biobank participants also tend to be healthier than the overall population, which could limit the ability for the finding to be generalized to wider populations.
The authors called for high-quality randomized studies to confirm the differences in how drinking habits reflect mortality risk.

title: 5-step sleep reset could promote healthy weight loss, nutritionist says
summary: A dietitian's seven-day SLEEP reset helped test panelists lose up to seven pounds by combining meal timing, light exposure and blood sugar balance.
story: Registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade, author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," reveals how meal timing, natural light exposure and nighttime routines can help support healthier circadian patterns.
One weekly routine could help foster better sleep and promote healthy weight loss, according to a New Jersey-based registered dietitian.
Erin Palinski-Wade, who is also a certified diabetes care specialist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," shared her "seven-day reset" in an interview with Fox News Digital.
The reset combines sleep, nutrition and lifestyle strategies into a five-part system represented by the acronym SLEEP.
SKIPPING SLEEP MAY PACK ON POUNDS FASTER THAN YOU THINK, NEW STUDY FINDS
In a test panel conducted in connection with her seven-day program, Palinski-Wade said participants reported improvements in sleep, blood sugar and weight.
Registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade joined Fox News Digital for an interview to discuss her new book, "The Sleepdemic Solution." (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

Experts recommend consulting a healthcare professional for individualized guidance before making significant changes to diet, sleep or lifestyle habits, particularly for those with underlying health conditions.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Palinski-Wade emphasized that results varied among participants with different sleep challenges. The panel included shift workers, mothers and people with long-term insomnia.

Despite those differences, within the first two to three days, the expert said people "across the board" reported falling asleep faster, getting higher-quality sleep and feeling more rested the next day.
People "across the board" reported falling asleep faster, getting higher-quality sleep and feeling more rested the next day, the nutritionist said. (iStock)
Panelists with pre-existing insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes also reported improvements in blood sugar levels, Palinski-Wade said.
"Once they were resting better and those stress hormones were reduced, and the body was getting the rest it needed, we were seeing better balanced blood sugar throughout the day," she noted.
Participants also reported improvements in hunger and satiety.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
"They weren't having those cravings, especially in the evening, especially those sugar cravings," Palinski-Wade said. "When they were eating, they were feeling more satisfied."
"I had a few test panel members who lost as much as seven pounds in the first seven days," she said, noting that some of the loss was water weight.
Participants reported reductions in weight and waist circumference and improvements in blood sugar, sleep and next-day energy.
The Reset
Below, Palinski-Wade breaks down the five components of the SLEEP system.
S – Set your rhythm
Setting a rhythm involves timing meals consistently to help improve sleep. This means avoiding skipped meals, which can lead to blood sugar fluctuations throughout the day. (iStock)
Setting a rhythm involves timing meals consistently to help improve sleep. This means avoiding skipped meals, which can lead to blood sugar fluctuations throughout the day, Palinski-Wade said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We want to be fueling our body all throughout the day so that our body is expecting to sleep in the evening," she said.
Skipping meals and consuming excess food and calories in the evening tells the body that it's time to burn energy, which is not going to be conducive to sleep, according to the expert.
L – Leveraging light
Getting exposure to sunlight in the morning and limiting exposure at night will help set a natural circadian rhythm. (iStock)
Exposure to sunlight within the first hour of waking can help set the body’s circadian rhythm, Palinski-Wade noted.
"When your body gets that natural light, whether you go outside or put your desk by the window, that's helping your body get more in tune with that rhythm where you're awake," she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In the evening, Palinski-Wade recommends dimming the lights and avoiding electronics and bright overhead lighting, which helps the body wind down and prepare for restful sleep.
E – Eat with intention
Eating with intention means choosing meals and snacks with nutrients that support healthy sleep, the expert said. (iStock)
Eating with intention means choosing meals and snacks with nutrients that support healthy sleep, according to Palinski-Wade.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Whether it's serotonin and tryptophan, anti-inflammatory nutrients, we want to make sure that we're eating with intention, so we're giving our body the building blocks it needs to create sleep in the evening," she said.
E – Evening out blood sugar
Palinski-Wade recommends combining lean protein, healthy fats and fiber to help keep blood sugar steady throughout the day and support better sleep.
P – Powering down your night
Powering down electronics at night will help induce more sound sleep. (iStock)
Powering down involves creating a consistent nighttime routine, including limiting electronics and caffeine and maintaining regular sleep and wake times, according to Palinski-Wade.
"That also applies to having a set bedtime and a set wake time ... in those seven days to reset that circadian rhythm, so we can have the best results moving forward," she said.
"We want to be fueling our body all throughout the day so that our body is expecting to sleep in the evening."
For those who are "trying everything," like diet and exercise, without seeing results, Palinski-Wade stressed that it is "not because you don’t have enough willpower."

"It could just be your biology working against you, and many times it's as simple as improving your sleep," she said. "If you start to improve your sleep within just a few days, you can see major changes in how you feel, how your body is processing food, in your metabolism, and then ultimately in your body weight."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
External research by the National Institutes of Health has also linked adequate sleep with appetite regulation and healthy weight management.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute states that sleep helps regulate hormones involved in hunger and fullness, while sleep deficiency can affect the body's response to insulin and has been linked to a higher risk of obesity.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Birth order linked to 150 health conditions in study of 10 million American siblings
summary: First-born children showed higher rates of autism, ADHD and food allergies, while second-born siblings faced more substance use disorders and migraines.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel analyzes a study of 10 million children indicating that birth order shapes health risks. First-born siblings show higher rates of ADHD and autism, while second-born children face increased risks for migraines. Siegel joins Ainsley Earhardt to explain how parental attention and immune system development drive these stark differences.
Whether someone is the older or younger sibling may be linked to certain health outcomes later in life, according to a massive new study.

Analyzing medical data from 10 million U.S. siblings over two decades, researchers from the University of Chicago and Columbia University found links suggesting that birth order may be connected to specific long-term health risks.
Researchers examined 569 disease categories across families and among siblings, identifying 150 conditions that were significantly associated with birth order.
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
First-born children showed a higher likelihood of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric diagnoses, including autism, ADHD, Tourette's and OCD, as well as immune-allergic conditions like food allergies.
Second-born children were statistically more prone to migraines, shingles, substance use disorders and gastrointestinal issues like gastritis.
First-born children showed higher rates of neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, ADHD, Tourette's and OCD, as well as an increased prevalence of allergies. (iStock)
Discussing the findings on "Fox & Friends," Dr. Marc Siegel, senior medical analyst for Fox News, noted the value of such a wide-scale study.
"I love this study because it opens a lot of questions more than it gives answers, but I think I have some answers," the doctor said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Regarding the heightened prevalence of ADHD among first-borns, Siegel offered his own hypothesis about parental behavior.
"My theory, they get more stimuli. The parents are like hovering over them, helicoptering them ... and they don't know where to look," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Addressing the disparities in allergic conditions, Siegel pointed to early environmental exposure, stating, "I think it's because the firstborn's immune system hasn't seen the environment before. And if it's not set properly, you get an allergy."
Differences in parental focus, early microbial exposure and maternal biological changes between pregnancies could help explain the distinct health patterns, the doctor said. (iStock)
Siegel also touched on biological and psychological factors when evaluating differences between siblings.
"I think the womb changes after you have your first child, and the second child gets a womb that's already been used. So therefore, it's more set for it," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Regarding the higher rate of substance use disorders among second-born children, Siegel suggested emotional drivers, saying, "it may be the same idea: 'I want attention. I'm looking for attention. I wanna do something to get a rise out of you.'"
While the research highlights patterns across a large population, the study comes with limitations.
The study highlights population-level statistical correlations, but it does not prove that birth order directly causes any specific medical condition. (iStock)
The findings demonstrate correlations rather than direct causation, meaning the trends don't necessarily stem from physiological changes, early microbial exposures or social dynamics.

Additionally, the data relies on commercial health insurance claims, which can reflect differences in diagnosis, healthcare-seeking behavior and parental attention rather than true biological functions alone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Factors such as the age of parents between births and varying age gaps between siblings also complicate these associations. Ultimately, researchers emphasized that birth order serves as a modest population-level risk marker rather than a definitive health predictor.
The research was published in the journal Nature Health.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Cancer warning signs may appear in DNA years before blood tests detect trouble
summary: DNA changes in certain blood cancers may signal progression to acute myeloid leukemia or myelofibrosis years before routine blood tests detect them.
story: Dr. Trisha Pasricha, a Harvard Medical School assistant professor, discusses a newly FDA-approved blood test designed to detect colorectal cancer early with Ainsley Earhardt.
DNA patterns could reveal whether certain blood cancers are progressing years before routine tests detect those changes, new research suggests.

A study, published in the journal Cancer Discovery by the American Association for Cancer Research, followed 30 people with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), a group of blood cancers in which the bone marrow produces too many blood cells.

Researchers monitored DNA in the patients’ blood and bone marrow for genetic changes, then examined whether those changes were associated with blood counts, stable disease or progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia.
MAN WHO BEAT RARE CANCER CELEBRATES BY CANOEING 2,000 MILES WITH HIS DOG

People who stayed stable often had stable DNA without cancer-related genetic changes. This suggests a genetically "quiet" MPN is more likely to remain stable, according to the researchers, who are based at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute in the U.K.
Patients whose disease remained stable often showed little genetic change over time, the researchers found. (iStock)
Patients whose disease worsened often showed DNA changes years before routine blood tests detected progression as new groups of abnormal cells emerged and grew, according to the study.
Nine participants eventually developed acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but their disease did not progress in the same way.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In some, MPN cells gradually accumulated harmful mutations; in others, the leukemia appeared to arise from a separate group of abnormal blood cells. Similar differences were seen in those who developed myelofibrosis.

The researchers also found that hydroxyurea, a common medication used to control blood counts in people with MPN, leaves a recognizable pattern of small DNA changes in blood cells. There was no evidence, however, that the drug causes leukemia. A similar pattern was linked to azacitidine, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers.
Genetic changes sometimes emerged years before routine blood tests detected disease progression, the study found. (iStock)
Three participants had "triple-negative" essential thrombocythemia, a condition generally classified as a blood cancer, yet researchers found no genetic signs of cancer in their samples.
The finding raises the possibility that some patients given this diagnosis may not have a malignant disease and may not need long-term cancer treatment.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The study was limited by its small sample size, and the findings show associations rather than establishing cause and effect.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Abhishek Chilkulwar, an oncologist with Orlando Health, noted that most people with MPNs can live with them "for decades."

"This research shows that these blood cancers may reveal their future course in a person's DNA long before any symptoms appear, a genuinely exciting scientific insight, and a step toward precision medicine in blood cancer care," an expert said. (iStock)

The doctor, who was not involved in the study, called the findings a "striking demonstration" that DNA changes may signal the development of certain cancers a decade before diagnosis and that their future path may "already be 'written' in a patient's cells long before doctors can see any outward sign."

"More broadly, it's an early example of what could become precision medicine for blood cancer prevention, using a patient's own genetic data to predict risk years in advance, then someday intervening before disease progression rather than only treating it after the fact," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"That's the direction this kind of research is pointing, even though the tools to act on it aren't fully built yet."

The results suggest that periodically retesting a patient’s DNA over time could give doctors a "heads-up" that someone’s disease is heading in a dangerous direction, "well before" it shows up in routine blood work, Chilkulwar added.

The next step, according to one doctor, would be pairing early genetic detection with drugs designed to act on those specific mutations, which could potentially prevent or delay disease progression. (iStock)

"In the near term, the realistic use of this is modest: closer monitoring, not new treatment," he said. "A patient found to have acquired a high-risk mutation could be shifted to more frequent blood counts and, if warranted, more frequent bone marrow checks. So, if progression does happen, it's caught earlier.

"It would not be a reason to start stem cell transplant evaluation; transplant is a serious procedure appropriately reserved for patients who have actually progressed to myelofibrosis or AML, not something to prepare for based on a mutation that might cause problems years down the line," the doctor cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The next step, Chilkulwar said, would be pairing early genetic detection with drugs targeting those specific mutations, potentially preventing or delaying disease progression.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Deadly disease outbreak kills 2,000 as experts reveal what Americans should know
summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed over 2,000 people. Experts say the average American faces very little threat while sharing key information.
story: David Wohl, MD, a professor of medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, spoke with Fox News Digital about whether the fast-growing Ebola virus poses a risk to Americans.

As the death toll from the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) surpasses 2,000 people, infectious disease experts say Americans should remain aware of the humanitarian crisis overseas while understanding the reality of domestic risk.
The virus has spread rapidly across parts of eastern and northeastern DRC, with earlier cross-border cases in Uganda. Published government data shows a total of 4,381 confirmed cases.

"There's a lot of people who live there. So this is not breaking out in a town of 50, but in rural cities of hundreds of thousands," David Wohl, M.D., a professor of medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told Fox News Digital.
FAUCI TEXTS SUGGEST OFFICIALS WERE ‘TOO SLOW TO PIVOT' AMID PANDEMIC, SAYS DR MARC SIEGEL
"Compared to previous outbreaks, the pace at which this is moving is unprecedented," he went on.
"The slope is just so catastrophic, with more and more people getting infected at a very significant pace without much slowing down."
A healthcare worker prepares a patient's blood sample for testing at Bunia General Hospital in Bunia, Congo, on June 11, 2026. (Moses Sawasawa/AP Photo)
Controlling transmission has proven particularly difficult in the DRC due to what Wohl calls a "perfect storm" of adverse conditions.
MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL
Dense populations and limited access can complicate efforts to deliver medical care, track contacts and establish quarantine protocols, he noted.
"There's conflict in and around these areas, which makes getting in and out of them … really tough," Wohl said.
What the outbreak means for Americans
Despite the escalating death toll in Africa, health officials emphasize that the average American faces very little threat from Ebola.

"This is not something that I think the average person has to worry about acquiring here in the United States," Wohl said, noting that transmission requires close physical contact with bodily fluids from a severely ill or deceased individual.

The current outbreak involves the Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain, which is genetically distinct from the 2014 Zaire strain and renders standard past treatments and vaccines less effective, the doctor said. (iStock)
"It doesn’t travel across the air and across a room," he added.

Even during the massive 2014 West Africa outbreak, which Wohl said infected more than 28,000 people, only four Ebola cases were diagnosed in the U.S. Two were imported cases, and two nurses contracted the virus while caring for an infected patient in Dallas, according to the CDC.
"The average person who gets a headache or a fever does not need to worry about Ebola."
Several other Ebola patients who had been infected and diagnosed overseas were medically evacuated to the U.S. for treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We just have so much better public health, healthcare systems, hygiene, access," Wohl said. "It's a very different environment."
Viruses such as measles, influenza, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 pose more immediate public health concerns for Americans, he added.

Researchers are actively evaluating novel therapeutics in clinical trials and leveraging advanced mRNA technology to rapidly develop targeted vaccines for the Bundibugyo strain. (Dirole Lotsima Dieudonne/AP)
"The average person who gets a headache or a fever does not need to worry about Ebola," the doctor said.
For the U.S., potential concerns include the risk to healthcare providers traveling to Africa to assist with containment efforts and the possibility of further instability in the region.
The treatment challenge
Medical researchers are also navigating challenges with virus variants, according to Wohl.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

While treatments and vaccines were successfully deployed against the Zaire strain during the 2014 crisis, the doctor said the Bundibugyo virus circulating in parts of the DRC is genetically different.
As a result, approved Ebola therapeutics are not approved for Bundibugyo-related disease, and their effectiveness against it has not been established.

The average American faces virtually no threat of catching Ebola domestically because transmission requires direct contact with bodily fluids and the U.S. maintains robust public health systems, the doctor said. (iStock)
Researchers are actively evaluating new treatments and vaccine candidates for Bundibugyo virus, Wohl said.
Emerging technologies, including mRNA platforms, could potentially help researchers more rapidly develop vaccines against specific viral threats, according to the doctor.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Global agencies, including the World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, continue to monitor the region closely.
Wohl emphasized that international support and resource deployment remain critical to stopping the surge.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"This is a fire that’s raging that continues to be out of control," Wohl said.
"There’s lots of people suffering ... and I think more can be done."
