title: Teacher busted under Kentucky's new anti-grooming law as advocate warns schools can't ignore red flags
summary: Kentucky's new grooming law lands its first arrest after a school employee allegedly had an improper relationship with a minor student in Graves County.
story: Kentucky child advocate Laura Wills-Coppelman breaks down how grooming can begin with seemingly explainable behavior, the red flags adults should not ignore and what the state’s new law means for protecting children.

What can look like innocent attention toward a child can mask something far more sinister, a Kentucky advocate warns as the state’s new grooming law lands its first arrest just weeks after taking effect.

Laura Wills-Coppelman, founder of ICKY, or Institutional Complicity Kentucky, told Fox News Digital that she sees the arrest as evidence of what the new grooming offense was designed to provide — an earlier opportunity for authorities to potentially intervene before alleged conduct escalates into sexual abuse.

"For the first time, Kentucky has a legal ability to intervene in a situation where a child could potentially face irreversible harm," Wills-Coppelman said. "It's a massive step forward in an effort to prevent child abuse."
KENTUCKY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER ACCUSED OF CROSSING THE LINE WITH STUDENT, ARRESTED UNDER NEW ANTI-GROOMING LAW
Authorities arrested Graves County Middle School teacher Sadie Flores after an investigation into an alleged improper relationship with a student. (Graves County Detention Center)
The new law was invoked just weeks after taking effect July 15, when 25-year-old Sadie M. Flores of Mayfield was arrested and charged with grooming a minor, a Class D felony.
The Graves County Sheriff's Office said Flores, an employee at Graves County Middle School, allegedly had an improper relationship with a minor student in the district.
The allegation was initially reported to Graves County Schools, which immediately turned the information over to the sheriff's office, according to authorities.
Detectives seized electronic records, conducted interviews and took other investigative steps before interviewing Flores and arresting her around 3:30 p.m., the sheriff's office said.
HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP

A woman poses with a sign as members of the public queue to enter a council meeting during a protest calling for justice for victims of sexual abuse and grooming gangs, outside the council offices at City Centre on Jan. 20, 2025 in Oldham, England. (Anthony Devlin/Getty Images)
Wills-Coppelman cautioned against drawing conclusions about Flores, saying the evidence and allegations in the case must now be evaluated through the court system.
But she said the arrest illustrates the significance of creating an earlier point at which authorities can investigate conduct that may precede abuse.
Wills-Coppelman said one of the biggest misconceptions about grooming is the belief that one questionable interaction can be viewed in isolation and labeled grooming.
Instead, she said grooming often unfolds gradually, with behaviors that may seem explainable on their own becoming increasingly concerning when they form a pattern.
"Grooming is a pattern of behavior that is intended to build trust, erode boundaries, and create conditions for a child to be exploited or abused," she said.
Potential warning signs, she said, can include excessive attention or favoritism, gifts, secrecy and increasingly isolating a child from other trusted adults or peers.
Individually, some of those behaviors may have innocent explanations. The alarm, Wills-Coppelman said, comes when adults begin seeing them develop into a broader pattern over time.
And from the child's perspective, she warned, grooming may not feel threatening at all.
TEACHER WHO SERVED AS GOP STATE LAWMAKER ALLEGEDLY USED ROBLOX TO LURE STUDENT INTO SEXUAL RELATIONSHIP

Brandon Matthews says he remains unable to determine whether his children could be expected to share school restrooms or locker rooms with members of the opposite sex, according to court filings. (Houston Chronicle via Getty Imag)
"Grooming is a form of manipulation," Wills-Coppelman said, explaining that a child may instead feel "special and seen and validated" by the attention.
"It doesn't often register as dangerous until it's too late," she said.
For parents watching from the outside, however, the same relationship may begin setting off alarm bells.
"Why does this adult need so much access? Why are they being isolated so much? Why so much excessive attention?" Wills-Coppelman said parents should ask themselves.
Wills-Coppelman said survivors her organization has spoken with have repeatedly described another troubling pattern — adults who recognized something felt wrong but did not speak up at the time.

"A lot of people, bystanders, in their situations in retrospect look back and say, 'I had an icky feeling,'" she said. "I saw something or I heard something that made me feel uncomfortable. I wish I would have spoken up."
She stressed that reporting concerning conduct is not the same as declaring someone guilty.
Instead, she said, authorities are responsible for examining the evidence and determining whether conduct meets the threshold for criminal charges.
"The point of awareness can be the point of prevention," Wills-Coppelman said.

That distinction has become particularly important amid concerns that ordinary interactions between teachers, coaches, youth leaders and children could be mistaken for grooming. The law makes clear that legitimate school, work and volunteer-related communications are not what it is designed to criminalize.
Wills-Coppelman rejected that characterization, calling appropriate adult-child boundaries "common sense."
"Healthy adult-child mentorship respects appropriate boundaries. Grooming erodes them," she said.
NEW MISSISSIPPI LAW EXPANDS DEATH PENALTY TO INCLUDE INMATES ON CHILD SEXUAL BATTERY CONVICTIONS
The president of a Georgia teachers union told Fox News Digital that public schools have "been grossly underfunded" due to school choice policies. (Getty Images)
"The intent of the law is to create an earlier intervention point, not to criminalize ordinary relationships between adults and children."
Wills-Coppelman said the legislation received unanimous support in both chambers of the Kentucky legislature and bipartisan backing.

House Bill 4, primarily sponsored by Republican state Rep. Marianne Proctor, passed the House 98-0 and the Senate 38-0 before the House unanimously approved the Senate's changes. Gov. Andy Beshear signed it into law April 10.
"This is not a political issue. This is a human issue," she said.
RITZY PRIVATE ACADEMY ATTENDED BY KARDASHIAN KIDS FACES TRIAL IN BIZARRE 'KISSING CLUB' SCANDAL

Kentucky's new grooming law is putting a spotlight on warning signs, appropriate adult-child boundaries and early intervention in schools. (Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)
The pushback she has encountered, she said, has instead largely centered on due process and concerns about what happens after someone reports suspected grooming.

Wills-Coppelman said due process remains an essential part of the law because a report alone does not automatically trigger criminal charges. Investigators must evaluate the evidence before determining whether charges are warranted.
"We can preserve and respect due process and also prioritize the prevention of abuse and the protection of our children," she said. "They are not competing principles."
Wills-Coppelman said she ultimately hopes the law results not in more arrests, but fewer children ever reaching the point where alleged abuse occurs.
"The ultimate goal of this law is not more prosecutions," she said. "It's earlier recognition, awareness and understanding of what these behaviors look like and ultimately prevention."
For Wills-Coppelman, passing the grooming law is only one piece of a larger fight.

She said she now wants Kentucky's educator code of ethics brought into alignment with the new law and is pushing for greater accountability when people in positions of authority become aware of disturbing patterns but fail to report them.
That includes situations in which institutions attempt to handle serious allegations internally rather than referring them to the appropriate authorities, she said.

"My efforts are focused not only on the obvious villain, which is the perpetrator in these cases, but also turning some attention toward enablers, systems and institutions and the people within those organizations that had the capacity and the ability to take action and made a deliberate choice to not do so," Wills-Coppelman said.
In the Flores case, Graves County Schools said administrators contacted law enforcement immediately after becoming aware of the allegation.
Sadie Flores, a teacher at Graves County Middle School, was arrested after authorities charged her with felony grooming of a minor. (X/@KyDeptofEd/Graves County Detention Center)
Superintendent Matt Madding said the district has since been informed that charges were filed against the teacher and pledged continued cooperation with investigators.
"We take any allegation involving the safety of a child or the professional conduct of an employee extremely seriously," Madding said in a statement.
The district said it is limited in what it can disclose because the case remains an ongoing legal and personnel matter.
Wills-Coppelman hopes Kentucky's approach eventually reaches far beyond the state.
She said Ohio has legislation similar to Kentucky's, but her goal is for protections against grooming to ultimately become a nationwide standard.
"A child's protection from grooming and abuse should never depend on geography," she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For now, Kentucky's first case under the new law will move through the courts, while the legislation itself faces its first real-world test.
And for Wills-Coppelman, its success won't ultimately be measured by the number of people put behind bars.
"If it prevents even one child from the horrific consequences of abuse," she said, "that makes it all worth it."

title: Mexican national faces federal charges after CBP finds $238K in fentanyl inside electric moped
summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers found seven packages of fentanyl hidden inside an electric moped at the San Ysidro border crossing.
story: President Donald Trump highlights a massive drop in fentanyl deaths and illegal drugs entering the country by sea in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher. Trump claims border security measures have reduced maritime drug smuggling by 97 percent, saving thousands of lives. The president questions why mainstream media outlets are not covering this positive development at the southern border.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers discovered more than 16 pounds of fentanyl – with an estimated street value of nearly $240,000 – hidden inside an electric moped attempting to enter the U.S. at the southern border, authorities said.
CBP said a 22-year-old Mexican national is facing federal charges following the seizure earlier this month.
Officials said the man was driving a 2024 Revoo electric moped when he applied for admission into the United States on Aug. 3 and was referred for a secondary inspection.
CBP SEIZES MASSIVE METH HAUL WORTH MILLIONS STASHED IN SECRET TILE SHIPMENT

National Guard officers install a checkpoint to inspect motorists before crossing into the United States at San Ysidro Port of Entry on February 6, 2025, in Tijuana, Mexico. (Francisco Vega/Getty Images)
According to CBP, officers used a nonintrusive imaging system that detected anomalies beneath the rear of the moped.
After a CBP canine alerted officers to the area, a physical inspection uncovered seven packages containing 16.53 pounds of white fentanyl powder with an estimated street value of $238,032.
"Smugglers are employing innovative tactics to smuggle lethal drugs into the country," San Ysidro Port Director Mariza Marin said in a statement.
"Despite these challenges, officers remain vigilant while effectively utilizing their training, canine resources, and nonintrusive technology to thwart these smuggling attempts," Marin added.
TWO SUSPECTS ARRESTED AFTER CRASHING THROUGH CAMP PENDLETON GATE WITH 112 POUNDS OF COCAINE AND FENTANYL

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers discovered more than 16 pounds of fentanyl hidden inside an electric moped during a secondary inspection, authorities said. (U.S. Customs and Border Protection)
CBP officers seized the fentanyl, moped, a GPS tracker and a cellphone.
The driver was arrested and will face federal prosecution for narcotics importation, officials said.
The seizure comes after CBP officers stopped two separate vehicles and confiscated more than $300,000 worth of narcotics in a single day in May.
Officers at the San Ysidro Port of Entry referred a 2013 Honda Civic for secondary inspection on May 17 after a scan detected anomalies in the vehicle's firewall.
FEDS SEIZE $6.4M WORTH OF COCAINE ABOARD OIL TANKER AT PORT OF LOS ANGELES, ARREST SUSPECTED CARTEL SMUGGLER
CBP officers seized seven packages containing 16.53 pounds of fentanyl powder with an estimated street value of $238,032, according to authorities. (U.S. Customs and Border Protection)
Officials discovered six packages containing white fentanyl powder worth an estimated $113,600, along with 8.4 pounds of cocaine valued at approximately $161,600.
That same day at the Calexico East Port of Entry, about 100 miles away, officers referred a 2011 Nissan Cube for secondary inspection.
A scan detected anomalies in the vehicle's flooring, where officers subsequently discovered 63 packages of methamphetamine, according to CBP.

title: NYPD cop found guilty of chokehold in first conviction since restraint tactic banned after George Floyd death
summary: A NYPD officer is the first convicted under New York City's chokehold ban enacted after George Floyd's killing, facing up to seven years in prison.
story: NYPD Detectives' Endowment Association President Scott Munro criticizes the reported attempted use of NYPD detectives to secure Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, during her personal travel to Syria, a country currently under a Level 4 travel advisory.

A New York City Police Department officer was found guilty on Thursday of strangulation and using a prohibited chokehold, marking the first time an NYPD officer was convicted under the city's 2020 chokehold ban, enacted after the 2020 murder of George Floyd by Minneapolis police Officer Derek Chauvin.

Omar Habib was convicted of the misdemeanor established under the law prohibiting certain restraint tactics by police officers. He was also found guilty of second-degree felony strangulation and third-degree misdemeanor assault.
The felony strangulation conviction carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison. Bronx Criminal Supreme Court Judge Cynthia Isales ordered him held without bail.
Habib, who was earlier suspended without pay, was terminated from the police department following his felony conviction after serving since 2007. The NYPD said his termination was required by law.
NYC JUDGE SEEKS TO MAKE EXAMPLE OF OFFICER WHO THREW COOLER AT FLEEING SUSPECT, CAUSING FATAL CRASH
A New York City Police Department officer was found guilty on Thursday of strangulation and using a prohibited chokehold. (Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

He was responding to a 911 call at a Bronx catering hall on July 28, 2023, when a drunk and disorderly man resisted arrest, according to Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark. Prosecutors said Habib put the man in a chokehold so tight that it impeded his breathing and circulation and caused him to lose consciousness.
Habib’s attorney argued during the trial that other factors could have caused the man to pass out, such as drinking without eating enough food.
Before his arrest, Habib had a history of substantiated misconduct complaints about excessive use of force and abusing his authority.

The Civilian Complaint Review Board substantiated an allegation that Habib used a chokehold in a separate 2017 encounter. Habib was also accused of lying under oath and tampering with evidence in a 2016 gun raid, resulting in several defendants withdrawing their guilty pleas.

Before his arrest, Omar Habib had a history of substantiated misconduct complaints about excessive use of force and abusing his authority. (Luiz C. Ribeiro for New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
The president of the Police Benevolent Association of the City of New York, Patrick Hendry, denounced Thursday's verdict.

The officer's conviction was "further proof of a grim reality: every second police officers spend on this job puts them at risk of criminal prosecution, and pervasive anti-police propaganda has made it incredibly difficult to receive a fair trial," the police union boss said, according to the New York Daily News.

Habib was charged under a 2020 city law that was passed after Floyd's murder in May of that year, sparking racial justice protests and a push for police accountability across the country. The New York City measure criminalizes chokeholds and certain forms of pressure on an arrestee’s chest or back that compress the diaphragm while an officer is making or attempting an arrest.
MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS
Omar Habib was charged under a 2020 city law that was passed after George Floyd's murder in May of that year, sparking racial justice protests. (Emilie Richardson/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The law was challenged by police unions but was upheld by New York state’s highest court in 2023.
Police use of chokeholds was already prohibited in most cases by NYPD policy when the law was enacted, but officers who used them were almost never prosecuted.

NYPD Officer Daniel Pantaleo lost his job but faced no criminal charges after a department disciplinary proceeding found that he used a prohibited chokehold on Eric Garner, who died during a 2014 arrest after repeatedly saying he could not breathe, fueling protests over police use of force.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Murder suspect captured following 45-day, 3-state manhunt after victim discovered in shallow grave
summary: Isabelle Johnson was arrested in Cottondale after a 45-day multistate manhunt spanning Florida, Georgia and Alabama for the suspect accused in Jason Coulthart's murder.
story: The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses the active search for Isabelle Rose Johnson, dubbed a 'master manipulator,' in connection with the gruesome murder of Jason Coulthart in Florida.
Murder suspect Isabelle Johnson was arrested Thursday following a weekslong multistate manhunt spanning Florida, Georgia and Alabama, authorities said.
A U.S. Marshals task force arrested Johnson, 38, at a home in Cottondale, about an hour west of Tallahassee, according to the Walton County Sheriff's Office.
She was wanted on a murder charge in the death of Jason Coulthart, whose body was found buried in a shallow grave in Florida on June 25.

Authorities said Johnson was taken into custody without incident Thursday afternoon, capping a 45-day manhunt. She was booked into the Jackson County Jail and is expected to be extradited to Walton County. Officials said she could face additional charges.
ACCUSED KILLER'S ALLEGED DISGUISES UNRAVEL AS SHERIFF RELEASES NEW CLUES IN MONTH-LONG MANHUNT
Law enforcement officers took Isabelle Johnson into custody Thursday following a weeks-long search that spanned Florida, Georgia and Alabama. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)
"We got her," the sheriff's office said. "Isabelle Johnson is in custody."
Officials said the arrest stemmed from information developed by the Walton County Sheriff's Office Cyber Crimes Unit about Johnson's whereabouts.
Jackson County Sheriff Donald Edenfield said that after receiving the information, his deputies and members of the task force responded to an address off Peanut Road, just outside Cottondale.
Walton County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Dustin Cosson praised the cooperation among local, state and federal law enforcement agencies that led to Johnson's arrest.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN
A U.S. Marshals task force arrested murder suspect Isabelle Johnson at a home near Cottondale, Florida, on Thursday, according to authorities. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)
"It's absolutely a good day," Cosson said. "It's really important, again, just want to stress to the public. She's here, she's in custody."
"We can't express the amount of appreciation for the work that's been done," he added.

Cosson said investigators put in "tons and tons of man hours" during the roughly 45-day search for Johnson, while noting that the broader investigation has involved more than 40 subpoenas and over 20 search warrants.
Coulthart was reported missing May 24 after he was last seen leaving the College Condominiums on East College Boulevard in Niceville.
FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED AFTER SUSPECTED HUMAN REMAINS FOUND BURIED AT PROPERTY WHERE HIS FATHER LIVED

Isabelle Johnson, 38, was taken into custody Thursday after a roughly 45-day manhunt spanning Florida, Georgia and Alabama. She is charged with murder in the death of Jason Coulthart. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)

During the missing-person investigation, detectives developed information that led authorities to a property off Sunset Lane in Freeport. Investigators obtained a search warrant and found Coulthart's body buried in a shallow grave on June 25, according to the sheriff's office.

Five other people have been arrested in connection with the case. Michael Ray White, Kathleen Morris, Bobbi Wagstaff, Martin Leaverton and Sandra Leaverton have been charged with accessory to a capital felony after the fact.
Authorities said Thursday that they expect additional arrests in the case.
Law enforcement escorts Isabelle Johnson following her arrest Thursday in Cottondale, Florida. Johnson is charged with murder in the death of Jason Coulthart. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)
During the manhunt, the Walton County Sheriff's Office described Johnson as "cunning" and a "master manipulator" while warning anyone who may have been helping her to stop.
Officials said additional details surrounding Johnson's arrest could not immediately be released because the investigation remains active.

title: Live bullet found aboard United flight forces passengers off plane for security sweep at Denver airport
summary: A live bullet discovered aboard United Airlines Flight 1302 forced 178 passengers to deplane the Boeing 737-900 at Denver International Airport.
story: 'JFK Jr.'s Fatal Flight: ‘The Last Witness’ author Kyle Bailey joins ‘Fox Report’ to discuss the Frontier Airlines incident at Denver International Airport.

A United Airlines flight from Denver to San Diego was delayed Thursday after a live bullet was discovered aboard the plane before departure, prompting passengers to deplane while security personnel swept the aircraft.

United Flight 1302 was preparing to leave Denver International Airport when the bullet was found during routine checks before the plane taxied to the runway, according to FOX31 Denver, which had a member of its news team aboard the flight.
"The bad news is we found a live round, a bullet on the airplane," the speaker said. "This is a security breach here, and everybody is going to have to deplane."
PASSENGER ALLEGEDLY BOARDS FLIGHT WITH FAKE BOARDING PASS, FORCING PLANE BACK TO GATE

A United Airlines plane at Denver International Airport March 23, 2026. A separate United flight was delayed Aug. 13 after a live bullet was discovered aboard the aircraft before departure. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
Passengers were instructed to leave the Boeing 737-900 with their carry-on bags while security personnel searched the aircraft.

"We need everybody to deplane the aircraft with your carry-on bags. We’re going to have to carry out a security sweep of the aircraft after the plane is empty," the speaker said. "We apologize for this."
The crew said at the time that it did not know how the bullet got aboard the aircraft or where it came from, according to FOX31.
United Airlines confirmed the incident in a statement to Fox News Digital.
UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT

Travelers move through a concourse at Denver International Airport. A United Airlines flight departing Denver was delayed Thursday after a live bullet was discovered aboard the aircraft. (Denver International Airport)

"United flight 1302 from Denver to San Diego underwent a security sweep after a bullet was discovered on board prior to the flight’s departure," a spokesperson wrote. "Security personnel cleared the aircraft, which later departed for San Diego."
United said the Boeing 737-900 was carrying 178 passengers and six crew members. The airline directed additional questions about the incident to the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).
Flight 1302 had been scheduled to depart Denver at about 1:25 p.m. It took off at about 3:41 p.m., more than two hours after its scheduled departure, according to FOX31.
It was not immediately clear who the bullet belonged to or how it ended up on the aircraft.

A United Airlines Boeing 737-900 at Newark Liberty International Airport Jan. 15, 2026. A United 737-900 carrying 178 passengers underwent a security sweep in Denver Aug. 13 after a live bullet was found aboard the plane. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

title: HHS warns Texas hospitals against denying life-saving care to newborn with disability
summary: HHS warned Children's Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern they cannot withhold treatment from baby Gabriel based on his heart defect.
story: Fox News correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on a legal battle involving surrogate mother McKenna West, who traveled to Texas to give birth after refusing the intended parents' request to abort the baby over a congenital heart condition diagnosis.
The Trump administration is stepping into the battle over a Texas newborn with a severe heart defect, warning two hospitals they cannot withhold medical treatment because of his disability.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights told Fox News Digital Thursday it is sending a letter to Children’s Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern Medical Center outlining their obligations under federal disability civil rights laws as doctors make treatment decisions involving baby Gabriel.

The federal intervention comes after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton took action to ensure the newborn receives medically necessary care after a dispute that began when his biological parents allegedly asked their surrogate to abort him after he was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION
Surrogate mother McKenna West fled to Texas after her baby's birth parents allegedly asked her to abort the child (Live Action)
Surrogate mother McKenna West refused the request and traveled to Texas, where Gabriel was born Wednesday and taken to a neonatal intensive care unit.

In its letter, HHS' civil rights office makes clear that federal law prohibits withholding medical treatment based on a person's disability, including based on judgments that the life of someone with a disability has less value or that the individual would impose a burden on others.
Those federal protections extend to decisions involving life-sustaining treatment, according to HHS.
The agency said it is monitoring Gabriel's case and offering technical assistance to Children’s Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern as the hospitals determine his care.
HHS OFFICIAL WARNS OF IRREVERSIBLE RISKS AS TRUMP ADMIN RESTRICTS FUNDING FOR YOUTH GENDER PROCEDURES
A newborn baby boy in a small transparent portable hospital bed. (iStock)

HHS is also urging the hospitals to seek a review by an infant care committee if doctors consider withholding or withdrawing medically indicated treatment. The agency said life-sustaining treatment should continue during that review.
The federal action marks the latest intervention in the dispute over Gabriel's medical care.

West was around 20 weeks pregnant when Gabriel was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped. The diagnosis allegedly prompted the intended parents to ask West to have an abortion, according to Paxton's office.

West instead traveled to Texas, and Paxton formally notified UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children’s Medical Center of Dallas of what his office said were their legal obligations to provide Gabriel with "medically necessary, life-saving care upon birth."
TEXAS AG PAXTON DEMANDS DALLAS SHERIFF PURSUE ICE AGREEMENT AS DEADLINE DISPUTE SPARKS LEGAL THREAT
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton makes a statement at his office May 26, 2023, in Austin, Texas.  (AP Photo/Eric Gay, File)
Paxton later secured a court order aimed at ensuring the baby received care after birth.
"The court has made the right decision in immediately acting to protect baby Gabriel’s life and ensure he receives the care he deserves," Paxton said.

"My office utilized every tool at our disposal to protect life, and we will not back down in continuing to support baby Gabriel’s well-being," he added. "Every child in our state deserves to be cared for and protected, and that’s exactly what I’ll fight for."
The case has drawn an outpouring of support for West from conservative and pro-life advocates, who praised her decision to continue the pregnancy and fight for Gabriel's care.
SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY SLAPS DOWN BLUE STATE TARGETING PRO-LIFE GROUP
Andrew Kolvet, a spokesman for Turning Point USA, called West a "hero" on X, writing that she "saved this baby's life" and saying he hopes she is ultimately able to keep Gabriel.

Alliance Defending Freedom, which represents West, celebrated the court order requiring Gabriel to receive the surgery. ADF Senior Counsel Erik Baptist praised West's "courageous stand" for Gabriel and said "every child deserves a chance at life."

Pro-life group Live Action also praised West for resisting pressure to abort Gabriel but said the fight is not over. The group raised concerns that a court order is preventing West from having contact with the newborn, saying Gabriel "needs the comfort of the only mother he's ever known" and that his needs should remain the priority.
Gabriel was born Wednesday and transported to a neonatal intensive care unit, where doctors could perform surgery to treat his heart condition.

"Baby Gabriel deserves a chance at life, and I will not allow anyone to unlawfully deny him medically necessary care," Paxton previously said. "My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives and ensure that every child receives the care required under Texas law."
Fox News Digital reached out to Children’s Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern Medical Center for comment.
Fox News Digital's Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Speaker Johnson slams Dems after noncitizens were charged with illegally voting in battleground state
summary: Michigan AG Dana Nessel charged five noncitizens and one U.S. citizen with election crimes after reviewing 38 suspected cases of illegal voting.
story: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt highlighted the administration's commitment to investigating and preventing illegal aliens from voting in U.S. elections. She points to a letter from the Secretary of Homeland Security requesting states, including New Jersey, remove noncitizens from voter rolls.

House Speaker Mike Johnson slammed Democrats Thursday over election security after noncitizens were charged with illegally voting in Michigan, warning that similar cases across the country pose a growing threat to the integrity of American elections.
"From New Jersey to Michigan, the evidence continues to mount: Illegal aliens are registering and VOTING in American elections," Johnson said in a post shared on X.
"Democrats know this — which is why they want OPEN BORDERS and OPPOSE voter ID" he added before stating that it is a "clear and present danger to the integrity of our elections — and our Republic.
"All Americans DESERVE secure elections, and Republicans are the ones fighting to make it happen."
HASAN PIKER WARNS ‘THE KNIVES WILL BE OUT’ AFTER SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG FALLS IN WISCONSIN UPSET

Johnson's remarks came as five non-U.S. citizens who allegedly voted in the 2024 presidential election — along with a U.S. citizen accused of registering her noncitizen husband — were charged with election crimes, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced.
The charges follow a state review of 38 suspected cases of noncitizen voting or related conduct from 2009 to 2025.
Of those cases, six resulted in criminal charges, 10 were closed without charges and 22 remain under active review.
BOMBSHELL VOTING SCANDAL ADDS TO PATTERN OF NONCITIZEN VOTERS AS TRUMP WARNS OF THREAT TO ‘HEART' OF DEMOCRACY
Dana Nessel (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"In my office, we’ve always taken election crimes seriously and prosecute attacks on our voting systems to the fullest extent of the law," Nessel said in a statement.

"We’re upholding election integrity by investigating all claims of noncitizen voters, as rare as they are, and holding bad actors accountable when they refuse to abide by the laws that keep our elections safe and secure."
More than 5.7 million ballots were cast in Michigan during the November 2024 general election.
State officials have said illegal voting by noncitizens remains rare.
TRUMP INTERVENES AS HOUSE GOP REVOLT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AT CENTER OF SPENDING SHOWDOWN
A voter drops a ballot into a ballot box at the Minneapolis Elections & Voter Services building Sept. 20, 2024, in Minneapolis. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
The charges come as President Donald Trump’s administration has made preventing illegal voting a priority.

He signed executive orders in March 2025 and March 2026 to strengthen citizenship verification for federal elections and directing agencies to give states greater access to citizenship and immigration data.
Trump's administration has also backed legislation requiring proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
Nessel's announcement included Robert Piva, 67, of Roseville, a permanent resident charged with election law perjury, attempting to vote unqualified and fraudulent registration.
NONCITIZEN EX-KANSAS MAYOR PLEADS GUILTY TO ILLEGALLY VOTING MULTIPLE TIMES

"I Voted" stickers are ready to be given out as citizens go through the voting process at Scheig Center & Gardens on Election Day Nov. 5, 2024, in Appleton, Wis. (Dan Powers/USA Today Network Wisconsin)
He allegedly voted early in October 2024. Piva claimed his vote was an "experiment" concerning voter fraud.
Michael Akioya, 39, of Oak Park, also a permanent resident, was charged with allegedly making false statements on an absentee voter application and ballot envelope during the 2024 election.

Alondra Harker, 26, of Three Rivers, is a limited-term alien resident charged with misdemeanor fraudulent registration, which is punishable by up to 90 days in jail, for allegedly registering and voting in person in 2024.
SKID ROW ELECTION SCHEME ALLEGEDLY FUELED BY POCKET-CHANGE PAYOFFS BUSTED BY TRUMP DOJ

Republican presidential nominee former President Donald Trump and former first lady Melania Trump walk after voting on Election Day at the Morton and Barbara Mandel Recreation Center, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024, in Palm Beach, Fla. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

Harumi Michael, 60, who lives in Wolverine Lake, is a permanent resident who faces three felonies — two counts of election forgery and one count of attempting to vote unqualified — plus one misdemeanor for allegedly registering and voting in Commerce Township.

Basanth Sadasivian, 29, is a noncitizen living in the United Kingdom who was charged with felony attempting to vote unqualified, punishable by up to four years in prison, for allegedly registering and voting in 2024 through the Federal Post Card Application system using a Bloomfield Hills address.
And Kimberley DiDonato, 60, of Rose Township, is a U.S. citizen charged with election forgery and computer crime after allegedly posing as her noncitizen husband to register him online.
Authorities said DiDonato claimed she wanted to test system vulnerabilities before asking to cancel the registration.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS DOJ ACCESS TO NJ VOTER ROLLS AMID STATEWIDE CONTROVERSY
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel attends an event for Democratic presidential candidate Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., in Clawson, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya File)

Nessel’s office declined to charge four referred people after determining that two were U.S. citizens, one was an American citizen through an international adoption and another was a federally recognized American Indian born in Canada.
Six additional cases were closed without charges because of a lack of evidence of criminal intent or potential registration errors.
Nessel also said delays in federal cooperation affected the timeline of the state’s investigations.
"While the question of whether any given resident is a citizen may feel simple, some cases are nuanced in unexpected ways," Nessel said.

"The federal government has not always provided easy or open access to certain necessary citizenship records, and so our investigators had to spend considerable time and effort coaxing cooperation from the federal agencies."

title: WATCH: Terrifying moment spear-wielding man lunges at California cops before shots ring out
summary: Dramatic video captures Oakland police repeatedly ordering Jose Angel Castillo to drop weapons near a homeless encampment before the fatal shooting.
story: Newly released police video shows Jose Angel Castillo, 43, carrying multiple weapons as Oakland officers repeatedly order him to drop them.
An armed man's confrontation with Oakland police came to a deadly end after he ignored repeated commands to drop a collection of weapons and lunged at officers, authorities said.

Dramatic video captured the minutes leading up to the shooting of Jose Angel Castillo, 43, who authorities alleged was carrying two makeshift spears when officers encountered him near a homeless encampment at 40th Avenue and International Boulevard, according to KTVU.
The video shows officers trailing Castillo down the street and repeatedly ordering him to drop the weapons before gunfire erupted.
WISCONSIN PROTESTER BRANDS MADISON AS 'CORRUPT CITY' DURING ANTI-POLICE TIRADE FOLLOWING DEADLY SHOOTING
Bodycam video shows Jose Angel Castillo holding a bladed weapon during his confrontation with Oakland police. (Oakland Police Department)
The deadly encounter unfolded just after 2 p.m. on July 13 after the California Highway Patrol (CHP) called the Oakland Police Department (OPD) for assistance, according to police.

Video of the ordeal begins with a request for backup as an officer reports being with a man armed with two knives and behaving aggressively. As police confront him, officers can be heard ordering him to drop multiple objects, including what one officer identifies as a hammer, offering an early glimpse at the array of weapons involved in the encounter.
"We're out with the subject holding two knives, being aggressive," an officer can be heard telling dispatch.
The footage then captures officers repeatedly ordering the man to drop what he is holding as the confrontation escalates.
VIDEO SHOWS UNDERCOVER COPS SHOOTING MAN THREATENING SHOPPERS WITH FAKE GUN IN ‘JUSTIFIED’ DEFENSE: OFFICIALS
Police bodycam video shows Jose Angel Castillo holding two weapons before his deadly encounter with Oakland officers. (Oakland Police Department)

Two cars overturned on Los Angeles’ 405 Freeway during the Thursday morning rush hour, closing several northbound lanes and triggering a major traffic backup.

The agency extended the SigAlert for another 30 minutes at about 8:30 a.m.

A Florida father who had just dropped off his daughter for her first day of elementary school was shot and killed after trying to intervene in a fight between a man and a woman, police and reports said.

After the fight in the bushes, Hill began running away from Vazquez and Honaker, yelling "help" with his hands in the air, the affidavit said.

title: Three death row inmates executed by lethal injection in rare same-day string across US

title: Former Chicago detective says one city's murder plunge offers Windy City crime blueprint
summary: A retired Chicago detective says the National Guard deployment that cut Memphis homicides by 43.7% could solve Chicago's worsening crime crisis.
story: Retired Chicago Police Chief of Detectives Eugene Roy tells Fox News Digital the city should look to Memphis, where homicides fell sharply after the National Guard moved in.
A former Chicago detective says the Windy City should look to a southern city where murders have plunged since the National Guard members moved in to find a way out of its crime crisis.

Homicides in Memphis, Tennessee, fell 43.7% during the first half of 2026 compared to the same period the prior year, according to data from the Major Cities Chiefs Association. President Donald Trump had signed an executive order in September 2025 authorizing the deployment of the National Guard, allowing troops to arrive in Memphis that fall.

On Monday night alone, nine people were shot across Chicago, including three who were killed. In one incident, two men were critically injured after gunfire rang out in the city's Near North Side neighborhood.
CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED

A police officer works at the scene where a 47-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were shot on the 2400 block of West Monroe Street on July 7, 2024, in Chicago. (Armando L. Sanchez/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"When we were in our living room, and we thought that another sporadic rainstorm hit Chicago, so we go outside in the windows, next thing you know, we just hear like lights everywhere," one person told FOX 32.
Retired Chicago Police Chief of Detectives Eugene Roy told Fox News Digital that Chicago officials aren't utilizing federal resources to clean up the city's crime problem amid a shortage of officers.

"Chicago has just 2,500 fewer police officers than it did just two or three years ago. You can't keep doing more with less. It's got to come down," Roy said. "As far as cooperation in preventative levels, which involves street-level policing, there's very little cooperation, if any, between Chicago and the federal authorities."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

The city's police officer shortage has been exacerbated by a November 2025 decision to pause classes at its training academy and slow hiring to roughly 50 recruits per month, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. The cut in training and hiring was made to address a $1.2 billion budget shortfall that the city faced.
MEMPHIS PIZZA JOINT SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER OWNER REFUSES TO SERVE NATIONAL GUARD TROOPS
Historic Beale Street, known as the Home of the Blues in Memphis, Tennessee, USA. (Ron Buskirk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images))

Roy pointed to Memphis in particular as a "success story" about what happens when local and state governments effectively partner with the federal government, as the National Guard and federal law enforcement agencies surged into the city.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"Memphis is a success story on how this can work out. From the material I've looked at, they had cooperation from the governor on down, some reluctance at the city level, but they've done the right things the right way, and it results in the… it's produced the results," Roy said.

"The mere presence of police serves as a disincentive to commit crime. You want people to say, 'Hey, people are going out to do something, a robbery, a burglary or whatever. Man, it's hot out here. The police are everywhere. Let's forget about it. Let's do it a different time, a different place. Let's move on.' That's how you prevent crime."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"Done right, done properly, it is a godsend," he said.
SEND US A TIP
Memphis recorded 67 homicides in the first six months of 2026, down from 119 during the same period in 2025, according to the Major Cities Chiefs Association.
GOT A TIP?
Chicago Police Department headquarters on May 17, 2021. (Chicago Tribune via Getty Images)

If done properly in Chicago, Roy said, bringing in the National Guard to help would "mirror those in Memphis and other locations where there's been a truly cooperative effort between the federal and local government."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Roy said it's not entirely unprecedented for a Democratic governor to deploy its National Guard to deter crime.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

New York Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul deployed at least 1,000 National Guard members to New York City's subway system in March 2024 following a series of high-profile crimes, saying it creates a deterrent effect.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For people who are thinking about bringing a gun or knife on the subway, at least this creates a deterrent effect. They might be thinking, 'You know what, it just may just not be worth it because I listened to the mayor and I listened to the governor, and they have a lot more people who are going to be checking my bags,'" Hochul said.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Chicago Police Department and the Illinois governor's office for comment.

title: Luigi Mangione plea buzz raises potential Paul Manafort problem for prosecutors
summary: Luigi Mangione's federal case conference Friday sparks plea deal speculation that could trigger New York's double jeopardy law and upend state charges.
story: Fox News contributor and "Crime & Justice" host Donna Rotunno explains the unique New York law that Luigi Mangione's defense could lean on if he does reach a plea deal in his federal case before the state trial.

Prosecutors with the Southern District of New York and defense attorneys for accused assassin Luigi Mangione asked a U.S. judge Tuesday to set a conference Friday morning — prompting speculation that the 28-year-old could agree to a plea deal in his federal case days before he's set to go to trial on state murder charges.

The timing could have major implications for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's state case. New York's double-jeopardy protections previously led Big Apple courts to toss charges against former Trump campaign Chairman Paul Manafort after his federal convictions.

After similar reports of a potential plea deal emerged earlier this year, Manhattan prosecutors indicated that they could "advise" the federal judge if any potential plea agreement would put the "just outcome" of his state case in jeopardy.
LUIGI MANGIONE HEARING SET FOR FRIDAY STIRS PLEA DEAL SPECULATION IN HIS FEDERAL CASE
Luigi Mangione attends a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan Criminal Court, in New York City on Aug. 11, 2026. (REUTERS/David Dee Delgado/Pool)

"If Luigi Mangione takes a plea federally, then the question is, does this state double jeopardy law get triggered?" said Donna Rotunno, a Chicago-based defense attorney, Fox News contributor and the host of "Crime & Justice."

New York has broader double jeopardy laws than the federal government, she said. A federal resolution first could therefore put the state case at risk in a way that a state conviction would not necessarily jeopardize the federal prosecution.
PROSECUTORS WARN LUIGI MANGIONE SUPPORTERS MAY INTIMIDATE WITNESSES AND JURORS AT MURDER TRIAL

UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson is pictured in an undated portrait provided by UnitedHealth. The executive was shot from behind and killed on his way to an investor conference in New York City in what prosecutors have described as a politically motivated assassination. (AP Photo/UnitedHealth Group via AP)

"The prosecutors reached out to Judge Carro via letter back in July when they were talking about which case should be set for trial first and the importance of setting the state case for trial before the federal one," Rotunno told Fox News Digital. "So now here we are in a situation where the state is saying wait, wait, why is the government allowing Luigi Mangione to possibly take a plea on the federal side? Because if that's the case, it could potentially upend our case on the state side."
Read the July letter from Manhattan prosecutors to Judge Carro:

Shortly after Friday's pre-trial conference appeared on the docket, speculation swirled that it could involve a potential plea deal. However, neither side has commented, and the purpose of the conference remains unclear.
EX-TRUMP CAMPAIGN CHAIRMAN PAUL MANAFORT OPENS UP ABOUT 'SCARY' TIME SPENT IN SOLITARY CONFINEMENT

While Mangione is currently scheduled to go on trial on the state charges next month and see a federal trial next year, his lawyers could potentially make the double jeopardy argument in New York, if the federal case results in a conviction first.
President Trump's one-time campaign manager, Paul Manafort, arrives at Manhattan Supreme Court June 27, 2019, for his arraignment on mortgage fraud charges. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)
In the 2019 Manafort case, he was charged at the state level with fraud crimes that were similar to those he had already been convicted of federally.
New York Judge Maxwell Wiley agreed to dismiss the state charges.
LUIGI MANGIONE'S FEDERAL TRIAL PUSHED TO NEXT YEAR IN ASSASSINATION OF UNITEDHEALTHCARE CEO
The factual overlap between the state and federal cases was "extensive — if not total," Wiley wrote at the time. Then-Manhattan District Attorney Cy Vance Jr. appealed the ruling unsuccessfully.

Paul Manafort's then-attorney Todd Blanche delivers a speech to the press members at New York State Supreme Court in Manhattan in New York, United States on June 27, 2019. Blanche is now the U.S. attorney general. (Atilgan Ozdil/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)
An appellate court unanimously upheld Wiley's decision.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

The question in the Manafort case was whether the federal and state laws were "designed to prevent very different kinds of harm or evil." Both Manafort cases involved the same fraud and the same victims, and the courts found that the laws were not aimed at "very different kinds" of offenses.

The suspect in the UnitedHealthcare CEO assassination, later identified as Luigi Mangione, is pictured by a taxi cab's security camera looking into the front from the passenger seat in the rear. (FBI)

In Mangione's case, should he actually reach a federal plea deal before his state trial, the question might boil down to whether a federal charge of stalking resulting in death is "very different" from New York's second-degree murder charge.

"There's a little bit of an argument to be made there, but again, if that was not an issue, then why were the prosecutors so concerned about making sure they go first?" Rotunno asked. "If you look at this law, this law really has to do with the state going first because the feds can prosecute any charges they want, even if they're based on the same conduct."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Luigi Mangione’s attorneys, Jacob Kaplan, Karen Friedman Agnifilo and Marc Agnifilo, arrive at court in Manhattan, New York, on April 1, 2026. A hearing for Mangione is held regarding the 2024 shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)
"If the charges were so different, they wouldn't worry about it," she added.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Manafort's lawyer at the time, Todd Blanche, is now the U.S. attorney general. At an unrelated Justice Department news briefing Wednesday, he declined to answer a question about whether Friday's hearing would be related to a potential plea deal.
WATCH: DOJ questioned on possible Mangione plea deal
SEND US A TIP

The top charge Mangione faces federally, stalking resulting in death, carries a maximum sentence of life in federal prison, without the possibility of parole, if convicted. At the state level, he faces a maximum of 25 years to life if convicted of the second-degree murder charge.

Even if convicted at trial, however, Rotunno said he might not get the maximum sentence based on his lack of a prior criminal history. Any plea deal that leads to less than a life sentence could be considered a win for the defense, she said.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

A split image showing Luigi Mangione in court and his alleged handgun and 3D-printed silencer. Mangione is accused of assassinating UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. (Curtis Means/Pool via Reuters)

"Odds of him getting life are probably slim even after a trial, given the fact that he had no background, and the maximum is life," she said. "But either way, he would’ve gotten such a big number that odds of him getting out would be very slim."
Carro had previously rejected a double jeopardy claim from Mangione's defense, and Mangione himself in February claimed he was being subject to "the same trial twice" in a courtroom outburst.
"One plus one is two," he complained, while being escorted out of the courtroom. "Double jeopardy by any common sense."
Mangione has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges against him in both cases.
Luigi Mangione speaks to a police officer in Altoona, Pennsylvania. (Manhattan District Attorney's Office)

Back in May, another disparity between state and federal law left a potential impact on the case. Carro ruled that some key evidence recovered from Mangione's backpack during his arrest at a Pennsylvania McDonald's would be inadmissible at trial. Judge Margaret Garnett, who is overseeing the federal case, rejected the defense team's argument that the search was improper.

At the same time, Garnett threw out the potential death penalty when she ruled that the underlying stalking charge didn't qualify as a "crime of violence." And that decision could fuel arguments from Manhattan prosecutors against any potential double jeopardy claims, according to Paul Mauro, a retired NYPD inspector and Fox News contributor.

"The federal judge has already found, thanks to Mangione's own arguments, that stalking is not a 'crime of violence,'" he told Fox News Digital. "And if that's the federal position, then you have to ask yourself, is the harm of a nonviolent crime, is the potential harm trying to be prevented by the stalking charge, different enough from what the statute for murder 2 is trying to prevent so that you can say the two statutes are distinct enough that the state case could go forward."

"But that said," he added, "the New York state double jeopardy law is very defendant-favorable. So who knows? Maybe Luigi has just decided he prefers federal prison to state prison. Because of generally better conditions."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News' Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

title: Police rescue 60 cats and kittens from abandoned sailboat off Washington beach after 6-day operation
summary: Tacoma police spent six days rescuing 60 cats from an abandoned 40-foot sailboat off Owen Beach, with many animals found frightened and malnourished.
story: Bodycam video shows Lee County deputies arresting a Fort Myers father accused of killing two family kittens and injuring a third as a form of punishment against his teenage daughter, according to authorities.
An abandoned sailboat off a Washington beach was home to an unexpected crew: 60 cats and kittens, many of them some frightened and malnourished.
The Tacoma Police Department said the unusual rescue began Aug. 6 when its Marine Services Unit responded to reports of an abandoned 40-foot sailboat in the waters off Owen Beach.

Officers initially discovered more than 30 cats and kittens living in unsafe conditions aboard the vessel, with many appearing frightened and malnourished. Marine Services began coordinating with Animal Control and the department's Forensics Unit to safely remove the animals.
What initially appeared to be a rescue involving more than 30 cats eventually grew to 60 over the course of a rescue effort spanning six days.
FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS
Tacoma police rescued 60 cats and kittens from a 40-foot sailboat located off Owen Beach after a six-day rescue effort. (Tacoma Police Department)
"That's a wrap! The final cat is off the boat. Fur real this time!" police wrote. "Final cat count: 60!"
Police said Animal Control was "as certain as they can be that all cats have officially disembarked."
"That's all for meow!" the department joked online.
Despite believing all 60 cats had been rescued, police said they would continue making trips to the boat this week as a precaution.
HERO SHEEPDOG BECOMES UNLIKELY RESCUE PARTNER AFTER UNEXPECTED MOVE AIDS FIRST RESPONDERS
Tacoma Animal Control and Marine Services worked to safely remove 60 cats and kittens from a sailboat anchored off Owen Beach. (Tacoma Police Department)

"While we believe we have safely removed all of the cats from the boat, as any cat owner knows, cats are exceptionally good at hiding," police said. "Because there is always a possibility that a cat may remain onboard, our work isn't quite finished."
The department said the additional searches would be conducted under the authority of a search warrant.
Police said Marine Services has also begun the process of having the legally registered vessel moved.

Authorities asked people visiting Owen Beach or boating nearby to notify Animal Control if they spot another cat aboard the vessel, while warning members of the public not to attempt their own rescues.
FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE
Tacoma police rescued 60 cats and kittens from a 40-foot sailboat anchored off Owen Beach in Washington after a six-day operation. (Tacoma Police Department)

"We know many animal lovers in our community want to help, and we appreciate the concern for these cats," the police said. "However, this remains an active criminal case. Our teams are working hard to protect the animals while also protecting the integrity of the investigation."
"PLEASE DO NOT BOARD THE VESSEL unless you are the legal owner," police added.
The warning followed an incident in which private cat rescue trapper Camille Sutherland told KING 5 she boarded the vessel overnight and captured two cats, which she took to the Humane Society.
Some of the cats and kittens discovered aboard the sailboat were frightened and malnourished, Tacoma police said. (Tacoma Police Department)
Sutherland told the outlet she was trying to help and believed authorities were taking too long to rescue the animals.
Police told KING 5 that the unauthorized boarding complicated their investigation into the vessel's owner.
Police have not announced any arrests or charges in connection with the case.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tacoma Police Marine Services responded to reports of an abandoned sailboat off Owen Beach before discovering dozens of cats and kittens aboard. (Tacoma Police Department)
More than 40 of the 60 rescued cats were taken to the Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County, while the remaining animals were placed in foster homes in the area, according to KING 5.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: US Ambassador Huckabee slams extreme group of Israeli settlers for seizing Palestinian homes on West Bank
summary: Settler violence in the West Bank prompted U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee to call the perpetrators "Israeli terrorists" after they besieged a Palestinian American's home near Nablus.
story: ‘Fox News @ Night’ panelists Jessica Millan Patterson and Elizabeth Pipko discuss Rep. Ro Khanna’s, D-Calif., claims that Israeli settlers detained him during his West Bank visit.

JERUSALEM: In a rare statement of anger and criticism directed at a small group of extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemned their attacks against a home being built by a Palestinian American from Ohio.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) managed to evict the lawbreakers who seized the house and arrested one person. But the group, mostly young, disaffected youths, who have set up unauthorized outposts and engaged in violence targeting Palestinians and their homes in the West Bank are becoming a growing problem for Israeli authorities who are being criticized for not doing enough to stop their violent actions.

Ambassador Huckabee posted on X in response to criticism that his team had not done enough, "The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem has been VERY involved & the IDF & Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this. The actions of those doing this to this family’s home is criminal. The WH hasn’t "intervened" because we have kept DC apprised of the situation already. Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."
HOUSE DEMOCRAT RO KHANNA SAYS HE WAS DETAINED BY ARMED ISRAELI SETTLERS IN WEST BANK
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee speaks to Fox News Digital during an interview at the American embassy in Jerusalem, Israel. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL for Fox News)

According to The Associated Press, Israeli settlers have besieged three homes in the occupied West Bank for several days, including one owned by Palestinian American Loui Ridi. The seizure of Ridi’s home took place in Qusra, in the northern West Bank.

A senior Israeli official from the prime minister's office said, "Israel doesn’t accept vigilantes or any form of violence by juvenile delinquents. We are investing a lot of efforts to curb such sporadic violence. The IDF sent an additional battalion to Judea and Samaria to address the issue. We don’t take violence lightly. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, there were over 350 investigations opened, leading to 35 arrests. Putting things in perspective, Jews are attacked almost daily by Palestinian terrorists. There were over 300 Palestinian terrorist attacks against Jews in May of 2026 alone. The attempt to draw a false symmetry between sporadic violence and Palestinian terror is hypocritical."

The official added, "We do not accept vigilantes. Judea and Samaria is our ancestral homeland. It's where Jews came from and have a right to live. The Jewish community in Judea & Samaria is a law-abiding community. We are addressing the juvenile delinquents."
HOLY LAND BATTLE: SOLOMON'S POOLS BECOME FLASHPOINT IN FIGHT OVER ISRAEL'S BIBLICAL HERITAGE

Israeli settlers run as they are chased by an Israeli military vehicle around Palestinian houses in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank, on Aug. 13, 2026. (Zain Jaafar / AFP via Getty Images)

Nadav Eyal, a prominent Israeli columnist for the large Hebrew daily Yedioth Ahronoth, told Fox News Digital, "There is an extending consensus in the Israeli political sphere, stretching from the left to the right, that some of the actions we are seeing in the West Bank, in Judea and Samaria, are, in actuality, Jewish terrorism. It is more widespread than it was ever before. It is considered by Israeli defense apparatus to be a serious problem."
In another post on X, Huckabee stated, "Settlers" are not the problem in Judea/Samaria. "Unsettlers" are. Very small minority who do great damage to Palestinian families & to Israel."

With over 500,000 Israelis living in Judea and Samaria, more commonly known as the West Bank, leaders of the settlement movements slammed the violence. The Jerusalem Post reported that the head of the Yesha Council, Yisrael Ganz, said, "There is no place for privately deciding to establish a hilltop outpost in the yard of a house, even when it is an illegal house or there is an attempt to take control of the area," he said. "There is absolutely no justification for violence against uninvolved people or against the security forces."

The newspaper also quoted Beit El Council head Shai Alon, who said they were causing "irreversible damage" to Israel and to the settlement movement, and described those responsible for attacks on innocent Palestinians as criminals.
Israeli settlers gather in front of Palestinian houses in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, in the West Bank, on August 13, 2026. (Zain Jaafar / AFP via Getty Images)

Wafa, the Palestinian News & Info Agency, reported on Thursday that the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates "condemned the escalation of Israeli colonist terrorism and attacks against the town of Qusra." According to the Ministry’s statement, the "crimes were part of systematic policies aimed at displacing Palestinians and uprooting them from their land while imposing a reality that serves plans to annex the West Bank."

Israel's Channel 12 News analyst, Amit Segal wrote on X that "Settler violence is a sensitive issue in Israel. Only a vanishingly small share of the settler population supports or takes part in such acts, but because the problem is exaggerated and used to obscure Palestinian violence against them, they bristle at hearing about it — even from Israel’s greatest friends."

Israeli soldiers patrol a street as they are deployed during an operation in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on Aug. 13, 2026. Israeli forces moved against rogue settlers laying siege to Palestinians amid unusually strong U.S. criticism. (Zain Jaafar/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Segal said that "The most damning verdict of the event comes from Israel’s most faithful friend, Mike Huckabee. The most pro-settlement ambassador in the history of the post, a man who will not so much as use the word 'settler'— called the men at Qusra ‘Israeli terrorists.’"

He added that "For four days, the most capable military in the Middle East could not clear a path for a family to reach its own front door. The family lives on the outskirts of Qusra, south of Nablus. On Sunday, settlers from the encampments seeded by the Tel Talpiot outpost sealed the entrance to their home and would not let them in or out."
Fox News Digital sent a press query to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
