Germany’s federal interior ministry, which publishes the annual domestic intelligence threat report, notes that crimes attributed to "religious ideology" have climbed from 134 in 2022 to 998 last year. Radical Islamist crimes are reportedly understood to make up the main portion of the "religious ideology" category.

Germany’s neighbor, France, experienced another stabbing just days after the attack in Germany. A suspect reportedly stabbed three women in Paris and, as people captured him after the attack, declared, "It is Allah who commanded me."

AMERICAN ‘JIHAD’ FUELED BY 'RISKY SOURCE' INSIDE US BORDERS, WARNS NATIONAL SECURITY EXPERT

Austria’s intelligence agency announced in May on its website that it had arrested a group of suspected Islamist terrorists, which included five males between the ages of 14 and 45 and one 16-year-old female.

To address the threat at its source, European governments need to focus on preventing radicalization and disrupting foreign funding and ideological networks that fuel extremist movements. Without tackling these root causes, the risk of future terrorist attacks will remain."
SENATE CLEARS WAY FOR TRUMP'S TOP SPY AS KEY ANTI-TERROR PROGRAM REMAINS IN LIMBO
A map depicting Spain, Morocco and Spain's Cueta, which borders Morocco. (2026 EarthStar Geographics, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap contributors)

"The United States should learn from Europe’s experience rather than simply criticize it," Mahmoud said. The United Kingdom’s judicial system recorded a series of convictions of Islamist terrorists in July. Late last month, in Wigston, Britain, the authorities arrested a 27-year-old man for supporting the Islamic State.
According to the Crown Prosecution Service, Mohammad Bashir, 31, "pleaded guilty to preparing an act of terrorism" against a British defense target.

A spokesperson for the British Home Office told Fox News Digital, "The United Kingdom has one of the most robust counterterrorism systems in the world. We remain committed to ensuring our Police and Security Services have the tools and powers they need to prevent the spread of violent ideologies and keep the country safe.
UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC
Prime Minister Keir Starmer visits the Hatzola Northwest independent ambulance base after a terrorist incident April 30, 2026, in Golders Green, England. (James Smith/Sam Snap/Getty Images)

"This includes a wide range of terrorist offenses and specialized powers designed to risk, support prosecution and strengthen management of terrorist offenders. Northern continental Europe is also facing a serious Jihadi terrorist threat. According to a late May Danish Security and Intelligence Service statement, the "CTA [Center for Terror Analysis in Denmark] assesses that the terrorist threat from militant Islamists remains at the level of significant."
Vidino said there has been a silver lining since the outbreak of the Islamic State terrorist attacks in Europe.

He cited Switzerland, Austria and the Scandinavian countries.
"They did not have legal capabilities and mindset. That has changed and it is not perfect."

story: Keeping gas prices low is now the United States’ “goal No. 1” in the Iran war, Vice President JD Vance has said, as Washington threatened an indefinite naval blockade and signaled it would soon intensify economic pressure on Tehran.
The comments appeared to be the latest shift in the public rationale for the conflict, with Vance ranking Iran’s nuclear ambitions second.

The vice president’s remarks came as the Trump administration embraced a long-term effort to inflict more damage on the Islamic Republic, despite growing signs of strain on American forces and domestic pressure ahead of the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has suggested a shift away from military force in favor of “low-keying it” with economic pressure. That followed a deadly cycle of tit-for-tat exchanges that produced no clear resolution and depleted U.S. reserves of missile interceptors.

He added that “obviously goal No. 2 is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” Tehran insists it has no desire to develop one.

title: Trump asks Supreme Court to allow White House ballroom construction to continue
summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday asked the Supreme Court to allow him to continue construction of a sprawling ballroom adjacent to the White House.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday asked the Supreme Court to allow him to continue construction of a sprawling ballroom adjacent to the White House.
The emergency application follows an August 7 ruling by an appeals court in Washington upholding a federal judge’s decision that would block work on site while litigation moves forward.

“If allowed to go into effect, the injunction would wrongfully install a single district judge as sole arbiter of what further construction is ‘strictly necessary’ to protect the safety of the President, his family, staff members, and visitors to the White House, including foreign dignitaries, and presidents and prime ministers of other countries,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer said in the filing.
The appeals court decision has yet to go into effect, meaning construction continues while the Supreme Court decides what to do next. The deadline for the justices to act is Aug. 21.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld an injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Richard Leon.
He had originally said that the White House could move forward with below-ground construction of security and medical facilities, but not the ballroom itself.
Leon later ruled that all construction would have to stop, but the administration immediately appealed, and his ruling has not gone into effect.

One key issue in the case is whether the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the underlying lawsuit, has legal standing to sue based on its members being harmed by construction of a building they object to on aesthetic grounds.

title: Selena Gomez and her mom accused of fraud over their mental health startup
summary: Superstar Selena Gomez and her mother are accused of defrauding investors of their mental health startup, Wondermind, in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday.
story: Superstar Selena Gomez and her mother are accused of defrauding investors of their mental health startup, Wondermind, in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday.
Wondermind, which was co-founded by Gomez; her mother, Mandy Teefey; and Daniella Pierson in November 2021, touts mental fitness practices and tools.
The suit accuses Wondermind and its founders of falsely representing the company’s infrastructure, leadership and partnerships to investors and concealing the alleged fraud for more than three years.
The founders told investors they would build a Wondermind app, boasted advertising deals and secured celebrity cover stories, none of which came to fruition, the complaint says.
Investors poured nearly $1.2 million into Wondermind, but the trio falsely represented the company’s plans to make it profitable, the suit says.
It alleges that investors were kept in the dark until two bombshell media reports portrayed Wondermind as a company in utter disarray.
The suit was filed in federal court in Delaware by Wondermind SRS 44 LLC and Bespoke Wondermind SPV I LLC, limited liability companies that invested in the startup.

They accuse the company and the founding trio of securities fraud, common-law fraud, and breach of contract, and are seeking rescission — meaning a legal cancellation of the investment contract — as well as damages.
In a statement, Pierson says she categorically denies the allegations against her and “welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.”

“To be clear, she has never used investor funds for personal expenses. Quite the opposite: Daniella invested her own money into the business and did not draw a salary from the company,” she said in a statement.
Representatives for Wondermind, Gomez and Teefey did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.
No products, no updates — and no Selena

Investors say in the suit that they believed the money they gave  Wondermind would rapidly scale and build a full suite of company products, including an app, a podcast, an editorial publication and other wellness products.

They also believed that the company’s value lay in Gomez’s involvement as a celebrity with a massive, loyal fan base. The suit alleges that Wondermind had indicated that Gomez would be “intimately involved in the Company” as head of marketing and involved in publicity.
But none of those things happened, the suit says.

“Gomez purported to sign a contract obligating her to perform and then ignored it. The partnerships did not exist. The initiatives never materialized. The app was never built,” it says. “And for three years, while the Company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse.”
The investors also allege in the suit that the defendants did not provide timely updates about the status of their investments and the company’s operations unless they were pressed.

In the limited updates they did provide, “they both affirmatively misrepresented the status of the Company’s operations and concealed material information about ongoing issues at the Company,” the complaint says.
Media articles allege a company in disarray
Investors were kept in the dark, the suit alleges, for more than three years.
Then came an August 2025 Forbes article focused on Pierson with the headline “‘Smoke And Mirrors’: How This Entrepreneur Exaggerated And Self-Promoted Her Way Into Turmoil.”

Pierson was described to investors as a millionaire executive whose past business, the daily newsletter The Newsette, of which she was CEO, generated $40 million a year, the suit says. Investors were also told she had secured partnerships with JPMorgan and Fidelity.
But the Forbes report cast scrutiny and said Pierson exaggerated her readership and the valuation of her newsletter.

The suit says that investors contacted Teefey for an explanation after the article published and that she responded that Pierson had allegedly “misappropriated investor funds — including the Plaintiffs’ funds — to fund her lavish lifestyle,” including her $60,000 monthly rent for her New York City apartment and monthly expenses, before she was ousted from the company in January 2023.
Yet Teefey had never informed investors about the alleged misappropriated funds before the article was published, the suit says.
An article in The Cut published Sept. 3 titled “What Happened at Wondermind?” based on interviews with current and former employees, alleged the company was falling apart.
“The accounts in the Cut article collectively show that, from the outset, Wondermind had no plan for its future — much less a plan for achieving a multi-billion dollar valuation,” the suit says.

That article alleged that Teefey had a long-running substance abuse problem that impeded her capacity to helm the company, that Gomez sought to distance herself from Wondermind “based on a long-running family dispute” with Teefey and that Pierson had been ousted from the company based on a dispute with Teefey, the suit says.
The article, the suit claims, proved that the company was “in a state of financial calamity” and that “there was no legitimate enterprise in the works.”

Two months later, in November, investors sent the defendants a notice of rescission, demanding the return of their funds, they say in their suit. The defendants did not respond “in substance” to the notice, the suit says, but “continued to lull and mislead the plaintiffs.”

After the notice of rescission was sent, Teefey allegedly contacted Bespoke’s representatives suggesting that investors should not file a suit claiming the company had an escrow account to return the investments, this week’s lawsuit says. When Andrew Resnick, part of Bespoke, followed up for details of the account and the return of funds, “Teefey disappeared,” the suit says.
“In short, there was no ‘escrow account’ or a plan to return the Plaintiffs’ investments,” the complaint says.
Misleading updates
The suit details several allegations of investors’ being given updates that ended up being misleading or false.

In June 2022, it says, Pierson told the plaintiffs that Wondermind had grown to more than 150,000 subscribers in one month, that she had met with executives at other companies regarding “large advertising deals” and that she anticipated closing “at least $5M in ad revenue this year.” She also said the company had “interest or confirmation for ‘Cover Story’ features from major celebrities including Camila Cabello, Tim Cook, Elton John, Drake, Megan Thee Stallion and more,” the complaint says.

She said the company was starting to build its “online editorial experience” and an ambassador/referral program, the complaint says. She is alleged to have touted that the company had a potential future value of more than $4 billion.
That led the investors to believe the company had the foundation to operationalize, the suit says.
The suit says that from 2022 to 2025, the plaintiffs “proactively” contacted Teefey and Pierson for updates.

“When the Defendants would provide updates — either by email or on a phone call — they concealed the significant operational and financial issues at the Company. Indeed, the Defendants affirmatively misrepresented that the Company was performing well,” the suit says.

Overall, the suit accuses Wondermind and all defendants of securities fraud, alleging they misrepresented the company’s finances, Gomez’s involvement, Pierson’s business background and Teefey’s fitness (as she had never held a similar startup CEO role). They are further accused of common law fraud and equitable fraud.
Pierson in addition is accused in the suit of securities fraud for what it alleges were misstatements to investors, conversion for wrongfully using investment funds and unjust enrichment.

Wondermind is also accused in the suit of breach of contract-use of investor proceeds, rescission-failures to satisfy conditions precedent, and breach of contract-breach of express representations and warranties.

title: Luigi Mangione expected to plead guilty during Manhattan federal court hearing
summary: Mangione was charged with two federal stalking counts and faces a maximum penalty of life in prison in the 2024 killing of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
story: The man charged with gunning down UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a New York City street two years ago is expected to plead guilty in Manhattan federal court Friday, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Luigi Mangione, 28, has a pretrial conference scheduled for 11 a.m.

The terms of a potential plea agreement remain unclear. Sources familiar with the matter said Thursday that negotiations were ongoing and nothing was final until Mangione accepted a deal. That potential decision could be reversed during the hearing.
Federal prosecutors and defense attorneys declined to comment Thursday.

Mangione was charged with two federal counts — interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death — though it isn’t clear if he will plead guilty to both. The charges carry a maximum penalty of life in prison and are separate from the state allegations, which include second-degree murder and firearms crimes.
What Luigi Mangione could gain from plea negotiations
Mangione’s trial in the state case is expected to begin early next month.

He pleaded not guilty in both cases and previously faced two additional federal counts, including using a firearm to commit murder, which carried a maximum penalty of death. A judge dismissed that charge earlier this year.

The brazen killing of Thompson — a father of two who led the nation’s largest healthcare insurer — put a spotlight on the country’s health insurance industry and widespread frustration over denied claims.
Mangione was arrested at a Pennsylvania McDonald’s on Dec. 9, 2024, five days after Thompson was fatally shot outside a Manhattan hotel that was hosting an investors’ conference.

Among the pieces of evidence found by authorities in Mangione’s backpack was a notebook that detailed his apparent grievances against the industry. At the scene, authorities found a bullet and two shell casings that had the words “delay,” “deny,” “depose” written on them.

Mangione’s attorneys had sought to bar the notebook from being introduced as evidence at his trials, arguing authorities obtained it during an illegal search. Judges in both cases rejected that argument.

title: Perez Hilton has long road to recovery, had struggled with depression, sister says
summary: Barbara Lavandeira recalled finding her brother in a state of distress on Aug. 4 and said “we remain hopeful” as he recovers.
story: In her first public interview, Perez Hilton’s sister opened up about discovering her brother during his self-harm incident, revealed he had been grappling with depression and offered thoughts about his long road to recovery.
Barbara Lavandeira told the New York Post’s Page Six that Aug. 4 “will forever be one of the darkest days my family and I have ever experienced.”
That was the evening Hilton, who rose to fame in the early 2000s as a celebrity gossip blogger, appeared to engage in self-harm during a livestream.
Police responded to his Miami home, and Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, was hospitalized for treatment.
Lavandeira was staying with her brother at the time and noticed his bedroom door was closed and locked, which she said “wasn’t like him,” Lavandeira told the outlet.
She called out to him, but he stopped responding.

“When I knocked, he said he was fine, but I could barely hear him,” she said. “After I knocked a few more times and asked him to open the door, he stopped responding. I tried calling his cellphone in case he couldn’t hear me, but he wouldn’t answer. Something just felt wrong.”
She said that she unlocked the bedroom door and saw he was inside the bathroom and that when he didn’t answer, she unlocked that door, too.
“When I opened the door, my nightmare became a reality,” she told Page Six. “Mario was standing in front of the shower, naked, cut up, covered in blood, with a box cutter in his hand.”

“What I can say with certainty is that I didn’t recognize my brother when I looked at him. I saw it in his eyes. They didn’t look the same. Then, a split second later, he smiled at me. It felt like I was staring at someone else,” she continued.
Lavandeira said she left the bathroom and corralled her daughter and Hilton’s three children out of the home, put them in the car and called 911.

“The first call I made was to the police. Then I messaged my best friend, who lives nearby, while I was on with dispatch, and asked her to please come get the kids and take them away from the scene,” Lavandeira said.
With the kids safe, she tended to her brother.

“Eventually, I was able to go back into the house while I waited for the ambulance and place towels over Mario to help stop the bleeding. He had already lost a significant amount of blood, yet he was somehow still able to speak, although his voice was very faint,” she said.
Finally, an ambulance arrived and took him to a hospital.
She said Hilton had checked himself into a hospital for “severe depression” shortly before the Aug. 4 incident. That came on the heels of “an extremely difficult year” of health issues, she said.
About two weeks earlier, Hilton approached her and their mother and opened up about his mental health.

“He told us that a few days earlier, he had felt empty, hopeless and like he was a burden on everyone. He then admitted that one night when he couldn’t sleep, he had taken the remaining painkillers from his surgery in March. He said he just wanted to sleep,” she told Page Six.
Lavandeira told her brother he needed “proper psychiatric help.” Hilton agreed, and she took him to the hospital that same day, she said.
“He went voluntarily,” she said. “After several days of evaluation and treatment, the facility determined that he could be discharged.”
Hilton seemed to be on the up, spending time with the family and using coping mechanisms and grounding techniques he learned at the hospital, she said.

On Aug. 3, Hilton returned to his regular therapy sessions, and the next day he “completed an intake call for an intensive outpatient program and was supposed to begin outpatient group therapy the following week,” his sister said.
“Later that same afternoon, our lives changed forever,” she added.

In March, Hilton said in a series of posts that he had been hospitalized for three weeks with an ulcer and sepsis. He said in a YouTube video addressing his hospitalization that his condition was a result of taking medication without eating.
“He was hospitalized for close to a month. Doctors initially didn’t know what was wrong. His body became septic, he coded and he nearly died several times,” Lavandeira said.
“He underwent abdominal surgery, had fluid drained from around his lungs twice and then had to recover from surgery and begin physical therapy,” she said.
Hilton was back in a hospital a few weeks later for deep vein thrombosis, he said in an interview with NBC South Florida last month.
After he was released, “he began struggling with depression, anxiety, stress and overwhelming thoughts,” Lavandeira said.
She said that the family took those signs seriously and that he saw a therapist and a psychiatrist to get better.
He moved from Las Vegas to his hometown, Miami, in June to be closer to his family.

“Soon after arriving in Miami, Mario started having doubts. He worried that moving had been a mistake, a financial drain and an impulsive decision. He wondered whether he should have stayed in Las Vegas, and those thoughts wouldn’t leave his mind,” Lavandeira told Page Six.
She said Hilton was prescribed a low dose of antidepressant.
She said that while things “seemed to be looking better,” when it came to Aug. 4, “my brother was not well that day. He needed help, and he still needs help.”
She said that Hilton remains hospitalized and that the family’s priority is the health and safety of him and his children.
“His physical and mental recovery is going to take a lot of time, but we remain hopeful,” she said.

“He did sustain cuts to his face and other areas, but it’s still far too early to know the extent of any lasting damage or scarring,” she told Page Six. “What I can say is that he has a long road ahead of him, both physically and mentally.”
She said he has no cellphone or internet access in the hospital.
Lavandeira said she decided to speak out as the “only person who witnessed what happened from the beginning to the end.”

“I’m talking now for everyone who cares about him and has been sending their best wishes, but also because of all the rumors, false reporting, fake exclusives and made-up quotes going around,” she told Page Six. “I can only share what I personally witnessed and experienced, but I want people to hear directly from someone who was actually there.”
Lavandeira stressed that Hilton’s kids love their father and that the family’s goal is for him to get better and care for his children again.
“In the meantime, our mother is caring for them, and our entire family is helping provide the love, stability, privacy and professional support they need,” she said.
Lavandeira also stressed that her brother isn’t the same person he was when he launched his gossip website and condemned people who were casting judgment or making jokes about his experience.
“I don’t believe someone should be reduced forever to the worst things they did in their past, especially when they’ve admitted the harm and genuinely tried to grow.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7, to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: Cuisinart’s popular 10-cup food processor is 50% off — it’s a meal prepper’s dream appliance
summary: Cuisinart’s popular Core Custom food processor is perfect for dicing, chopping and more, and it’s up to 50% off right now.
story: Similar to a stand mixer, Dutch oven and cast-iron skillet, a food processor is a kitchen accessory you’ll almost always have a use for. Right now, you can get Cuisinart’s Core Custom 10-Cup Food Processor for up to 50% by using a promo code at Kohl’s, making it more than $100 off.

The food processor is perfect for mincing, dicing and chopping almost any vegetable, but it’s also the best appliance for making things like salad dressings, salsas, dips, pasta sauces and if you’re NBC Select senior editor Shalwah Evans, your dog’s food. title: 21 products you actually need when your kid starts school for the first time — from a mom of 3

To get ahead of lunch box spills, wardrobe malfunctions, and double booking mistakes, I tested a bunch of school supplies and related items earlier this year and through the summer to get us ready for this special time in his life.

The products below made our mornings easier, stood up to beatings from three kids, and outlasted their competitors. title: How often do you really need to wash your jean shorts? Experts weigh in
summary: Learn how to wash jean shorts the right way, including how often to wash them, the best detergent, drying tips, and a clever freezer trick — straight from denim experts.
story: We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if lip balm is actually bad, how often you should wash your hair and more.

Summer has a way of putting your jean shorts through the ringer. Between the sweat, the sunscreen, the grass stains from picnics and the sand that somehow ends up in every pocket, your favorite cutoffs earn their keep. And because they’re basically a warm-weather uniform — worn on repeat from the first hot day in May until the leaves start turning — they need a little more love (and likely washes) than their full-length denim cousins.

The good news? Washing jean shorts isn’t all that different from washing regular jeans. Same fabric, same care principles, same instinct to protect that perfect fade and fit. The main difference is frequency: where a pair of jeans might go weeks between washes, your shorts are working overtime in the heat and need to hit the laundry basket more often. Here’s how to keep them clean without wearing them out, according to an expert on textiles and a laundry services CEO.
How often should you wash your jean shorts?

Unlike regular jeans, which can often go weeks between washes, jean shorts call for a bit more attention once the temperature rises. “Sweat, sunscreen, saltwater, sand and body oils build up more quickly during the summer, so you’ll likely need to wash jean shorts more often than a pair of jeans you wear in colder weather,” says Courtney Barriger, a sustainable fashion designer and founder of ReFashion Workshop, an educational platform exploring fashion, retail, and sustainability.

So what’s the magic number? “Typically, you’ll want to wash jean shorts [after] every three to five wears,” says Ashley Kidder, founder and CEO of laundry service Mountains of Laundry. But that’s just a guideline, you may need to wash them more frequently depending on your activities. “Use your best judgement here, if it was a sweaty day of digging in the garden and you can smell them, give them a wash.” Kidder adds.
How to wash your jean shorts

When it’s time to actually wash your jean shorts, a few small habits go a long way. “Before washing your jean shorts, turn them inside out — this can help reduce fading,” says Kidder. “Then put them in the washing machine on a gentle cycle and go easy on the detergent. Using too much detergent  (and using fabric softener in general) can cause product to build up on your jeans over time, which can wind up making your jeans smell funky.”

When it comes to drying, both experts point in the same direction, which is away from the dryer. “Whenever possible, skip the dryer,” says Barriger. “Hanging your jeans to dry helps preserve the color, shape, and fabric while reducing energy use.” If time is an issue you can tumble dry them, just make slight modifications from how you dry other types of clothes., “If you have to use the dryer for efficiency, use low heat,” says Kidder.
The best products to help you wash your jean shorts
To choose these products, I looked for highly-rated options that align with Barriger’s and Kidder’s advice — including mild detergents and dryer alternatives that help preserve color and fit.
Seventh Generation Free & Clear Concentrated Laundry Detergent

Kidder suggests using a mild detergent to avoid buildup on jean shorts, and this pick fits the bill. This option from Seventh Generation is fragrance-free and plant-based, gentle enough for sensitive skin while still lifting sweat, dirt, and odor from denim without leaving behind harsh residue.
Woolite Darks Defense Liquid Laundry Detergent

Great for dark denim shorts specifically, this detergent is formulated to prevent fading and color loss wash after wash. In addition to keeping darker washes looking fresh and new, it is gentle on fabric fibers and free from hash additives.
Amazon Basics Foldable Portable Drying Rack

For anyone following Barriger’s advice to skip the dryer, this drying rack is a simple solution. It folds flat for easy storage, offers ample space to air-dry several pairs of jean shorts without heat damage, and helps preserve color, shape, and denim fibers over time.
Honey-Can-Do Heavy-Duty Gullwing Drying Rack

This gullwing-style drying rack offers sturdy, space-saving support for air-drying. Its wing design maximizes surface area for faster drying, while the durable steel frame folds flat for easy storage between laundry days. There is also a mesh panel near the bottom that allows you to lay things like sweaters flat for drying.
Grandma's Secret Spot Remover

I’ve used Grandma’s Secret Spot Remover on denim for everything from grease stains to red wine spills, and it’s consistently effective. Just a small amount worked into the fabric before washing lifts stubborn stains without harsh chemicals — it’s a handy pre-treatment step for keeping jean shorts looking clean all summer.
Does putting jeans in the freezer clean them?

A piece of denim care folklore is that you can toss jeans in the freezer to clean them — which, as it turns out, has some validity to it. “Freezing temperatures can slow bacterial activity and reduce some odor causing bacteria, but they won’t remove dirt, body oils, food spills, or stains,” says Barriger. “I think of freezing as a refresh button, not a replacement for washing. If your jeans just need a quick reset after a few wears, an overnight stay in the freezer can buy you a little more time before laundry day. If they look dirty or smell dirty, the washing machine still wins.”
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
Frequently asked questions

Experts I spoke with agreed that you should ideally wash new jean shorts before wearing them. This removes excess surface dye that can rub off and stain your skin or furniture, washes away chemical residues and sizing agents left over from the manufacturing process and cleans away germs from being tried on in stores. It’s an easy step to skip when you’re excited to wear something new, but one quick wash — following the same gentle-cycle, cold-water approach as usual — helps your shorts feel (and smell) like they’re actually yours.

Trust your senses first. “Smell and visible dirt or stains are the first things I look for,” says Kidder. Fit matters too — if your shorts are starting to sag or lose their shape, that’s another cue to toss them in the wash. “Some jeans stretch out quicker, which is another sign to give them a wash so they fit how you like them.”

title: Judge shows signs of frustration with DOJ attorneys over handling of Epstein files
summary: The judge said he had “absolutely no desire” to go down the road of holding government attorneys in contempt but gave a history lesson on when he has done so.
story: WASHINGTON — A federal judge overseeing a case focused on the Justice Department’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files pressed government attorneys Thursday about their compliance with his court orders and warned that he has held lawyers in contempt before.

U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan, a 41-year veteran of the bench, convened the hearing seeking answers about whether the Trump administration had complied with his previous orders in the case, including one about the need for the Justice Department to publish justifications for the numerous redactions in the released Epstein files.
Justice Department official Andrew Block told Sullivan he was not in a position to commit to a time frame, saying that it was out of his control and that information would be “forthcoming.”
“Christmas is forthcoming,” Sullivan quipped.
Sullivan called his orders “straightforward” and said he was willing to work with the government to obtain compliance.
“You want me to issue another order and say, ‘I really mean it this time’?” Sullivan said at one point.

The case stems from a lawsuit journalist Katie Phang filed against Attorney General Todd Blanche in April, arguing that the Justice Department had failed to comply in full with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which was passed by Congress and signed into law last year. The suit alleges the government failed to make some key redactions, inappropriately redacted other information and improperly withheld documents that referred to President Donald Trump.

The Justice Department had argued that Phang lacked standing to bring the case, and it has said it is “absurd” to claim the Justice Department violated Sullivan’s order in June requiring more information surrounding specific redacted files.

Former Attorney General Pam Bondi, who led the Justice Department when millions of Epstein files were made public, told lawmakers after Trump fired her that “redaction errors” occurred during the records’ release.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

At Thursday’s hearing, Sullivan embarked on a history lesson about a previous case before him in which the Justice Department withheld exculpatory evidence: the prosecution of Sen. Ted Stevens, R-Alaska, whose conviction the Justice Department moved to reverse in 2009 not long before Stevens died in a plane crash. Sullivan recalled that he held government attorneys in contempt for withholding information and that an appeals court upheld his decision.
Sullivan said it was important for attorneys to know he was a judge willing to “enforce legitimate judicial orders” with the means available to him.
“I’m not in a habit of blindsiding people,” he said.
He added that he had “absolutely no desire to go down that road again” but wanted to make sure the attorneys were aware that it has happened before.
Attorney Brendan Ballou, who is representing Phang, said in a statement after the hearing that Blanche had “failed to follow the law.”

“He has failed to produce its redaction log. He has failed to begin producing foreign language documents. He has failed to produce notes concerning Donald Trump,” Ballou said. “The Justice Department’s strategy here is endless delay, and we’re glad that the Court appears to recognize this. Our next step is to file a proposed order for how to handle the Attorney General’s noncompliance, which we plan to do shortly.”
The hearing took place shortly after Blanche, who was recently confirmed as attorney general, addressed Justice Department employees at headquarters on Pennsylvania Avenue.

“We will always respect the role of the judiciary. We will not engage in or stand for any sort of performative attacks that undermine the institutions that we are sworn to uphold,” he said. “At the same time, we’re not going to be intimidated.”

title: Haitians in Ohio who lost protected status get ankle monitors instead of ICE detention
summary: The decision is due to a lack of detention space, sources say, and may clash with the White House’s hard-line immigration approach.
story: Haitians living in Ohio who’ve lost their protected status are increasingly getting ankle monitors instead of being detained by immigration officers, attorneys say.

ICE has been alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they are given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until an immigration judge can decide whether they may have a legitimate reason to remain in the country, such as an asylum claim, according to the lawyers.

The decision is often made over a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost Temporary Protected Status after a Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official said.

“We were really worried that this was going to be a mass enforcement, mass detention operation,” said Katie Kersh, an immigration attorney who represents Haitian clients as part of her work at the Ohio-based law firm Advocates for Basic Legal Equality.

Instead, Kersh said, several of her clients recently received ICE letters mandating the in-person check-ins. “And so we went,” she said. People were arrested but not detained for the long term. “They all have these ankle monitors and they’re not allowed to travel outside of a 75-mile radius from their home.”
DHS declined to comment on the ankle monitors. “DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
“What we would say now is it’s closing time, which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.”

It is the latest policy shift since DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over in March that could draw President Donald Trump’s ire. Last month, Mullin ran afoul of President Donald Trump when he announced a halt on vehicle pursuits by ICE after fatal shootings.

The ankle monitors and other trackers allow immigrants to continue to live in the U.S. while their cases play out. The program was bolstered during the Biden administration, but Trump’s immigration policy architect, Stephen Miller, prefers holding immigrants in detention.

A senior administration official and a DHS official told NBC News recently there was growing tension between the White House and Mullin, the administration’s second homeland security secretary, though Trump does not appear to be preparing to oust him.

Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian program created by Congress that allows people from countries ravaged by war, natural disasters or other extreme circumstances to come and live and work in the United States temporarily.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end the protections for more than 300,000 Haitians who came to the country following the 2010 earthquake, and the more than 50,000 Syrians who came when the civil war broke out in their country in 2015. Previous administrations and lower courts had determined the conditions in both of those countries were still too dire to end protections against deportations there.
The order has sowed confusion among business owners who employ Haitians, and employees who have been unsure when or how they should show up to work.

The senior DHS official said it would be impossible to hold the more than 300,000 Haitians in the U.S. who lost their protected status in ICE detention. ICE currently is holding about 65,000 immigrants in detention facilities across the country, until a judge can hear their case. NBC has reported ICE is working to open new detention facilities.

Last month, Mullin instructed ICE officers to pause vehicle stops following two fatal shootings of men in vehicles, but the policy was quickly overturned by Trump. Mullin had not run the pause by the White House, NBC News reported, citing a senior administration official.
Trump has repeatedly focused on Haitian immigrants in the United States.

On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump and his vice presidential running mate, JD Vance lent credence to false rumors that began on social media that a Haitian immigrant in Springfield, Ohio, had eaten a cat.
“In Springfield, the people that came in, they’re eating the dogs ... they’re eating the cats,” Trump said in a September 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris.
The Facebook post that sparked the rumor was later debunked, but Trump’s rhetoric fired up immigration hard-liners who supported him in the election.

title: Judge dismisses Trump admin lawsuit alleging Harvard failed to protect Jewish students
summary: The judge called alleged incidents of antisemitism “too isolated and episodic” to support a claim of ongoing civil rights violations.
story: WASHINGTON — A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit Thursday by the Trump administration ‌that alleged that Harvard University failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.

U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston said in his ruling that the administration’s lawsuit, which was filed in March, had not plausibly shown an ongoing violation of ​federal civil rights law on Harvard’s campus.

Stearns said the government’s allegations focused largely on incidents ​amid protests over Israel’s war in Gaza during the 2023-24 school year, with only ⁠a handful of later incidents alleged in March 2025 that were “too isolated and episodic” to support a ​claim of ongoing civil rights violations.

The judge said the lawsuit did not adequately allege failures by the ​Ivy League school after the government told Harvard in June 2025 that it was not complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bans discrimination based on race, color and national origin in programs that receive ​federal funding.
The White House and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit came amid ​an escalating clash between the administration and Harvard, a leading target of President Donald Trump’s campaign to overhaul major U.S. universities. ‌The ⁠administration said in court papers that it was suing to “recover billions of dollars of taxpayer subsidies awarded to a discriminatory institution.”

The administration in December appealed a judge’s order that found it unlawfully terminated more than $2 billion in grants awarded to Harvard and could no longer cut off its research funding. In another case, a ​federal judge last year blocked ​the administration’s efforts to ⁠revoke Harvard’s ability to enroll international students.
The civil rights lawsuit alleged that Harvard faculty and leadership “turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis.”

Harvard ​has denied the claims and in an earlier statement called the lawsuit “yet ​another pretextual and ⁠retaliatory action by the administration for refusing to turn over control of Harvard to the federal government.”
In a June court filing, Harvard urged Stearns to dismiss the administration’s lawsuit, saying the government had not alleged ongoing or ⁠imminent violations ​of Title VI.

“Harvard condemns antisemitism and is committed to ensuring ​that Jewish and Israeli students, like all members of the Harvard community, can learn and participate fully in campus life free from ​harassment or exclusion,” the university said.

title: Kennedy Center board votes to add president’s name again — and throw in a ‘Trump Plaza’
summary: The board also voted to close the center’s main building for renovations while keeping a smaller addition open in response to a court order.
story: The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted Thursday to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to a person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.

The decision would close the Kennedy Center’s main building and keep a smaller addition, known as the Reach, open for some events in response to a May court order requiring the board to maintain the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.

After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20-3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change.
Trump, who appointed himself chairman of the board last year, joined the call for several minutes, according to the source who attended the meeting.
The three people voting against it are the ex officio members from Congress, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio; Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; and Rep. Rick Larsen, D-Wash.

“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, who was one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the Kennedy Center’s renaming, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”

Attorneys for Beatty said in a statement that the new naming effort appears to defy a judge’s ruling this year that the center’s board does not have the authority to rename what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president.

“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained. Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” said the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s order in May, which temporarily blocked the Kennedy Center’s planned closure last month, also asked that the board provide a financial plan to justify the decision to close it. Keeping the smaller venue open would allow ticket sales for some events, including performances by the National Symphony Orchestra, which is the Kennedy Center’s chief tenant.
The orchestra has performed there since the early 1970s, when the center — conceived by Jaqueline Kennedy as a memorial to her slain husband — opened.

In recent years, under the baton of music director and principal conductor Giancarlo Noseda, it has been rising in stature — but its future is now uncertain because the Kennedy Center’s Concert Hall will not be available. A search for other venues in the area has been underway.
The Kennedy Center’s future has been in limbo for months as Trump moves to reshape the iconic art institution in his image, one of several major Washington renovation projects.
After Trump named himself the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year and filled its board with allies, the board voted unanimously in March to close the center for two years for renovations.
Cooper’s order temporarily blocked the construction work and ordered that Trump’s name be removed, which it was in June.
He also said the board could still ultimately close the center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.”
Cooper also found the board did not have the authority to rename the center or add a name to it without the approval of Congress, which initially named it.

“The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” Cooper said in his May decision.

“May the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts be renamed absent Congressional authorization? The answer, plain from the face of the statute, is no. Nor can any other individual be memorialized on the front portico of the building. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.”
The decision to close the center and add Trump’s name to the building has sparked outrage from the administration’s critics, as well as members of the Kennedy family.

Former Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, a grandnephew of the late president, said in a statement last year that the center “is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”

title: Two soldiers are dead after a military helicopter crashes in Texas, sparking a fire
summary: The fire prompted evacuations and “looks to be out of control,” an official said.
story: Two soldiers who were on a military helicopter were killed Wednesday when it crashed in Salado, Texas, the Bell County Sheriff’s Office said.
They were pronounced dead after officials responded to 911 calls around 1:30 p.m., sheriff’s spokesperson Cliff Coleman said. Salado is about 50 miles north of Austin.
The Army AH-64 Apache attack helicopter is based at Fort Hood, the military installation said.
The soldiers were taken to Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center at Fort Hood, and their names are being withheld until 24 hours after their families could be notified.

“Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the families, friends, and fellow Troopers of those involved during this incredibly difficult time,” Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general of the 1st Cavalry Division, said in a statement.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott asked for prayers for the soldiers’ families and the Fort Hood community. “Texas is forever indebted to those who serve our state and nation,” he wrote on X.
No structures were damaged, and no other injuries were reported, Coleman said.
“It crashed into a field, and you could tell it was a violent crash,” Coleman told reporters at the scene.
The crash caused a large fire that “looks to be out of control,” he said. It burned a large area of land and prompted some evacuations in the area.
As of 7 p.m., the fire had spread to 155 acres and was 85% contained, Coleman said.
Local emergency responders, military personnel and law enforcement officers all responded to the incident. The Criminal Investigation Division at Fort Hood is leading the inquiry.

The AH-64 Apache is a twin-engine, four-bladed, multi-mission attack helicopter designed as a highly stable aerial weapons-delivery platform, the Army says on its website, calling it “the most advanced aerial fighting vehicle in the world.”

title: The showdowns and reunions highlighting the NBA’s 2026-27 season
summary: After offseason moves to new teams, Jaylen Brown and Giannis Antetokounmpo will return to their former cities for the first time at the season’s midway point.
story: The NBA’s offseason was defined by team-switching superstars — which meant that when the league released its schedule Thursday, it was highlighted by those stars’ returns to the cities that once cheered for them.

During the 2026-27 season, Giannis Antetokounmpo will return to Milwaukee following a yearslong drama concerning whether he wanted to stay or leave. Jaylen Brown will play in Boston less than three years removed from bringing the Celtics an NBA championship. And Brown’s new Philadelphia teammate, LeBron James, will revisit Los Angeles after eight years as a Laker.
Whether they will be received warmly or not won’t be known until tipoff. But fans already know now when matchups like that, and other highly anticipated games, will be played.
Brown vs. Tatum in Boston

Only two years after Brown won NBA Finals MVP for Boston, the Celtics traded him to division rival Philadelphia in a move interpreted as the Celtics’ choosing Brown’s former running mate, Jayson Tatum, over him. Brown later said he “threw my phone across the room” after he heard he was being dealt. Rather than hold the juicy reunion early in the season, the league dated his Boston return for Jan. 21 (Prime Video). That game is one of four between the 76ers and the Celtics this season; the others are on Nov. 10 (Prime Video), Feb. 7 (NBC/Peacock) and March 7 (ABC).
More Sports from NBC News

Bob Iger once found it hard to root for the Lakers. Now he’ll own them.The WNBA is bigger than ever. But the attention is on anything but basketball.Are the Dodgers ruining baseball? Players union president pushes back on that theory
Bob Iger once found it hard to root for the Lakers. Now he’ll own them.
The WNBA is bigger than ever. But the attention is on anything but basketball.
Are the Dodgers ruining baseball? Players union president pushes back on that theory
Giannis returns to Milwaukee

Antetokounmpo’s breakup with Milwaukee, the team that drafted him and with which he won a championship in 2021, was long. The NBA didn’t rush his return to Milwaukee, either. Antetokounmpo’s Miami Heat first visit the Bucks on Jan. 28, near the midway point of the season, when it will be easier to gauge how successful his departure for Miami has gone (Prime Video).
Lillard’s Portland homecoming

After having spent the first 11 years of his career adored in Portland, guard Damian Lillard left the city in a cantankerous exit in 2023 for Milwaukee to give Antetokounmpo what was supposed to be a championship boost. That partnership never lived up to such expectations, however, and Lillard re-signed with Portland last season but never played a game while he rehabbed a long-term leg injury. That changes this season. If Lillard is healthy to begin the season, as expected, the first home game of his second Portland chapter will take place Oct. 21 against Phoenix.
LeBron returns to L.A.
The Christmas Day slate includes LeBron James in his first game facing the Lakers in Los Angeles since he decided to become a free agent and joined Philadelphia (ABC/ESPN).
Trae Young’s first game in Atlanta

Once an All-Star whom the Atlanta Hawks oriented their franchise around, guard Trae Young was traded unceremoniously to Washington last season and played only five games with the Wizards before he signed a long-term extension with the team this offseason. None of those games in a Wizards uniform was against his former team. Young will first play in Atlanta on Nov. 6.
How will Memphis welcome Morant?

Similar to Young in Atlanta, Ja Morant was once an untouchable trade asset when he launched to superstardom to begin his career in Memphis. Injuries and off-court discipline led the team to unload him this offseason to Portland. Morant will first play in Memphis on Feb. 6 (Prime Video).
A Knicks villain returns to New York

With big shots and brash confidence, Tyrese Haliburton became the player Knicks fans loved to hate as he led Indiana past New York and into the 2025 NBA Finals. After he spent all of last season recovering from an Achilles tendon tear sustained in the Finals, Haliburton is set to return to Madison Square Garden against the reigning champion Knicks on Nov. 22. Expect boos.
Three meetings between West finalists

The Western Conference’s path to the Finals last season was decided by a seven-game series between Oklahoma City and San Antonio, a pair of young rivals that could determine the conference’s fate for years to come, too. They will meet three times during the regular season in games that will instantly become circled on many fans’ calendars: Oct. 20 (NBC/Peacock), Feb. 11 (Prime Video) and March 14 (ABC).
Four games between perennial playoff foes

It wouldn’t be considered a historic rivalry, but Denver vs. Minnesota has become one of the best active matchups in the league after they met in the first round three times in the last four years. They will play four times in the regular season, on Dec. 28 (NBC/Peacock), Dec. 31 (Prime Video), Jan. 27 (ESPN) and March 7 (ABC).
The ‘what-if?’ games

Few would have considered LeBron James a potential teammate of Stephen Curry’s when they faced each other during four consecutive NBA Finals from 2015 to 2018. The two nearly joined forces this summer at Golden State, however, when James became a free agent and had the opportunity to ride out some of the last years of the aging superstars’ careers together. Instead, they continue to be on opposite sidelines, with Curry’s Warriors facing James and the 76ers twice, on March 24 and March 31.
No. 1 pick vs. No. 2
It’s not just the established superstars whom fans will want to watch. The first two picks in the most recent draft, Washington’s AJ Dybantsa and Utah’s Darryn Peterson, will first play Feb. 27.
Led by Wembanyama, the NBA takes Europe

As the NBA continues to build out its plan to operate a league in Europe, perhaps as soon as next year, it will take two regular-season games there. San Antonio’s French-born star, Victor Wembanyama, will be showcased when the Spurs play New Orleans in Paris on Jan. 14 and again Jan. 17 in Manchester, England. The latter will be the first regular-season game to be played in Manchester, in perhaps a test run for a market that is among the potential targets to host an NBA Europe franchise (both on Prime Video).

title: KATSEYE Says ‘We Stand By Sophia and Manon’ Amid Their Hiatuses: ‘We Ride for Them’
summary: During their TODAY appearance, KATSEYE members Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae Jeong, Megan Skiendiel and Lara Raj spoke about Sophia LaForteza and Manon Bannerman.
story: Although KATSEYE is currently down two members and performing as a quartet, the girl group is a unified front.
Four members of the Grammy-nominated group — Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae Jeong, Megan Skiendiel and Lara Raj — performed live on the TODAY Plaza on Aug. 14 as part of the Citi Concert Series.
The group, who sang hits like “Gabriela” and “Pinky Up,” also spoke about Sophia Laforteza and Manon Bannerman, two members who announced hiatuses from the band this year.
Craig Melvin asked, “Two of the group members are not here today: Sophia and Manon. We understand they’re taking care of themselves. Have you been able to talk to them? How are they doing?”
Raj responded, “As KATSEYE, it’s so important to us to always prioritize our well-being. We stand by Sophia and Manon through and through. We ride for them.”
Savannah Guthrie followed up by asking if the group had a message for Laforteza and Bannerman.
“We love you guys so much, always,” Raj said, and Skiendiel, Avanzini and Jeong next to her blew kisses.
Laforteza announced last week that she was stepping away from the band to prioritize her “mental health and wellness.” Bannerman announced her own hiatus in February.

In a statement on Weverse issued to their fans, known as Eyekons, the group said that Laforteza will be “temporarily unable to participate in upcoming promotional activities” and added that “it is imperative that her mental health and wellness are prioritized.”

“Sophia has been receiving the utmost support, and following thorough consultations with medical professionals, it has been advised that she take dedicated time for extended rest and ongoing care to ensure a full recovery,” the statement continued. “While Sophia herself is eager to perform alongside her members, the health, safety, and long-term well-being of our artists will always remain our highest priority.”
The group said they will monitor Laforteza’s progress and are supporting her from afar.

“We plan to reassess her condition in September and will share a further update with fans at that time. We sincerely appreciate your understanding and continued support for Sophia, and we look forward to her being back with KATSEYE,” they told their fans.
Laforteza penned a separate message on her Instagram story.

She said, in part, “It truly breaks my heart to have to miss out on a lot. You know how much I love being on stage, performing, and sharing these moments with you. Making this decision wasn’t easy, but I’m learning that health has to come first. I’m realizing that if I don’t take care of my mind and body now, I won’t be able to keep doing what I love the most for so long.”
The 23-year-old said she will be cheering on the band as they perform without her.
In February, the group shared on Weverse and their social media platforms that Bannerman was taking a hiatus from the band.

“After open and thoughtful conversations together, we are sharing that Manon will be taking a temporary hiatus from group activities to focus on her health and wellbeing,” the group said in a statement. “We fully support this decision. KATSEYE remains committed to showing up for one another and for the fans who mean everything to us. The group will continue scheduled activities during this time, and we look forward to being together again when the time is right.”
The news came after all members took the stage at the 2026 Grammy Awards, also in February. The sextet was nominated for best new artist and best pop duo/group performance for their song “Gabriela.”

title: ‘Camp Rock 3’ Ending Includes a Sweet Demi Lovato Cameo and New Final Jam Winner
summary: What to know about the “Camp Rock 3” ending, including Jonas Brothers, Demi Lovato’s cameo, who wins the Final Jam.
story: Warning: Spoilers from “Camp Rock 3” below.
Turns out the final jam wasn’t all that final, because camp is back in session with “Camp Rock 3.”
“Camp Rock 3” premiered on Disney Channel Aug. 13, 18 years after the 2008 release of the original, with “Camp Rock 2: The Final Jam” just two years after.

The original musical served as a catapult into stardom for original cast members Demi Lovato and the Jonas Brothers. The fictional camp, meanwhile, has always been a place for similarly aspiring young performers to come together and learn what it takes to be a rocker.
This new reboot inducts rising stars Malachi Barton, Disney’s newest male lead from the popular “Zombies” franchise, and Liamani from “Descendants: Wicked Wonderland.”

“Camp Rock 3” picks up many years after the sequel, with the Jonas Brothers reprising their role as the members of the fictional boy band Connect 3: Shane Gray (Joe Jonas), Jason Gray (Kevin Jonas) and Nate Gray (Nick Jonas). When Connect 3 loses the opening act of their “Reconnected” reunion tour, they turn to the place they went from reluctant campers to pivotal counselors in search of the next greatest voice.
Maria Canals-Barrera reprises her role as Connie Torres, mother to Lovato’s character Mitchie Torres.

Unlike her former co-stars, Lovato was listed solely as an executive producer of the film. However, fans online weren’t so convinced — and the instincts were right! Lovato makes a surprise cameo towards the end of the movie, making for a full-circle moment with both old and new castmates. News of Lovato’s return was revealed Aug. 10 across social media, including a post from the star herself.

“She’s an amazing producer,” Canals-Barrera tells TODAY.com about reuniting with Lovato. “She’s so talented. Even at 15, she just grabbed people’s hearts and they never let her go through all the ups and downs in her life and her success.”
Here’s everything to know about “Camp Rock 3,” from Lovato’s surprise appearance, all the new Disney Channel faces and how the movie expands on the beloved franchise’s legacy.
What Happens In ‘Camp Rock 3’?
“Camp Rock 3” combines nostalgic callbacks to the glory days with the introduction of some new voices.

Comedian and actor Sherry Cola comes in as Lark, Connect 3’s tour manager who has little patience for their brotherly band drama. Competition is always an element of Camp Rock, and when campers are faced with a series of challenges to determine who will open for Connect 3, Lark is roped into judging. Despite being hesitant to spend tour prep time in the woods, the catchy songs grow on her, and the excitement of the contest wins her over.

Barton’s character, Fletch, wears the “bad boy” shoes of Shane Gray, as he mysteriously shows up late to camp in a cop car. Fletch, like Shane, immediately bumps into the outgoing aspiring frontwoman Sage, played by Liamani. The two align on their shared passion for using music as a cathartic means of connectivity during times of uncertainty.

Liamani, 17 — just two years older than Lovato was when she first stepped foot on camp — nearly manifested her leading role in “Camp Rock 3.” Three years ago, during her time on “High School Musical: The Musical: The Series,” she covered Lovato’s iconic ballad “This is Me” from the original film. Sage is the girl who always has a plan, but influenced by the spontaneity of her brother Desi (Hudson Stone), she discovers newfound anchors of confidence and direction.

One of Sage’s discoveries includes an iconic reference to the first “Camp Rock.” Looking for inspiration, Sage stumbles upon Mitchie’s songwriting notebook, left under the floorboards of her cabin. When Connie spots Sage writing her own songs in the notebook, she gives Sage some words of wisdom.

Another familiar Disney Channel face (new to the “Camp Rock” universe) is Milo Manheim, the lead of Disney’s “Zombies” franchise and upcoming star in the live-action “Tangled” movie. Manheim portrays a former camper turned counselor who helps mentor campers through the various workshops and challenges.

Key newbies include Rosie (Lumi Pollack), who seizes the opportunity to break free from her parents’ classical expectations, Cliff (Casey Trotter), who finds friends who let him beat to his own drum, and Callie (Brooklynn Pitts), a dancer who discovers leadership skills as Lark’s assistant.

This summer, Connie trades in her chef coat for the camp director’s desk, and has the difficult job of enforcing a new rule: No phones. Like old times, when the competition turns up the heat, the campers must decide if certain rules are worth being broken and when revenge is necessary.
When Does Demi Lovato Make Her Surprise Cameo?

At first, “Camp Rock 3” seems to focus solely on the return of Connect 3 and Connie. Fans are in luck, however, because by the last 20 minutes of this trilogy film, Mitchie Torres indeed makes an appearance.
Once the five finalists are narrowed down — Sage, Fletch, Rosie, Desi and Cliff — and Final Jam approaches, Mitchie surprises Connie and Connect 3.
“This is their night, not mine,” Mitchie says to Connie about wanting to stay on the sidelines rather than make a big entrance during Final Jam.

Mitchie, who took a break from a tour to witness Final Jam, stays backstage and reminisces with her mom about how much camp still means to so many kids, who, like her, came here to discover their sound and kick off their dreams.

Mitchie also chats with Shane, Jason and Nate, and convinces them they don’t have to pick just one Final Jam winner. The former campers see themselves in these young newcomers, and Mitchie reminds them one of the greatest talents isn’t individual star power, but how artists can help each other shine.
After the announcement that all five campers will get to open for Connect 3 as a group, Mitchie and Shane fans get their moment.
“You think they know what they just got?” Shane asks.
“Not yet,” Mitchie responds. “But they will.”

As the new generation gears up to perform a finale duet of “We Rock” with Connect 3, Sage catches a glimpse of Mitchie, who gives the young (and starstruck) performer a wave and a smile before walking off camera.
Will There Be a ‘Camp Rock 4’?
While there is no major cliffhanger moment, the end of the scene between Lovato and Joe Jonas does leave open the possibility of a future for the franchise.
“So, same time next summer?” Joe Jonas’ character poses, to which Lovato answers back, “You’re on.”
“Camp Rock 3” will stream on Disney+ on Aug. 14.

title: Tony Goldwyn Has the Cutest Response to Becoming a Grandpa
summary: Tony Goldwyn is going to be a grandpa and he couldn’t be happier.
story: Tony Goldwyn is going to be a grandpa and he couldn’t be happier.

The “Scandal” star’s daughter Anna Musky-Goldwyn is expecting her first child with husband Billy Durden. The writer shared the exciting news on her Instagram, along with a slew of photos of her baby bump and sonogram.
“New project, currently (and probably forever) known as Goobey, debuts next month,” she captioned the joint post with Durden, before seemingly confirming it’s a girl. “We expect her to be a hit.”
In the comments section, Goldwyn expressed his excitement for his first grandchild, sharing that he’s already proudly printed out a copy of the sonogram.
“We already have her picture up on the mantle (ultrasounds look good these days),” he wrote, adding a heart-eyes emoji.
Goldwyn’s former “Scandal” co-stars Bellamy Young and Katie Lowes also commented on Musky-Goldwyn’s post.
Young wrote, “I can’t wait to meet Goobey!!!!!!!!!,” along with many red hearts and smiling faces with hearts emoji.
Lowes added, “Aaaaah!!!! Yayayay! Congrats!!!!”
Goldwyn shares Musky-Goldwyn and daughter Tess Goldwyn with wife and production designer Jane Musky. The couple have been married since 1987, welcoming Musky-Goldwyn in 1990 and Tess Goldwyn in 1995.
In a 2019 interview with TODAY, the “Hacks” actor spoke about his then-32-year marriage and shared how he knew Musky was the one.
“Jane is just the most incredible human being that I know,” he said. “I knew when I was 21 when I met her that I’d better hang on because I’ll never come across this again.”
When asked why he thinks they’ve had such a successful and long marriage, he told Hoda Kotb that during difficult times, they would ask each other: “Are you willing to work on this?”
Their response was always, “Yeah.”
He added that “it takes both people to look at each other” and mutually agree to talk things out.

title: Krispy Kreme Launches Pokémon Doughnuts: How to Catch ’Em All
summary: To celebrate the 30th anniversary of Pokémon, Krispy Kreme is releasing six new doughnuts inspired by the franchise’s beloved characters.
story: Krispy Kreme’s latest doughnut collection is giving us a major dose of nostalgia.
To celebrate Pokémon’s 30th anniversary (how is that possible?!), the doughnut chain is releasing six new sweet treats inspired by the franchise’s beloved characters.
On Tuesday, Aug. 18, Krispy Kreme will debut doughnuts featuring Pikachu, Bulbasaur, Charmander, Squirtle and Jigglypuff, plus a bonus Poké Ball Doughnut.

It’s hard to believe that it’s been three decades since kids were first introduced to Ash Ketchum and his adorable sidekick, Pikachu. After Pokémon trading cards debuted in the 1990s, the imaginary universe quickly expanded to a cartoon, merchandise and more.
Ready to learn more about Krispy Kreme’s Pokémon collection?  Here’s everything you need to know in order to catch ’em all:
Customers Can Preorder the Collection This Week
Don’t want to miss out on the sugary, supercharged fun? Krispy Kreme customers can preorder Pokémon doughnuts by the dozen starting Aug. 13.

When the collection officially debuts on Aug. 18, it will be available for a limited time in shops and for pickup/delivery in the chain’s app/website. Customers can purchase the doughnuts individually and by the dozen.
The collection will be available in a custom Pokémon Dozen box at participating shops and a six-pack box in select retailers.
The Doughnuts Look Equally Adorable and Delicious
Krispy Kreme’s Pokémon collection brings several characters to life. Here’s a little bit more about each of the doughnuts:

Bulbasaur Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut is dipped in vanilla-flavored icing, topped with frosting then finished off with a Bulbasaur piece.Charmander Doughnut: This unglazed doughnut is coated in chocolate and toasted marshmallow-flavored filling, dipped in orange-colored caramel icing plus red and gold sugar, then topped with a Charmander piece.Squirtle Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features swirls of cotton candy-flavored buttercreme, sugar, nonpareils and a surfing Squirtle piece.Pikachu Doughnut: This unglazed doughnut is full of lemon-flavored Kreme filling, dipped in vanilla icing, then decorated with drizzle, nonpareils and a Pikachu piece.Jigglypuff Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features strawberry-flavored buttercreme, a strawberry-flavored cookie and a Jigglypuff piece.Poké Ball Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features vanilla-flavored icing, red sprinkles and chocolate icing.
Bulbasaur Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut is dipped in vanilla-flavored icing, topped with frosting then finished off with a Bulbasaur piece.

Charmander Doughnut: This unglazed doughnut is coated in chocolate and toasted marshmallow-flavored filling, dipped in orange-colored caramel icing plus red and gold sugar, then topped with a Charmander piece.
Squirtle Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features swirls of cotton candy-flavored buttercreme, sugar, nonpareils and a surfing Squirtle piece.
Pikachu Doughnut: This unglazed doughnut is full of lemon-flavored Kreme filling, dipped in vanilla icing, then decorated with drizzle, nonpareils and a Pikachu piece.
Jigglypuff Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features strawberry-flavored buttercreme, a strawberry-flavored cookie and a Jigglypuff piece.
Poké Ball Doughnut: This Original Glazed doughnut features vanilla-flavored icing, red sprinkles and chocolate icing.
Krispy Kreme Is Also Releasing Pokémon Cups

As part of the collection, Krispy Kreme is also debuting special-edition Pokémon cups available in five exclusive Pokémon designs. Each cup will be filled with 10 Original Glazed Gold Dots (aka mini doughnuts).
Krispy Kreme is Giving Out Free Doughnuts on Aug. 22

On Saturday, Aug. 22, Krispy Kreme customers who show up to their participating shops wearing Pokémon attire will score a free Original Glazed Doughnut. The single-use offer is available in shops and at the drive-thru.

title: The Osage Story ‘Little House on the Prairie’ Never Told — Until Now
summary: The Osage people’s story is finally incorporated into Little House on the Prairie thanks to the new movie. Here’s what to know.
story: In 1868, the Drum Creek Treaty pushed the Osage Nation from Kansas to present-day Oklahoma, then known as Indian Territory.

More than 150 years later, roughly 200 people gathered in Pawhuska, Oklahoma to revisit that history. Osage individuals, Netflix producers, actors and cultural and historical consultants filled the Osage Casino and Hotel for a screening of Episode 7 of the streamer’s new adaptation of “Little House on the Prairie,” which dramatizes the treaty’s signing.

Unlike the original stories, Netflix’s new eight-episode adaptation, which premiered July 9, highlights the story of the Osage people, whose land Laura Ingalls Wilder’s family illegally settled on in 1869, and were later pushed off of by the U.S. government.
The series primarily represents the Osage perspective through the fictional Mitchell family, whose storyline runs nearly parallel to the Ingalls family and provides an Indigenous lens on the story.
For the cast and crew who spent months trying to wrestle an erased history onto the screen, earning the Osage Nation’s approval was more important than that of any fan or critic.

The long-awaited verdict arrived when the credits rolled, and the Osage Nation principal chief approached actor Meegwun Fairbrother, who portrays farmer and father William Mitchell in the series. Fairbrother recalls the Chief telling him, “‘This is our stamp of approval. We like it,’” he tells TODAY.com.

Indigenous stories weren’t only left out in the original books and adaptation. In recent years, Wilder’s stories have also been criticized for including depictions of Indigenous people that reflect racial attitudes common among white settlers of the 19th century.

Production sought to strike a delicate balance: accurately portraying the Osage Nation’s fight to stay on their own land while also preserving the heart and “overall sensibility” of Wilder’s tales that drew readers to the stories in the first place, Robert Warrior, an Osage historical consultant and professor of American literature who worked with the show’s creators, tells TODAY.com.
Read on to learn more about the historical moment the series stepped into, and what it was like for the actors to depict Osage culture and history onscreen.
Bringing Osage History to Screen

When the Ingalls family made their famous journey to present-day Kansas, they arrived on land that wasn’t legally open to settlement. But Pa didn’t know that when he arrived, and neither did many of the settlers who showed up to claim land they had been told was available, Warrior explains.

Railroad companies also wanted access to the region, he says, and those economic interests often benefited from encouraging settlers to move into the area before legal questions about land rights were resolved.
The tensions in the region weren’t just between settlers and Indigenous people. Competing claims to land, political power and economic opportunity collided across the territory.

Facing displacement and hostility, Osage people were forced to make difficult decisions about survival, identity and their futures, the historian explains. Roughly 4,500 Osage people ultimately left their homeland and way of life in Kansas, and relocated to Oklahoma, what was then called Indian Territory, Warrior says.

But not all families made the choice to leave. About 19 Osage families chose to remain in Kansas, which is the historical basis for the Mitchell family storyline depicted in Netflix’s series. The few who stayed encountered intense discrimination: two heads of those families were killed by settlers, Warrior says, and nearly all eventually fled Kansas and joined the broader Osage community elsewhere.
Really, one of Warrior’s most important goals in consulting for the show was depicting that Osage people, like the Ingalls family, had their own ambitions, disagreements and family dynamics.
He sought to ensure they were afforded the same depth in the show’s storytelling as settler families.
“They’re not just 4,500 nameless people who are standing in the way of a railroad,” he says. “They are actual real people.”

Bringing complex Osage history, stories and culture to the screen entailed far more than just recreating historical events. Actors spent weeks studying cultural practices, learning the Osage language and building characters grounded in lived experience.
